description_block:
Kamal Khojandi, Diwan, poetry, copied by Mun'im al-Din al-Awhadi, resident of Shiraz, perhaps for a royal library 
Persia, Shiraz, dated the last day of Ramadan 902/1st June 1497
Persian manuscript on paper, 255 leaves, 14 lines to the page written in fine nasta'liq in black ink in two columns, intercolumnar rules in gold, inner margins ruled in gold, blue and black, headings written in nasta'liq in gold surrounded by floral illumination, one double-page illuminated frontispiece, preceded by an illuminated shamsa containing a dedication, perhaps contemporary gold embossed covers incorporated in modern binding 
240 x 145 mm.

Kamal Khojandi (d. 1400) was a Persian poet and Sufi. His Divan is written in ghazals, totalling 980 poems. 

The opening cartouche contains a dedication: be-rasm-e khazaneh al-sultan al-a'zam al-a'dal abu'l-fath sultan ahmad khallada mukuhu: 'For the library of the Most Great Sultan, the most Just, Abu'l-Fath Sultan Ahmad, May (God) make his kingdom everlasting'. However, there is no Sultan Ahmad who appears to fit the date of the manuscript.

Mun'im al-Din is recorded as a calligrapher of the 15th-16th Centuries. His recorded work is dated between AH 894/AD 1488-89 and AH 927/AD 1520-21. See Mehdi Bayani, ahval va athar-e khushnavisan, vol. 3, Tehran 1348 sh, pp. 921-922.

For a manuscript of the same text, formerly in the library of Sultan Mehmed the Conqueror, Ottoman Turkey, circa 1460, see Christie's, Art of the Islamic and Indian Worlds including a Private Collection Donated to Benefit the University of Oxford, 10th April 2014, lot 184; and the same manuscript subsequently at Sotheby's, Arts of the Islamic World and India, 27th October 2020, lot 408.

description_block:
An illustrated album page depicting the creation of Iblis and his refusal to bow before Adam alongside the angels, from the Qisas al-Anbiya, The History of the Prophets, by Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Nishaburi 
Persia, Isfahan, circa 1610
Arabic and Persian manuscript on paper, pasted down on board, panel with five lines written in nasta'liq and naskhi in black, blue and gold, painting in gouache and gold, inner borders with sections excised from another manuscript written in small nasta'liq, stencilled foliate border in green also excised from elsewhere 
page 323 x 217 mm.

The heading reads: 'the story of the creation of Iblis, curse be upon him'.

The citations from the Qur'an consist of suras XVIII, al-Kahf, part of verse 50, and sura II, al-Baqarah, verse 34.

The Qisas al-Anbiya, by Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Nishaburi, a 12th Century scholar, is a collection of narratives focusing on the lives of the Islamic prophets up to Muhammad, incorporating stories from historical and mythological personalities from the Qur'anic traditions, and also from the Rabbinic and Biblical traditions. The style and content of this literary tradition was standardised by the 11th Century.

An illuminated manuscript of the text, with 22 miniatures, copied in Shiraz in 1577, is in the Staatsbibliothek, Berlin.

For a further discussion of the text see Milstein, Rührdanz and Schmitz, Stories of the Prophets, California, 1999.

description_block:
An early copy of the Du'a-name (Book of Supplication) of the Shaykh al-Islam and jurist, Ebusu'ud Efendi [Muhammad Abu al-Su'ud (Abu Su'ud Efendi)] (d. 1574) 
Ottoman Turkey, late 16th/early 17th Century
Ottoman Turkish manuscript on paper, 36 leaves, 13 lines to the page written in nasta'liq in black ink, further text written diagonally within panels in margins, headings in red, inner margins ruled in gold, blue and black, one illuminated headpiece, further illumination on last page, prayers at end, contemporary binding with central stamped medallion, with flap 
180 x 108 mm.

Provenance
Acquired in an estate sale, Washington DC, in February 2026.
Private collection, USA.

A fine copy of this famous text, possibly copied in the author's lifetime, or soon afterwards.

On the front flyleaf, in a late 16th or early 17th Century naskhi hand, is a description of the work: müfti-i sekalayn ebu's-su'ud efendi hazretlerinin vezir-i a'zam 'ali paşa'ya te'lifen irsal ve ihda buyurdığı du'a-namedur: 'This is the Du'a-name written by His Excellence the Mufti of the Men and of the Jinn, Ebussu'ud Efendi, sent to and dedicated to the Grand Vizier 'Ali Pasha'.

The work consists of seven chapters and is on the subject of the importance and benefits of supererogatory prayer. It is written in plain Turkish, and is therefore considered to an important text in the development of Turkish literature. Judging by the number of surviving copies, it was extremely popular. As the note discussed above states, the work was dedicated to (Semiz) 'Ali Pasha, who was Grand Vizier in 1561-1565. For the work, see Abdullah Kaleli, Du'ânâme (İnceleme-Çeviri Yazılı Metin-Özel Adlar Dizini-Tıpkıbasım), MA thesis, Adıyaman University, 2014. 

For another early copy of the text, dated AH 1008/AD 1599-1600, signed by Muhammad Amin al-Husaini al-Tirmidhi, see Christie's South Kensington, Arts and Textiles of the Islamic and Indian Worlds, 11th April 2014, lot 265.

Ebusu'ud was the most famous of all Ottoman jurists and Shaykh al-Islam's. The standard English-language work on him is Colin Imber, Ebu's-Su'ud: the Islamic Legal Tradition, Edinburgh, 1997. The most up-to-date bibliography, in Turkish, is Pehlül Düzenli, 'Şeyhülislam ebus- suûd efendi: bibliyografik bir değerlendirme', in Türkiye Araştırmaları Literatür Dergisi, 3:5 (2005), pp. 441–75, esp. p. 453.

'Sultan Suleyman the Lawgiver respected and trusted Ebussuud Efendi the most among his friends. Ebussuud was his close friend and confidant. The Sultan asked for Ebussuud's opinion in many matters concerning his affairs. His high prestige by the Sultan, fame as a great scholar and wisdom made him a second 'Magnificent' person of the XVI century'. (A. Celebioglu, 'Turkish Literature of the Period of Sultan Suleyman the Magnificent I', in Divan Edebiyati Arastirmalari Dergisi 18, 2017, pp. 563-623).

description_block:
An illuminated Ruzname (almanac or calendar), in scroll form, copied by Sulayman, known as Hikmati 
Ottoman Turkey, not dated but circa AH 1200/AD 1785 or shortly before
Arabic and Ottoman Turkish manuscript on vellum, text and tables written horizontally and vertically in naskhi script in black and red ink, columns ruled in gold, these interspersed with further gold ground and panels of illumination, illuminated headpiece in colours and gold, gilt leather covering flap attached to upper edge, on a bone spindle with circular bone terminals 
80 long x 9 cm. wide; width when rolled including terminals 10 cm.

The colophon states 'Sulayman, known as Hikmati, wrote it'. The text at the end says that the calculations have been made for Istanbul and the surrounding area. It is not dated, but the earliest date to appear on the calendar is AH 1200/AD 1785, so it was presumably made then or shortly before.

Similar ruzname scrolls have appeared at auction: see the sale in these rooms, Bonhams, Islamic and Indian Art, 12th November 2024, lot 19 (dated AH 1233/AD 1817-18); 12th November 2025, lot 7 (late 18th/early 19th Century); and 1st May 2003, lot 72 (dated AH 1223/AD 1808); Sotheby's, The Shakerine Collection, 23rd October 2019, lot 39.

There is another in the John Rylands University Library (see J. Schmidt, A Catalogue of the Turkish Manuscripts in the John Rylands University Library, Leiden 2011, pp. 261-262, no. 157), dated AH 1199 AH/AD 1784-85; and another offered at Christie's, Islamic, Indian, Southeast Asian Manuscripts, Miniatures and Works of Art, 28th November 1983, lot 107, dated AH 1215/AD 1800-01. Another, dated AH 1220, is in the Cairo Museum.

For three ruznames in the Khalili Collection, see F. Maddison, E. Savage-Smith, Science, Tools and Magic: Part One, London 1997, pp. 280-281, nos. 170-172. While the first is early 17th Century, the others are dated 1805-06 and 1853-54. To quote the introduction to the three pieces: 'The known almanacs vary in length, but usually give tables of the times of Muslim prayers for each month of the solar year, and other times of religious importance; the length of day and night, and the time of nightfall; the time when the sun is in the direction of Mecca (data usable also for the orientation of mosques); and information for calendar-calculation correlating the lunar calendar with the days of the week, and with the Rumi calendar, which was the Syro-Arab version of the Julian calendar'.

description_block:
An illuminated scroll with five suras of the Qur'an 
Qajar Persia, 19th Century
Arabic manuscript on paper, in scroll form, text written in naskhi in black ink within cloudbands on a gold ground, margins ruled in black and gold, sura headings in red riqa' on a gold ground within illuminated panels in colours and gold, illuminated headpiece 
151 x 7.2 cm.

The five suras of the Qur'an of which the scroll is composed are as follows, each with its own benefits from recitation:

Sura XXXVI, Ya Sin, for forgiveness of sins.
Sura XLVIII, al-Fath, for triumph and relief.
Sura LVI, al-Waqi'ah, for protection from poverty.
Sura LXVII, al-Mulk, for bringing inner peace.
Sura LXXVIII, al-Naba', for encouraging righteousness.

For a discussion of the role of talismanic and amuletic scrolls of the text of the Qur'an in the Islamic world in general, see S. Vernoit, Occidentalism: Islamic Art in the 19th Century, The Khalili Collection of Islamic Art, London 1997, p. 46, with two Qajar examples, nos. 23 and 24. A grouping of seven suras was regarded as most efficacious - VI, XVIII, XXXVI, XLIV, LV, LXVII, LXXVIII (three of which appear in our scroll).

There is no scribe named or date given.

description_block:
A manuscript in scroll form on astronomy, calendars and the astrolabe, copied by Amir 'Abd al-Hamid Bahreyni 
Persia, dated Ramadan 1215/January-February 1801
Arabic manuscript on paper (several sections joined together), in scroll form, illuminated headpiece, text in thuluth in black ink within cloudbands on an illuminated floral ground, several illuminated roundels representing the planets and their courses, one human figure representing a constellation, inner margins ruled in colours and gold, light blue borders 
201 x 17 cm.

The manuscript begins by saying it relates to the planet Venus (kawakib al-thaniya), the planets more generally and their connection with calendars and the astrolabe. One image is described as the second Aquarius (dalw al-thani). In one place it says that the text was taken from the writings of Mir 'Abd al-Qadir Husayni Kazeruni (unidentified). At the end of the manuscript it is stated that it derives from discussion of the science of planets and the knowledge of the astrolabe by Tari Marakeshi (unidentified). The scribe Amir 'Abd al-Hamid Bahreyni is also unidentified.

description_block:
An illuminated Qur'an, copied by Murad Beg al-Bukhari al-Naqshbandi for a certain Shaykh 'Abd al-Latif 
Kashmir, dated Jumada II 1166/April-May 1753
Arabic manuscript on paper, 905 leaves, nine lines to the page written in bold naskhi in black with diacritics and vowel points in black and red, verse-endings marked with gold roundels, inner margins ruled in gold and blue, illuminated marginal devices, marginal commentaries, sura headings written in naskhi in blue and black within cloudbands in gold, double-page illuminated frontispiece, six further illuminated double-pages, several seal impressions indicating ownership in the 18th and 19th Century, perhaps contemporary binding with covers decorated with stamped silver central medallions and cornerpieces 
168 x 108 mm.

Provenance
Formerly in a private London collection, acquired in the early 1980s.

Neither the scribe Murad Bayg al-Bukhari al-Naqshbandi nor the patron 'Abd al-Latif is recorded at this date.

The seal impressions show that the manuscript belonged to a certain Jan Muhammad Qarani in the second half of the 18th Century (seal dated AH 1191/AD 1777-78) and a Mir 'Abbas in the 19th Century (seal dated AH 1287/AD 1870-71).

There is an opening note in nasta'liq on the benefits of reciting the opening sura, al-Fatiha.

At the end of sura XVI, al-Nahl, there is a note crudely written, perhaps of a later date: 'This Quran [belongs to] 'Abd al-Latif, whoever claims it, it will be void and God will barbecue his liver'. There is another note elsewhere: 'Abd al-Latif, his son Nur Muhammad and Nur Hamar (?) the two sons, the year solar (shamsi) year 1171 (?) (1791-2), again the name 'Abd al-Latif in black and the oval seal impression Mir 'Abbas, dated 1287 (?) (1870-71).

description_block:
A group of three Mamluk glass sprinklers (qumqum) 
Egypt or Syria, 12th/ 13th Century
each of flattened globular form, two of pale yellow glass and one of deep blue, each with a kick foot and narrow cylindrical neck, one with applied trail handles to shoulder 
the largest 18 cm. high(3)

description_block:
A Ghurid moulded glass roundel 
Afghanistan, 12th Century
of round form, impressed in relief to one side with a central roundel containing a rearing griffin, an inscription in naskh to border 
9.8 cm. diam.

Provenance
Formerly in a private collection formed between 1920 and 1950; thence by descent.
Christie's, Arts of Islam, 5th October 2012, lot 655. 

Inscription: Jahan Pahlawan 'Umar bin Husayn, 'Champion of the World 'Umar bin Husayn'.

With many initially rediscovered during the excavations at a palace at Old Termez (Tirmidh), Uzbekistan, these medallions are believed to have featured within stained glass windows of Ghaznavid and Ghurid rulers' palaces. This carries on from Sasanian tradition where mosaics and mould-pressed glass plaques were used in the walls of Ctesiphon Palace. Many of the recovered medallions are now in The al-Sabah Collection, Kuwait, two of which bear the same name inscribed upon this medallion. Stefano Carboni identifies 'Umar ibn al-Husain Nusra as Shams al-Din Muhammad Pahlavan, a Ghurid atabeg who is textually referenced in 1181 and 1182, suggesting that he lived at the juncture of Ghaznavid and Ghurid rule. For further discussion and examples of these medallions, see Stefano Carboni, Glass from Islamic Lands: The Al-Sabah Collection, Kuwait National Museum, London 2001, pp. 272-283.

description_block:
A Seljuk bronze mirror later converted into a talisman 
Persia, 12th/ 13th Century, the talismanic inscriptions probably 14th Century
of circular form, cast in relief to one side with two addorsed sphinxes with scorpion tails on a foliate ground, central raised knob, the border with an inscription in kufic, the reverse inscribed with concentric circles containing four smaller circles, all with magic numbers and inscriptions in naskhi 
11 cm. diam.

Inscriptions: undeciphered.

Beyond their function simply as mirrors, it has been suggested these items may have served as weights, or as magic talismans for divination given the benedictory inscriptions upon their reverse. These inscriptions were most probably added later, notably in the Safavid period. Such amuletic function is attested by the fact that many similar mirrors been found in burial contexts. For further discussion and other examples, see Sheila R. Canby, Deniz Beyazit, Martina Rugiadi and A.C.S. Peacock, Court and Cosmos: The Great Age of the Seljuqs, New Haven 2016, pp. 247-248.

description_block:
A Khorasan engraved bronze sprinkler in the form of a partridge 
Persia, 12th Century
of typical form, standing on two three-clawed feet, the beak hinged with pin, the hollow body with two openings to underside and tail, engraved and chased with chevron-filled bands and roundels containing knot motifs, the chest with inscription in kufic 
12 cm. high

Inscriptions: al-mulk li-llah, 'Sovereignty is God's'.

A similar bird is in The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, inv. no. 1948.458. A further example is illustrated in E. Atil, W.T Chase and P. Jett, Islamic Metalwork in the Freer Gallery of Art, Smithsonian Institution, Washington 1985, no. 11, p. 88.

These items were thought to have served as sprinklers, drinking vessels, or aquamaniles, in Seljuk homes. Liquid would have been poured from the beak of the bird having been filled via the hole to the underside, and stopped with a stopper. It is also possible that these birds may have held powdered incense. The sockets of their eyes would originally have been filled with glass beads. For further discussion, see Chase and Jett, pp. 88-90.

description_block:
A Seljuk niello and gilt silver amulet case 
Persia, 11th Century
of oblong form decorated in niello, gilt and repoussÃ© with arabesque sprays to central panel on both sides, inscription-filled bands to borders in kufic, the sides with a small opening surrounded by geometric motifs, hinges to upper part 
3.6 x 3.3 cm.

Inscriptions: to each side, Qur'an, chapter CXII (al-Ikhlas).

Only a handful of early medieval amulet cases remain in public collections, and only six examples exhibit niello inlay. One example is in the Metropolitan Museum, New York, (inv. no. 1978.415). Similarly gilded and executed in silver, the this amulet depicts an enthroned ruler in a courtly setting surrounded by libations. The scene is similarly framed by an inscription band in kufic. Another example is in the British Museum, London, (inv. no. 1939,0313.1). The example forms part of a Seljuk hoard found in Nihavand, Iran, with a peacock depicted in repoussé and a Qur'anic inscription to the borders. For further discussion on this amulet see Basil Gray, 'A Seljuq Hoard from Persia', The British Museum Quarterly, vol. 13, no. 3, 1939, pp.73-79, and R.H. Pinder-Wilson, 'A silver Ladle and Amulet Case from Persia', British Museum Quarterly vol. 25, no.s 1-2, 1962, pp. 32-34.

description_block:
A Khorasan bronze ewer 
Persia, 12th Century
the gadrooned body of globular form on a tall foot, the neck with lugs and terminating in a wide, upward-facing spout, the strap handle with thumb-rest, engraved and decorated with inscriptions to the body in kufic to four of the fluted panels, the neck and spout with bands of undulating scrollwork and knot motifs 
34 cm. high

Inscriptions: barakah li-sahibihi, 'blessing upon the owner'.

This ewer relates to a known group of globular or fluted bodied vessels that have upward pointing, zoomorphic spouts adorned with lugs for the attachment of rings. The group has been dated on accordance of its similarity with lustre pottery of similar form, datable to the second half of the 12th Century (for examples, see Oliver Watson, Persian Lustre Ware, London 1985, fig. 45). description_block:
A Kirman slip-painted pottery dish 
Persia, 17th Century
of shallow rounded form on a short foot with everted rim, decorated in white slip, cobalt-blue and manganese on a pale green ground with a floral spray to well, vegetal scrollwork to rim 
21.4 cm. diam.

Provenance
Christie's South Kensington, Arts & Textiles of the Islamic & Indian Worlds, 22nd April 2016, lot 349. In this instance, the vessel was catalogued as 'Kubachi' ware.

A dish with comparable elements is in the Victoria & Albert Museum, London (inv. no. 1355-1876). Arthur Lane categorised these vessels within the 'Kirman monochrome group', with their greenish hues imitating Chinese celadon. He notes that the glaze colour can vary from a straw-like brown to a greyish-blue, depending on firing conditions. For further discussion, see Arthur Lane, Later Islamic Pottery, London 1957, pp. 68-77 and pp.83-84.

description_block:
A Safavid lustre pottery dish with peacocks 
Persia, second half of the 17th Century
of shallow rounded form with everted rim on a short foot, decorated in a golden-brown lustre on a white ground with a pair of addorsed peacocks on a ground of floral sprays to well, cartouches containing vegetal interlace to rim, the exterior with floral and foliate sprays 
24.5 cm. diam.

Similar dishes are in the Ashmolean Museum, Oxford (inv. no.s EAX.1207, EAX.3081 and EAX.3070). James Allan notes these dishes form part of the renaissance of Persian lustre production that occurred after 1650. Unlike earlier Seljuq predecessors, these dishes emit a purple hue from their gold lustre and their iconography is more densely and naturalistically painted. Such imagery takes directly from manuscript illuminations, with the arabesque-filled cartouches deriving from framing ornamentation upon frontispieces. For further discussion, see James Allan, Islamic Ceramics, Oxford 1991, pp.56-57.

description_block:
A monumental Qajar brass bowl depicting scenes from Firdausi's Shahnama by 'Ali Asghar Kashi 
Persia, 19th Century
of rounded, deep form with an everted rim on a high splayed foot, profusely engraved with inscription-filled lobed cartouches interspersed with lobed roundels of hunting and mythological scenes, all on a ground of floral scrollwork, the body with Qur'anic and literary episodes notably from the shahnama, including Rustam shooting Isfandiyar in the eye and King Hushang discovering fire, the lower bands with mythical scenes and vegetal interlace

The opening reads: Events of Nasir al-Din Shah's travels to England and his return, taken from the Shah's notes, by al-Hajj Shaykh 'Abd al-Wahhab son of the deceased Shaykh Muhammad Mu'mim Shirazi, printed in Bombay together with images published in London newspapers and others.

The last page reads: Accounts of Nasir al-Din Shah's travels leaving Tehran on 21st Safar 1290/20th April 1873 and his return to the capital on 15 Rajab 1290/8th September 1873, taken from notes by Nasir al-Din Shah, together with what is published in newspapers of those countries. The note in the roundel on the last page must be a copyright note dated 25th of the year 1876, 'so that no one can print it'.

The illustrations include Zill al-Sultan, the Prime Minister, the deputy Minister, the Tsar of Russia, the King of Prussia, visiting an aquarium, being welcome by the German king; the arrival at Dover, at arrival at Charing Cross station, meeting the Queen at Windsor, image of the Prince of Wales, meeting the Duke of Cambridge, going to Liverpool to watch where ships are made, to Manchester where his image is woven in textile, in a Manchester factory to see how textiles are made, the ceremonial planting of a tree in London, visiting Napoleon's tomb in Paris, and an opera house in Italy.

description_block:
Habl al-Matin, a weekly illustrated Persian-language newspaper published in Calcutta, a complete one-year run, in one volume 
Calcutta, 16th Jumadi II 1327/5th July 1909 to 5 Jumadi II 1328/13th June 1910
lithograph, 52 issues, each of 24 pages, modern simulated marbled binding 
343 x 230 mm.

A lithographed copy of the newspaper Habl al-Matin, year 17, covering events between 16 Jumadi II 1327 (5 July 1909) and 5 Jumadi II 1328 (13 June 1910).

Habl al-Matin was an influential newspaper during the Qajar period, running from its first issue on 10 Jomada II 1311/19th December 1893 until 18 Adhar 1309 sh/ 9th December 1930 - though with occasional interruptions. It was founded by Sayyed Jalal-al–Din Muʾayyid-al-Islam Kashani and was published in Calcutta to avoid censorship by the Persian authorities.

It focused on the Persian Constitutional Revolution, advocating for democracy and modernisation, and attacked corruption and colonial influence. It provided uncensored news about Iran, advocating for constitutional rights and criticising royal authority.

A number of important events occurred during the period June 1909 to June 1910 covered by this run. In July 1909, constitutional forces from Rasht, Qazvin, and the Bakhtiyari tribal warriors marched on Tehran, forced the abdication of Mohammad Ali Shah Qajar on July 16, 1909, and re-established the parliament (Majlis). In the same month, the 11-year-old son of the deposed Shah, Ahmad Shah Qajar, was crowned as the new ruler while Sheikh Fazlollah Nouri, a prominent cleric who supported the coup of Mohammad Ali Shah and the bombardment of the first Majlis, was hanged in Tehran by the revolutionary forces. Continued insecurity and power struggles resulted in further British-Russian intervention in Persian affairs.

For further information, see https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/habl-al-matin/

description_block:
EugÃ¨ne Flandin (French, 1809-76) 
A Courtyard in Isfahan
watercolour and bodycolour heightened with white on card, signed lower right 
310 x 246 mm.

Provenance
Christie's South Kensington, Indian and Islamic Art, 15th October 2004, lot 506.
Purchased from the above by the present owner.
The Property of a Lady.

This view depicts the home of the prominent religious leader Aga Najafi (1846-1914) in Isfahan, during the time of Nasr al-Din Shah Qajar. The Masjed-e Shah Mosque can be seen in the background, built during the Safavid dynasty by order of Shah 'Abbas I, in the Naghshe Jahan Meydan. The house and its courtyard seen here still exists.

European artists were at work in Persia during the 19th Century, mostly French, such as Jules Laurens (1825-1901), Pascal Coste (1787-1879) and Eugène Flandin (1809-1889), all in Persia between the 1840s and 1860s, in the wake of French diplomatic missions at that time. For various examples and discussion, see G. Fellinger (ed.), L'Empire des Roses: chefs-d'oeuvre de l'art persan du XIX siècle, Lens 2018, pp. 26-35.

Eugène Flandin (1809-76) travelled to Persia in 1840, attached to the French diplomatic mission there. Alongside the architect Pascal Coste (1787-1879), he made hundreds of drawings of buildings and landscapes, both contemporary and ancient, and the result, on his return, was one of the finest records of the Persia of that time. Flandin received the Légion d'Honneur in 1842 for his part in the mission.

His Perse Moderne was part of a six-volume work, Voyage en Perse pendant les années 1840 et 1841, published in Paris by Gide et J. Baudry between 1843 and 1854. The six volumes were published serially in seventy parts issued over ten years, Perse Ancienne in fifty parts, Perse Moderne in twenty parts, each priced at 20 francs. The original is rare. The subjects include views in Tabriz, Tehran, Kashan, Isfahan, Hamadan, Shiraz, and the ancient site at Persepolis.

The Kiani Collection: Royal Jewels of Ahmad Shah QajarA fine Royal Qajar diamond-set silver brooch or headdress ornament (jeqqa) belonging to Ahmad Shah Qajar (reg. 1909-1925) 
Persia, 19th Century
in the form of an openwork crown surmounted by a plume, a pendent drop to upper feather, set with a large central rose-cut diamond and other smaller similarly cut diamonds 
5.1 cm. high; the central diamond 10.3 x 9.8 mm. approx.; 17 g.

Provenance
Ahmad Shah Qajar (reg. 1909-1925) and thence by descent.

The jeqqa, a jewelled aigrette worn on the front of a crown or cap, was an emblem of Qajar kingship. Set with precious stones and sometimes accompanied by feathers, it formed part of the ceremonial dress of shahs and princes at coronations, New Year celebrations and court audiences. Ahmad Shah continued the tradition of wearing the jeqqa. An eyewitness account of his coronation in 1914 describes a large diamond and aigrette on his black astrakhan cap, which he removed to receive the crown, and later put on again after the ceremony.

The Kiani Collection: Royal Jewels of Ahmad Shah QajarAn enamelled silver-gilt Grand Collar, Star and Breast Star of the Qajar Order of the Crown (Neshan-e Taj-e Iran) belonging to Ahmad Shah Qajar (reg. 1909-1925) 
by Arthus Bertrand, Paris, circa 1914
the star in the form of a five-pointed star with smaller rays between, the central enamelled medallion depicting a Qajar crown surrounded by a wreath, surmounted by the date AH 1332, verso with a sun, on a suspension loop in the form of a wreath; the collar with central element in the form of two confronting rampant lions with the suns behind lifting a crown, the chain with alternating elements in the form of lions, Taj stars and floral cartouches; the breast star in the form of a five pointed star with rays between, with central enamelled medallion depicting a Qajar crown surrounded by a wreath, surmounted by the date AH 1332, inscribed 'Arthus Bertrand rue de Rennes Paris' to reverse; original maker's red morocco box embossed with gilt lion and sun motif on lid, original fitted box 
46.5 cm. long from collar to bottom of pendent star; the breast star 9.6 cm. diam.(2)

Provenance
Ahmad Shah Qajar (reg. 1909-1925) and thence by descent.

Published
Gwenaelle Fellinger [ed.], l'Empire des Roses, 2018, p. 135, no. 140.

Exhibited
l'Empire des Roses, Louvre Lens, 28 March - 23 July 2018. 

The Order of the Crown (Neshan-e Taj) was founded by Ahmad Shah Qajar in 1913 (AH 1332) as Persia's highest dynastic and state order and comprised of two classes. The present lot, the Grand Collar of the first class, was an exceptionally restricted form of the order, worn only by Ahmad Shah and his brother, the Crown Prince Mohammad Hassan Mirza (1899-1943). It was produced in Paris by Arthus Bertrand, exemplifying the manufacture of Persian royal insignia by European specialists. Ahmad Shah is depicted wearing both the collar and breast star offered here in a well known photograph dating to circa 1916. A shorter, but otherwise identical, collar was offered in these rooms (Bonhams Islamic and Indian Art, 7 October 2014, lot 152).

The Kiani Collection: Royal Jewels of Ahmad Shah QajarAn enamelled gold collar of the Ottoman Order of the House of Osman (HÃ¢nedÃ¢n-Ä± Ãl-i OsmÃ¢n NiÅanÄ±) belonging to Ahmad Shah Qajar (reg. 1909-1925)

comprising a series of nineteen gold elements in the form of lobed cartouches decorated in red and white enamel with stars and crescents interspersed by gold elements in the form of quatrefoils decorated in red and white enamel with six pointed stars, the removable pendant in the form of an oval cartouche decorated in repoussÃ© with a tughra and further inscriptions, the border bearing the dates AH 699 and AH 1311, openwork ribbon and wreath to border, surmounted by a star and crescent, clasp to top elements

Inscriptions: al-mustanid bi'l-tawfiqat al-rabbaniyya malik al-dawla al-uthmaniyya, 'The one supported by divine success, the king of the Ottoman state', with the tughra of Sultan Abdülhamid II, the date '1311' and the date '699'.

Instituted by Sultan Abdülhamid II (reg. 1876-1909) in 1893, the Order of the House of Osman (Hânedân-ı Âl-i Osmân Nişanı) was a single-class distinction awarded to senior members of the Imperial family, statesmen, and foreign heads of state. The dates on the order relate to the foundation of the Ottoman Empire (AH 699/ AD 1299) and the date of the foundation of the order (AH 1311/ AD 1895). Ahmad Shah is recorded as receiving the order on the 19th of July 1914, two days before his coronation. Another example of the collar, from the collection a prince of the Egyptian Royal Family and an Ottoman Sultanzade was sold at Sotheby's, Arts of the Islamic World & India, 29 April 2026, lot 249.

description_block:
The Kiani Collection: Royal Jewels of Ahmad Shah QajarA diamond-set and enamelled gilt-silver Spectacular First Class Breast Star of the Ottoman Order of Osmanieh (Osmaniye NiÅanÄ±) belonging to Ahmad Shah Qajar (reg. 1909-1925) 
Europe, first quarter of the 20th Century
in the form of an eight pointed star, profusely set with old brilliant and rose-cut diamonds, the central element decorated in green and red enamel with inscriptions and a crescent, brooch pin and two hooks to reverse for suspension, with fitted box 
9.5 cm. diam.; 103.1 g.

Provenance
Ahmad Shah Qajar (reg. 1909-1925) and thence by descent.

The Order of Osmanieh (Nişân-ı Osmanî) was established by Sultan Abdülaziz (reg. 1861-76) in 1862. Conceived as a high Ottoman distinction, it was awarded for service to the state and also served as an instrument of diplomacy, its recipients included foreign rulers, ministers and ambassadors. Originally comprising three classes, it was subsequently expanded in 1867 to include four classes including an augmented First Class made with diamonds (murassa' or 'in brilliants'). Its insignia is distinguished by a red enamel centre bearing a gilt crescent and an invocation of divine assistance naming Abdülaziz as sovereign of the Ottoman Empire, surrounded by a green enamel band. Both the first and second classes included a breast star; under the regulations the first-class star was worn on the left breast with a sash, whilst the second-class star was worn on the right.

These textiles were sometimes left purposefully unfinished, signalling the continuation of happy marriages within the family home. Palyak is a designation for those embroideries produced in Tashkent and its surrounding area. Meaning 'firmament' or 'heavens' in Arabic, these linens accordingly portray stylised moon motifs with the number of medallions often indicating the fabric's age. description_block:
Pierre Vattier (trans.), L'Histoire du Grand Tamerlane, the first French translation of a history of the reign of Timur by Ibn Arabshah (15th Century) 
Paris, Chez Remy Soubret, 1658
first edition, three titles bound in one, pp. [xxiv], 248; [viii], 146, [1]; 44, 332, woodcut headpieces and endpieces, initial letters and title page decoration, contemporary (or slightly later) calf, neatly re-backed in morocco, all edges gilt, marbled end-papers 
4to, 230 x 185 mm.

Full title: Ibn Arabshah; al-Makin, Jirjis ibn al-Amad. L'Histoire du Grand Tamerlan divisee en sept livres, contenant l'origine, la vie, & la mort de ce fameux Conquerant, nouvellement traduite en François de l'Arabe d'Achmed fils de Guerapse; [together with] Portrait du Grand Tamerlan, avec la suite de son histoire iusques a l'establissement de l'empire du Mogol, nouvellement traduit de l'Arabe du fils de Guerapse; [and with] L'Histoire Mahometane, ou les Quarante-Neuf Chalifes du Macine. Divisez en trois livres, contenant un abrege chronologique de l'histoire Mussulmane en general, depuis Mahomet iusques au regne des Francois en la Terre-Saincte, nouvellement traduit d'Arabe en Francois; avec un sommaire de l'histoire des Mussulmans ou Sarrazins en Espagne, extraict de Rodrigue Ximines Archevesque de Tolede, et verifie sur la Macine.

The first translation into French of Ibn Arabshāh's (1389–1450) two histories of of Timur, 'Tamerlane the Great' (1336-1405). The first translation of Ibn Arabshah's history was by Jacobus Golius (1596-1667) into Latin in 1636, and this translation by Pierre Vattier (1623-1667) made the works much more accessible.

There were only three contemporary histories of Timur and Ibn Arabshah's directly opposed the other two Timurid-sponsored works, both titled Zafarnama. These painted Timur as a benevolent and glorious ruler, similar to how he is perceived by Islamic Central Asia today, while Ibn Arabshah described him as a deformed and ignoble man who desecrated many important Islamic cities, echoing the sentiments of many in Arabia and India. Vattier's translation from Arabic of al-Makin's (1205-1273) history of the Saracens, from the time of Muhammad to the accession of the Mameluke Sultan Baybars in 1260, is bound in the front of this work to provide a history of Timur's Islamic opponents and to emphasise Ibn Arabshah's point of view.

Pierre Vattier (1623-1667) was doctor to the Duke of Orleans and professor of Arabic at the College Royal from 1658. He published numerous translations from Arabic originals.

Roderick Whitfield, The Art of Central Asia: the Stein Collection in the British Museum, 3 volumes 
Tokyo, Kodansha International, 1982-1985
first edition in English, three volumes, pp. 344, 358, 362 respectively, 270 colour plates, 438 illustrations, one of 550 sets in English, red cloth covers, original silk slip-cases 
folio (397 x 285 mm.)(3)

A magnificently illustrated set depicting the art removed from Dunhuang by Stein and now preserved in the British Museum. Ninety packing cases from Stein's 1906-07 expedition were delivered to the British Museum in 1909. Unpacking and conservation took several years. Stein was not the first European to reach Dunhuang, nor the first to remove treasures from China. However, sponsored by the Government of India and the British Museum, he was impelled to collect on a vast scale, and justified his action thus: 'with the sad proofs of progressive damage before my eyes, I could feel no doubt that, as local protection was out of the question, careful removal of as much of these mural paintings as circumstances would permit and artistic or iconographic interest would warrant, offered the only means of assuring their security'.

The first two volumes are devoted to the paintings of Dunhuang, the third to textiles, sculpture and other arts.

Figurative illustration, from early Arab examples to Safavid and Qajar painting are a particular strength.

The first two volumes document acquisitions by Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan up to 1967; the third and fourth volumes acquisitions made between 1967 and 1976. This catalogue was privately printed in a limited edition; sets were presented to universities and museums at the time of publication, but it was never commercially distributed. description_block:
Mahmoud Farshchian (Iran, 1930-2025) 
A Harp Player seated in a rocky landscape, dated the month of Tir 1344/22nd June 1965
watercolour and gold on paper, signed and dated lower right 
68.5 x 48.5 cm.

Provenance
Presented to the seller by Prince Shahyar Pahlabod in the 1970s.
Private UK collection.

Prince Shahyar Pahlabod is the son of Princess Shams, who was the sister of Mohamad Reza Pahlavi and the daughter of Reza Shah.

Born in 1930 in Isfahan, Mahmoud Farshchian's oeuvre was greatly informed by the opulence of art and nature by which he was surrounded as a child. Farshchian's father, a carpet dealer, adorned their family home with Persian rugs, which provided a stimulating visual atmosphere for the young artist; it is to him that Farshchian's initial passion for art is owed. Memories of water and birds around which Farshchian would play in his local neighbourhood of Ahmedabad have served a central role in his paintings. The Royal Mosque in Isfahan was the inception of Farshchian's formal preoccupation with traditional Persian craft, particularly Safavid dynasty art and architecture, which lent itself to elaborate detail and intricate beauty. Farshchian attended the School of Fine Arts in Isfahan, where he studied the geometry of Islamic architecture, Persian miniature, and carpet design, and in his spare time explored the rich literature of Rumi and Hafiz. His first solo exhibition was held at the city's Iranian-British Cultural Association office in 1948. Farshchian's practical talent, intellect, and avid appreciation for culture lead him to the Academy of Fine Arts Vienna, where he furthered his studies before travelling to Paris and Munich. He was later Director of Tehran University's Department of National Arts.

In 2001, the Farshchian Museum opened in Isfahan to house a collection of the artist's works. The dedicated Farshchian Hall in the Astan Quds Razavi Museum, Mashhad, as well as the Museum of Contemporary Arts, Mashhad, also include permanent displays. Farshchian's paintings were acquired for the royal private collections of Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip, Queen Juliana of the Netherlands, Prince Agha Khan, and Emperor Akihito, as well as notable political leaders internationally. The artist currently resides in the United States.

For a large work by the artist sold at auction, Untitled (The Fifth Day of Creation), dated 1990, see Sotheby's, The Edith and Stuart Cary Welch Collection, 25th October 2023, lot 130.

An Ottoman steel chamfron 
Turkey, 17th Century
of typical form with an articulated triangular plate between former ear guards, ridge to centre of frontal plate, below, mark of Saint Irene Arsenal 
47.6 cm. long

Provenance
Acquired in London in February 1981.

Built originally as a church under Constantine I, the Saint Irene Arsenal was converted into a weapons repository after Sultan Mehmed II's (1432-1482) conquest of Istanbul in 1453. The building formally became a functioning arsenal under Sultan Ahmed III (1673-1736) in 1726. Soon after, the armoury was looted by its own armourers following the deposition of Sultan Selim III (1789-1807) and the disbanding of the Janissaries Corps. It would be revived as an arsenal once more under Sultan Abdülaziz (1861-1876).

description_block:
An Ottoman tinned-copper candlestick with dedicatory inscription to the shrine of Moses (possibly the shrine of Nabi Musa) in AH 1169/ AD 1755/6 
Turkey, 17th/ 18th Century
of splayed conical form with raised bands to rim and foot, the associated neck of cylindrical form with raised, beaded bands and a torus element decorated in openwork with geometric and foliate motifs, all rising to an everted rim, inscription to body 
34.7 cm. high

Provenance
Lieutenant Colonel Henry Courtney Brocklehurst (1888-1942).
His brother Lieutenant Colonel, Sir Philip Lee Brocklehurst Bt. (1887–1975), Swythamley Park, near Macclesfield until 1975.
Thence by descent.

Exhibited
On long term loan to West Park Museum, Macclesfield, c. 1939–1976.

Inscriptions: 'Umar ibn ... endowed this candlestick to the shrine of the one who spoke (al-kalim, an attribute of Moses) with the the Most Merciful (i.e. God), Musa ibn 'Umran, blessing and peace be upon him, the year 1169 (1755-6).

Brothers, Henry Courtney and Philip Lee Brocklehurst, were renowned travellers and explorers of the twentieth century, as well as Great War veterans. Sir Philip famously participated in Shackleton's 1907–1909 Nimrod expedition to the Antarctic. He would later travel through both the Middle and Far East. His brother, Courtney accompanied him on a trip to the Arctic in 1912. Courtney travelled extensively in China, Japan and Tibet in the 1930s, bringing the first giant panda from Tibet to the UK. Many of the artefacts collected on these travels were loaned to the West Park Museum, where they remained following Philip's death in 1975.

The inscription may refer to the celebrated shrine of Nabi Musa, traditionally identified with the burial place of the Prophet Moses (Musa ibn 'Imran), situated in the Judaean Desert between Jerusalem and Jericho. The sanctuary, an important Muslim pilgrimage site from the medieval period onwards, developed around a shrine established or substantially endowed under the Ayyubid sultan al-Malik al-Zahir Baybars (reg. 1260–77), and was subsequently enlarged and maintained under the Ottomans. The wording of the present inscription, describing its destination as the mashhad of kalim al-Rahman Musa ibn 'Imran, (Moses son of Amram, he who spoke with the Merciful [God]), is consistent with the veneration of Moses at the shrine. The use of mashhad ('shrine' or 'sanctuary') and the dedication of a candlestick as a waqf further support an association with a functioning pilgrimage sanctuary. Although the inscription does not appear to specify the location, the prominence of Nabi Musa as a major Ottoman shrine dedicated specifically to Moses makes it a plausible identification.

description_block:
A large bone and mother of pearl-inlaid olivewood model of the Aedicule from the Church of the Holy Sepulchre 
Palestine, 17th/ 18th Century
intricately inlaid in mother-of-pearl and bone, the roof lifting to reveal the Chapel of the Angels and the Holy Sepulchre Chapel, with hinged door at entrance, inscribed 'I' to base and to underside of roof 
29.3 x 11.8 x 9.4 cm.

The Aedicule at the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem is the small shrine enclosing the site traditionally identified as the tomb of Christ, from which Christ is believed to have risen following the Crucifixion. Olivewood and mother of pearl models were probably made in Bethlehem under Franciscan supervision as gifts for diplomats and rulers and as souvenirs for grand tourists. An early example of the entire Church of the Holy Sepulchre is in the National Museum of Denmark (Copenhagen 1996, p.344, no.317). Inventories record that this had entered the collection before 1674. Other examples are in the British Museum (museum nos. OA.10338 and 1983,0107.1), one of which was bequeathed by Sir Hans Sloane (1660-1753) and is listed in the Hans Sloane Manuscript Catalogue: 'The model of the temple of the Sepulchre of our Lord Jesus Christ & of Mount Calvary in Jerusalem - with an explication of the same, beads, measures &c.' Sloane had another model of 'The model of the temple at Bethlehem' with the price he had paid for it, £5, 7 shillings and 6 pence. This example measures 23 x 42 x 36.5 cm. A larger example, measuring 49 cm. max., was sold in these rooms (Bonhams, Fine European Furniture, Sculpture and Works of Art Including the Beurdeley Collection, 6 July 2011, lot 28). The large size of the present lot would suggest that it was made for a more monumental model, or perhaps as a stand alone piece.

description_block:
Four bronze medals relating to the Battle of Lepanto (1571), variously by Gianfederico Bonzagi and Giovanni Antonio de' Rossi 
Italy, the earliest dated 1571
each circular, to the obverse of each Pope Pius V Ghislieri; to the reverse of two depictions of the Battle of Lepanto inscribed respectively 'DEXTERA TVA DOMINE PERCVSSIT INIMCVM 1571' and 'A DOMINO FACTVM EST ISTVD 1571', signed 'F.P.' and '10 ANT R.F.'; the third with a representation of the Crusade fleet of 1455 inscribed 'HOC VOVI DEO UT FIDEI HOSTES PERDEREM ELEXIT ME'; the fourth with the three personifications of the Holy League inscribed 'FOEDERIS IN TVRCAS SANCTIO', signed '10 ANT R.F', dated 1571 
the largest 4.2 cm. diam.(4)

These medals chart a chronology of escalating conflict between the Roman Empire and the Ottomans. In May 1571, the Holy League was formed, comprising the Papacy, the Spanish Empire and Republic of Venice, to cease Ottoman expansion into the Mediterranean after Turkish forces had taken Venetian-controlled Cyrprus in 1570. The alliance went on to defeat the Ottoman fleet at the Battle of Lepanto on October 7, 1751. 

For other examples of medals commemorating the Battle of Lepanto, see the Royal Museums Greenwich (inv. no. MEC0227) and the National Gallery of Art, Washington D.C. (inv. no. 1957.14.966.b).

description_block:
A Veneto-Saracenic brass salver depicting tulips 
Italy or Eastern Mediterranean, 16th Century
of shallow rounded form with an everted rim, profusely engraved with geometric interlace within a roundel to well surrounded by scrolling tulip and split-palmette motifs, the walls and rim with vegetal guillochÃ© motifs interspersed with flowerheads, the reverse with interlocking floral motif to base and a band of pendant trefoils 
45 cm. diam.

Provenance
Formerly in a private collection London, acquired in the early 1980s. 

The 19th Century romantic conceptions that these vessels were made by Muslim craftsmen living in the Serenissima have been slowly eroded since the late 20th Century, most famously by Sylvia Auld in her work Renaissance Venice, Islam and Mahmud the Kurd, London 2004. She notably split these profusely engraved and, at times, inlaid brass vessels into three groups, positing that many were in fact made in Mamluk Egypt and Syria. She maintained, nonetheless, that Group C items were made in Italy in the late 15th and early 16th Century, emulating Levantine originals, and feeding European tastes for Islamic wares (pp. 8-9). We may posit that this salver forms part of this group given the presence of the tulip motifs, a sought-after commodity that was traded through Venice in the 1560s and which was largely absent from Mamluk iconography. Venice likewise saw the trade of richly decorated Iznik vessels and Ottoman textiles throughout the 16th and 17th Centuries, whose imagery no doubt inspired artists working in the city and beyond. The tulips depicted on the present lot have a characteristicly Ottoman look such as those depicted on Iznik and Damascus pottery of the 16th Century.

description_block:
A large Italian maiolica Iznik-style charger 
Padua or Bassano del Grappa, dated 1653
of shallow rounded form with everted rim on a shoot foot, decorated in orange, yellow, cobalt-blue and green with sprays of carnations and saz leaves to the outer band, the central roundel with architectural scene of a church surrounded by cypress trees and birds, the exterior with stellate motifs, date and cross motif 
44 cm. diam.

Italian maiolica inspired by Iznik pottery was traditionally attributed to Candiana, a municipality to the south of Padua. However, it is now understood that these vessels were produced in Padua itself. This is confirmed by the cross-shaped mark to the reverse of this bowl, a symbol attributed to the city, see Johann Georg Theodor Grässe, Führer für Sammler von Porzellan und Fayence, Berlin 1919, p.333. The earliest known examples of this type are recorded to 1613, with the latest recorded to 1705 in Ca' Rezzonico, Venice. New discoveries in the 1980s of Iznik maiolica in Bassano del Grappa dated to the late sixteenth century indicates the diffusion of the style across the Veneto. The scene upon this dish may take inspiration from this region, perhaps depicting the Basilica of San Antonio de Padua. For further discussion of these wares and other examples of this style, see Bernard Rackham, Catalogue of Italian Maiolica in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London 1940, vol. I, fig. 1082-1085; vol. 2, pp. 359-360.

description_block:
An Ottoman composite silk-embroidered cotton panel 
Turkey or Greece, 19th Century
of rectangular form, comprising alternating square panels embroidered in polychrome silks on a cotton ground, with flowerheads and geometric motifs, the border with floral interlace 
119 x 180 cm.

Provenance
Private UK collection, London.

The rigorous laundering to which Ottoman textiles were sometimes subjected, including beating garments against rocks and washing fabric panels with harsh lye, inevitably hastened their deterioration. Worn or damaged domestic textiles were therefore frequently repurposed, with surviving fragments patched together with other pieces of fabric to create new objects. Patchwork wall hangings consequently became increasingly popular, reflecting not only an economical approach to valuable textiles but also, perhaps, the survival of much older Turkic traditions in which garments assembled from disparate pieces of cloth were invested with spiritual significance. For further discussion and examples of such panels, see Roderick Taylor, Ottoman Embroidery, London, 1993, pp. 133–39.

Provenance
Presented in 1923 by Bekir Sami Günsav (1879–1934) to his daughter Azize Sami (b. 1908) and her husband Geoffrey Crabbe, on the occasion of their marriage; thence by descent to the present owner. 

Azize Sami, the vendor's grandmother, was the daughter of the Ottoman officer and Turkish nationalist commander Bekir Sami Günsav (1879–1934). In 1923 she married the British engineer Geoffrey Crabbe, who later served as chief advisory engineer to the Turkish Government. Their marriage was recalled fourteen years later in a profile of Azize by Ralph Hewins, published under the headline 'She Will Bring Ski To Turkey: "Modern Woman No. 1"', Daily Mail, Thursday, 9 December 1937. The article records that Azize had rebelled against the husband selected for her by her father and eloped with Crabbe in 1923, and describes her subsequent prominence in introducing European customs into Turkey. The present silver service was given to the couple by Günsav as a wedding present and has remained in the family by descent.

description_block:
An Armenian mother of pearl-mounted pastoral staff 
Ottoman Turkey, 18th/ 19th Century
the faceted octagonal shaft segmented by two knops, terminating in a steel tip to bottom end with possible inscription to upper socket, the mother of pearl finial carved in the form of two inward-curving serpents with coral-set eyes (corallium rubrum) on a balustered ferule 
155 cm. long

Provenance
Acquired by the owner's grandfather in Paris in the 1970s. 

Staffs such as the present lot were traditionally carried by Armenian bishops or priests with a single or double serpent signifying his office within the Eastern Orthodox church. The serpents resemble the Greek letter 'tau', a form traced back to both the cross of St Anthony and Moses and Nehushtan, as told in the Book of Numbers. Two other tau-headed staffs are in the Victoria & Albert Museum, London, see (inv. no.s 944-1904 and 343:1, 2-1903). These are said to have been produced in the Ottoman court in Constantinople in the seventeenth century, on account of their similarity to another staff in the Monastery of St Catherine on Mount Sinai.

description_block:
A monumental pair of post-Mamluk silver-inlaid brass Candlesticks from the Church of St. John the Divine in Lincolnshire 
Egypt or Syria, 19th Century or earlier
identically decorated, topped with circular rimmed trays with continuous Arabic inscription to the underside, detachable drip-trays, the shafts with openwork foliate arabesque detailing, three baluster-shaped sections with continuous Arabic inscriptions against openwork, interspersed with three hexagonal sections, the central one with further short Arabic phrases within cartouches, the cartouches in the other sections blank, the flaring base with nine quatrefoil cartouches containing inscriptions, below a band of nine pierced arrow-shaped cartouches, with church candle fittings 
236 cm. high; base 75 cm. wide(2)

Provenance
Sir Hickman Beckett Bacon (1855-1945).
The Church of St. John the Divine, Gainsborough, Lincolnshire, by 1882.
Bonhams, Islamic & Indian Art including Contemporary Indian and Pakistani Paintings,12th and 13th October 2005, lot 206.
Private UK collection, Chilham Castle, Kent.

Literature
Nikolaus Pevsner and John Harris, The Buildings of England, Lincolnshire, London, 1964, p. 242 ('CANDLESTICKS. Tall, C18(?), Italian(?), of wood. They are said to come from Egypt.')

Inscriptions: in Arabic, some appear to be Christian prayers and invocations, using metaphors of light (and hence highly appropriate for such objects). Those that have been deciphered read: 

to underside of trays, Qur'an, chapter IX (al-Tawba) part of verse 51; to horizontal bands to body 'We praise and magnify you... and joy to [all] men [...] Glory be to God on high and peace to people on earth [...] Exalted is the sublimity of your glory, we bow to you and we thank you and we thank...' [...] The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right until I make your enemies (your footstool)'; to cartouches around base, repeat of part of a Psalm of David, known as Zabur in Arabic.

Sir Hickman Beckett Bacon (1855-1945) was 11th Baronet of Redgrave and 12th Baronet of Mildenhall. He is best known as a collector of watercolours: the Hickman Bacon Collection consists of 400 works by various artists including Turner, Girtin, and Parkes Bonington. But he also travelled and collected abroad, especially in the Middle East. When a 'bazaar' was held in order to raise funds in 1882 on the consecration of St. John the Divine (the site for which had been donated by Sir Hickman in 1878), he presented, as his niece wrote, 'some brass candlesticks which he had brought back from Cairo'. (See Lavinia Gibbs, Uncle Hicky: Sir Hickman Bacon, an Edwardian Eccentric, Dougarie 2001, p. 38). The candlesticks remained in the church, which fell out of use in recent years, and are depicted in various postcards of the interior of the church dating to the early 20th century.

The candlesticks, or lampstands, predate the Mamluk Revival style which originated in the late 19th Century in Cairo and Damascus. The craftsmanship of the candlesticks is of a more conservative character which continues the tradition of earlier Mamluk metalwork, outlasting the Ottoman conquest of Egypt and Syria. Such a style might be described as 'post-Mamluk'. However, there is no precedent in Mamluk metalwork for the sheer variety of shapes of large candlesticks, suspension lamps, and standing lamps. There is evidence that comparable pairs of candlesticks possessing vase-shaped upper structures for holding a candle were already being used in mosques in the mid-17th Century, and a number of other similarly-decorated suspension lamps can be attributed by their inscriptions and signatures to early 18th Century Damascus. The timing of their arrival in England (not later than 1882) would also imply that they do not fall into the category of Mamluk Revival. In addition, Sir Hickman was an avid collector of tiles, rugs and textiles, amongst other things, and it would have been highly unlikely that he would have acquired newly-produced objects.

Very little scholarship exists on this subject: reference should in the first instance be made to Doris Behrens Abouseif, Mamluk and Post-Mamluk Metal Lamps (Institut Francais d'Archaeologie Orientale, Cairo, 1995).

It has been suggested that the Christian phrases relate to Coptic liturgy, and that the candlesticks may therefore have been initially made for a Coptic church.

description_block:
A large gold, silver and copper-inlaid brass tray depicting scenes from the Old Testament signed by Nu'man 
Damascus, Syria, dated AD 1913
of circular form with flattened rim, profusely engraved and decorated in silver and copper inlay with a large central roundel depicting Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden, details including the sun and hair inlaid in gold, surrounded by a band of cartouches containing inscriptions in Hebrew, a further band containing old testament scenes surrounded by vegetal motifs, and another band of cartouches containing inscriptions in Arabic, the rim with inscription-filled cartouches on a ground of geometric designs 
69 cm. diam.

Provenance
Acquired in Egypt during the First World War by Captain Thomas Colville (d. 1950) and thence by descent. 

Published
Canon Dr. Clare Amos in, A Damascene Plate, in Common Ground Magazine, winter 2023, pp. 38-41.

Inscriptions: in Arabic: 'The work of Nu'man and partners in Damascus of al-Sham, the year 1913'; in the small cartouches to rim, the story of Adam and Eve who were in Paradise, ate the forbidden fruit, repented, were forgiven by God and remained on earth; in Arabic and Hebrew, in the large cartouches, captions for the including 'the exit of Adam and Eve from Paradise', 'Qain (Cain) kills his brother Habil (Abel)', 'Noah at the time of storm', 'building of the tower of Babel', 'Lut flees the city', 'Moses is rescued from the sea', 'the exodus of Bani Isra'il from Egypt', 'Moses strikes the rock and water comes out', 'the Israelites leave the Holy Land and the death of Moses'.

Captain Thomas Richard Colville (1883–1950) served in the Duke of Cornwall's Light Infantry before being seconded to the Egyptian Army in July 1914, serving with the 14th Sudanese Infantry Battalion. He later settled at Sandywell Park, Gloucestershire, which he purchased in 1924, and pursued a wide range of sporting interests, including big-game hunting, fishing, foxhunting and racehorse ownership. His horse Angel Hill was entered for the 1950 Grand National.

description_block:
An unusual gem-set enamelled silver-gilt hilted steel ceremonial sword commemorating the family of the Shaykhs of the Al al-'Abid, the leaders of the Albu Diraj clan in Iraq, with the names of three of its recent leaders 
London, 20th Century, the hilt hallmarked 1995
the single-edged steel blade of curved form, engraved to each side with foliate motifs, inscription-filled cartouches and stylised palmettes, the gilt-silver hilt with pommel in the form of a lion wearing a crown, the eyes set with green gemstones, hallmark for London to lower mane, the knuckle-guard dividing into three parts towards the forte, one terminating in a single quillon in the form of a lion, the eyes set with green gemstones, inner guard with hallmarks for London, maker's mark 'CW' and date letter for 1995, circular green enamelled plaque to guard engraved with a tughra surrounded by a wreath, applied silver plaque in the form of a palmette engraved with tughra enamelled in green near forte, black leather and gilt-silver thread grips, gilt-silver thread braid to guard terminating in two brass elements decorated with gilt-silver thread and green silk; the wood scabbard clad in black leather, gilt-silver mount to top engraved with inscription-filled medallion of stellar form surmounted by a foliate motif, above an applied silver rosette engraved with inscriptions and decorated in green and yellow enamel, above a 'v' shaped band of green gemstones, four further silver mounts variously engraved with inscriptions and inscription-filled cartouches, gilt-silver chape engraved with foliate motif, two suspension loops; the wood stand with five applied silver plaques variously engraved with tughras and inscriptions, one with matching hall marks to hilt 
91 cm. long(2)

Provenance
Private UK collection. 

Three of the Shaykhs whose names are mentioned ruled over the family during the late 19th and 20th Century:
al-Sayyid al-Shaykh 'Ali al-Sayyid 'Abdullah al-'Abid' (whose dates are recorded as 1860-1940, but on the sword the dates are given as 1855-1940).
al-Sayyid al-Shaykh Husayn al-Sayyid 'Ali al-'Abid (whose dates are recorded as 1895-1978).
al-Sayyid al-Shaykh 'Abd al-Khaliq al-Sayyid al-Hasan al-'Abid (the most recent, though no dates are recorded).

The numerous inscriptions are as follows: 

To the guard, the basmala in tughra form. 

To the blade, to one side the names 'al-Sayyid al-Shaykh 'Abdullah al-Sayyid al-Shaykh ... al-'Abid' and 'al-Sayyid al-Shaykh 'Ali al-Sayyid 'Abdullah al-'Abid'; to the other side the name 'al-Sayyid al-Shaykh 'Abd al-Khaliq al-Sayyid al-Hasan al-'Abid'.

To the scabbard, in the lobed green device: a tughra (undeciphered); in the small roundel, possibly 'Sayyid al-'Abid'; to the border of the roundel, in black, the shahada, 'Wisam al-'Abid' and possibly the date 1291 (AD 1874-5); to the centre, in green Qur'an, chapter III (Al 'Imran), verse 8; to the pointed star, possibly the basmala in tughra form; around the roundel, 'Remember me al-Sayyid!', 'Husayn, 1319, 1897, 1976'; to the centre, 'The basmala, Sayyid al-'Abid'; to the device below the above, 'In the name of God, Sayyid al-'Abid'; to the long device below the above, the shahada, Qur'an, chapter XV (al-Hijr), verse 46, Qur'an, chapter XVII (al-Isra'), part of verse 1; to the device below, around the roundel 'remember me al-Sayyid!' 'Ali;' and the dates '1275, 1855, 1362, 1940'.

To the stand, the basmala in tughra form; to the octagonal plate, 'In the name of God, Sayyid al-'Abid'; to the rectangular plate, 'The sword of the Family of the Shaykhs of al-'Abid'; to the lobed plate, the basmala in tughra form; to the small roundel, 'In the name of God, Sayyid al-'Abid'; to the border of the roundel, the shahada, ' ... al-Sayyid al-'Abid', and the dates 1301 and 1881 (repeated); to the middle, Qur'an, chapter III (Al 'Imran), verse 8; to the star, possibly the basmala in tughra form, to the border of the roundel, 'Remember me al-Sayyid!', the name Husayn, with only two dates clear 1895 and 1978, to the centre, 'In the name of God, Sayyid al-'Abid'.

This is a sword bearing the names of the Shaykhs of the Al al-'Abid, the leaders of the Albu Diraj clan in Iraq, who played a prominent role in society and politics, particularly in the city of Samarra. The Albu Diraj are the descendants of the head (naqib) of the Sayyids (descendants of the Prophet) Durj al-Din, who protected the Sunni Sayyids and various shrines, including that of Abd al-Qadir Gilani, after the Shi'i Safavids took Iraq.

The heads of the clan from the 19th Century onwards were the Al al-'Abid, the Family of al-Abid, named after al-Shaykh 'Abd Allah b. Ahmad, known as al-'Abid, who was head of the Qadiriyya Sufi order in Samarra and whose own tomb is in that city. After a successful delegation was sent to Istanbul asking for permission from the Sultan Abdülhamid for the foundation of a madrasa in Samarra, the Shaykhs of the Al al-'Abid were awarded their own insignia and seal consisting of the basmala in tughra form which was used on the stick and sword they used on ceremonial occasions, and which appears to be the type here. He was succeeded by his son Shaykh 'Ali (1860-1940), who was undisputed chief of the shaykhs of Samarra and who hosted King Faisal when he visited the city. He was succeeded by his son Shaykh Husayn (1895-1978), who also played a leading political, social and charitable role in Samarra. For discussion of this family, see 'Abbas al-'Azzawi, Mawsu'at 'Asha'ir al-'Iraq, Beirut 2005, vol. 3, pp. 295-301.

description_block:
A rare album of photographs documenting an official mission to carry out restoration work in Mecca in 1951 
Saudi Arabia and Egypt, photographs taken March 1951, letter dated 4th December 1951
59 gelatin silver prints pasted down on 23 card album pages, handwritten captions in Arabic, typewritten letter in Arabic giving official confirmation of the mission issued by the Egyptian Ministry of Public Works, dated 4th December 1951, green leather album 
photographs 82 x 130 mm. and 88 x 82 mm.; album 245 x 345 mm.

Provenance
The seller's grandfather, Mohamed Abdel Fattah Helmy Bey (1905–1994), an Egyptian architect and senior heritage official who later became Director of the Administration for the Conservation of Arab Monuments in Egypt, and subsequently Director General of the Egyptian Antiquities Service.

This lot and the next (lot 112) document a restoration mission to the Hijaz undertaken in March 1951 and are accompanied by an official dedication issued by the Egyptian Ministry of Public Works, dated 4th December 1951, confirming Helmy's participation in the mission for the restoration of Al-Masjid an-Nabawi.

The letter is addressed to Mohamed Abdel Fattah Helmy Bey, sending two collections of his photographs of his visit to Mecca and Medina during the restoration of the Prophet's Noble Sanctuary in Jumadi II, 1370 (March 1951). The letterhead is that of the Ministry of Public Work, the Lawyer's Office, Cairo and is dated 4th December 1951. The signature of the sender is not clear, but may be that of 'Uthman Muharram Basha, Minister of Public Works in 1950-52.

John H. Harvey FSA (1911-1997) and thence by descent until sold at auction in June this year.

The Nusretiye Mosque (Nusretiye Camii) in Tophane, Istanbul, was commissioned by the Ottoman Sultan Mahmud II (reg. 1808–1839) and constructed between 1823 and 1826 by the imperial Armenian-Ottoman architect Krikor Balyan (1764–1831). Built to replace an earlier mosque destroyed by fire, its name, meaning approximately 'Mosque of Victory', commemorates Mahmud II's military reforms and victories. With its slender twin minarets and richly articulated Baroque and Empire-style architecture, the mosque became a prominent landmark on the Bosphorus waterfront.

description_block:
A Collection of Clocks and Watches for the Ottoman MarketA gilt-brass mantle clock designed by Adolphe-Victor Geoffroy-Dechaume accompanied by an original design drawing 
France, second half of the 19th Century
the 3.5 inch dial with enamelled-copper Arabic numerals, the case decorated in openwork with paired birds and palmettes, flanked by confronting dragons and surmounted by an openwork crest, inscribed 'GEOFFROY DECHAUME' to lower right, on a marble base, the twin train striking movement striking the hours and half hours on a polished bell mounted to the backplate; the design in pencil and watercolour on paper 
44.5 cm. high; the design 180 x 270 mm.(2)

For another example of this model, see the Garniture persane in the Musée des Arts Décoratifs, Paris, (inv. 2016.19.1–5), comprising a clock, a pair of two-light candelabra and two tazze, in gilt and silvered bronze, enamel and marble. The museum dates the garniture to circa 1852 and identifies Adolphe-Victor Geoffroy-Dechaume (1816–1892) as sculptor and Auguste-Maximilien Delafontaine (1813–1892) as founder, recording that it was executed by Delafontaine after designs by Geoffroy-Dechaume. The two men had collaborated from 1847, producing a series of works inspired by medieval and Islamic art. Geoffroy-Dechaume's accounts record the delivery to Delafontaine in 1852 of the design for a 'pendule dite persane', a drawing which is reported to remain in the Geoffroy-Dechaume archive at the Cité de l'Architecture et du Patrimoine, Paris. The same archive contains, according to the Musée des Arts Décoratifs, dozens of graphic studies and measured drawings of interlace, arabesques and friezes of stylised birds derived from the Islamic repertoire, documenting Geoffroy-Dechaume's researches for the garniture; a preparatory drawing for one of the accompanying tazze is also preserved and illustrated by the Cité de l'Architecture. The design is further documented in De plâtre et d'or: Geoffroy-Dechaume (1816–1892), sculpteur romantique de Viollet-le-Duc, exh. cat., Musée d'Art et d'Histoire Louis Senlecq, L'Isle-Adam, 1998, p. 88, figs. 25–26. See also Musée des Arts Décoratifs, Paris, Garniture persane composée d'une pendule, de deux candélabres et de deux coupes (inv. 2016.19.1–5).

description_block:
A post-Nasrid bone-inlaid taracea casket 
Spain, 16th Century or later
of rectangular form on four square feet, inlaid in the intarsia technique with bone, silver and wood with carved colonnades to the lid and body enclosing stellate motifs and arabesques in relief to the spandrels, striped inlay to rim of lid 
10.4 x 11.4 x 21 cm.

The Nasrids developed a distinct aesthetic defined by elaborate geometric motifs which evolved from North African and Iberian sources. It was in particular the Almoravids and Almohads whose courtly commissions incorporated these micromosaics, later coined by the Spanish as taracea from the Arabic tarsi or 'incrustation'. These Maghrebi dynasties had themselves borrowed the technique from earlier 10th century traditions, most famously evidenced in the minbar of the Great Mosque of Cordoba dated to the period of al-Hakim II (r.961-978 AD) (Jerrilyn D. Dodds, Al-Andalus: the Art of Islamic Spain, New York 1992, p. 373).

description_block:
The Alhambra Collection: Part IAn early photograph of the Court of the Lions (Patio de los Leones), The Alhambra 
Granada, Spain, mid to late 1840s
plain toned salted paper print, untrimmed and
unmounted

198 x 286 mm.

Provenance
Sotheby's, Valuable Printed Books and Maps, 16 November 2006, lot 129.

One of the earliest known photographs of the Alhambra, this anonymous image predates the photographs taken by Charles Clifford (1819–1863), who settled in Madrid in 1850 and photographed the palace in 1854 (see lots 142-145). The present image was printed from an unwaxed calotype negative. The absence of watermarks or other characteristic paper marks, together with the lack of visible low-density defects within the image area, indicates that the print is contemporary with the production of the negative. On the verso, in one corner, is a fragmentary ink stamp, too incomplete to be deciphered, which may relate to the photographer, their agent, the print seller or the paper supplier.

description_block:
The Alhambra Collection: Part IBisson FrÃ¨res, Choix D'Ornements Arabes de L'Alhambra, a rare copy of the first photographic publication devoted to the Alhambra 
Paris, Gide et J. Baudry, 1853
first edition, half-title, 12 albumen prints of architectural detail, each mounted on card with printed caption, contemporary green morocco-backed boards, spine in compartments gilt 
folio (380 x 290mm.)

Provenance
Acquired at Sotheby's Valuable Printed Books and Maps, 16 November 2006, lot 131.

Full title: Choix d'ornaments Arabes de l'Alhambra offrant dans leur ensemble une synthèse de l'ornementation Mauresque en Espagne au XIIIe siècle reproduits en photographs.

The first photographic publication devoted to the Alhambra, this work represents the earliest publication issued by the Bisson brothers and is also the first to incorporate albumen prints produced from albumen-on-glass negatives. The twelve photographs, numbered consecutively from 1 to 12 and each bearing the title Alhambra, are accompanied by the printed credit 'Bisson Frères Photog./Gide et J. Baudry, Editeurs/Imp. Photog. Lemercier, Paris on their mounts.

The work is exceptionally rare, with only five copies traced in institutional collections: the Library of Congress, Washington, DC; the New York Public Library; the Institut national d'histoire de l'art (Collection Jacques Doucet), Paris; the Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris; and Cambridge University Library.

The importance of the publication was recognised in the exhibition devoted to the Bisson brothers held in Paris and Essen in 1999, for which the copy belonging to the Bibliothèque Nationale de France was selected for display. For further discussion, see B. Marbot et al., Les frères Bisson photographes, de flèche en cime 1840–1870, Paris, Bibliothèque Nationale de France, and Essen, Museum Folkwang, 1999.

description_block:
The Alhambra Collection: Part IA photograph of The Gate of Justice (Puerta de la Justicia), The Alhambra by Charles Clifford (1819-63) 
Granada, Spain, 1859
albumen print, blindstamp credit, numbered '4' in red ink to lower right, misattributed to 'Laurent' and other miscellaneous annotations in later hand in pencil on mount 
293 x 410 mm.; the card mount 463 x 633 mm.

Provenance
Christie's, Photographs, 19 May 2004, lot 83.

Charles Clifford (1819–1863) was one of the foremost photographers working in 19th Century Spain and an important pioneer of architectural photography. He settled in Madrid in 1850 and travelled extensively throughout Spain, recording its monuments, landscapes and major public works. In 1858 he was appointed photographer to Queen Isabella II (reg. 1833-1868), subsequently accompanying the royal court on a number of official journeys. His large-format photographs, made from paper and later wet-collodion negatives and generally issued as albumen prints, are particularly admired for their exceptional clarity, careful composition and sensitive treatment of monumental architecture. For an important album of photographs by Charles Clifford see lot 145. 

Charles Clifford photographed the Gate of Justice in 1859. A print of the same photograph is in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London (accession no. 47788). It formed part of his Recuerdos fotográficos de la visita de SS.MM. y AA.RR. a las provincias de Andalucía y Murcia en setiembre y octubre de 1862, comprising photographs taken between 1859 and 1862. Another example is illustrated in Lee Fontanella, Clifford en España: Un fotógrafo en la corte de Isabel II (1999), fig. 81.

provenance: Christie's, Photographs, 19 May 2004, lot 83.

Provenance

Charles Clifford (1819–1863) was one of the foremost photographers working in 19th Century Spain and an important pioneer of architectural photography. He settled in Madrid in 1850 and travelled extensively throughout Spain, recording its monuments, landscapes and major public works. In 1858 he was appointed photographer to Queen Isabella II (reg. 1833-1868), subsequently accompanying the royal court on a number of official journeys. His large-format photographs, made from paper and later wet-collodion negatives and generally issued as albumen prints, are particularly admired for their exceptional clarity, careful composition and sensitive treatment of monumental architecture. For an important album of photographs by Charles Clifford see lot 145. 

The Court of the Lions in the Alhambra, Granada, was among Clifford's most important architectural subjects. He photographed the court and its pavilions in several compositions, exploiting the contrast between the brilliant Andalusian sunlight, deep shadows and the exceptionally intricate Nasrid plasterwork and slender columns. 

A cropped print of the same photograph is preserved in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London (acc. no. 35:506), where it is dated 1859–62. It is likely, however, that the negative belongs to an earlier photographic campaign. Clifford was already photographing the Alhambra by 1854, and the V&A preserves another of his photographs of the Court of the Lions, dated to that year (acc. no. E.1249-2000). Clifford subsequently returned to Granada and photographed the Alhambra on further occasions, including in connection with Queen Isabella II's celebrated tour of Andalusia and Murcia in 1862. Another example is illustrated in Lee Fontanella, Clifford en España: Un fotógrafo en la corte de Isabel II (1999), fig. 50.

description_block:
The Alhambra Collection: Part ITwo photographs of painted gesso plaques inspired by the Lindaraja Hall (Mirador de Lindaraja) of The Alhambra by Charles Clifford (1819-63) 
Granada, Spain, circa 1859
albumen prints, the first with blindstamp credit, on card mount, pencil inscription to lower right of mount 'Ventana Sala Albencerages. Alhambra'; the second with blindstamp credit to lower left 
201 x 217 mm.; the card mount 485 x 639 mm.; and 202 x 362 mm.

Provenance
Christie's, Photographs, 19 May 2004, lot 87 (one photograph).

These photographs depict painted gesso models of architectural details inspired by the Lindaraja Hall in the Alhambra's Palace of the Lions, constructed under Muhammad V (reg. 1354–59 and 1362–91). One presents a triple arcade beneath four pierced windows; the other isolates a single scalloped arch beneath two windows. The models belong to the 19th Century practice of reproducing the Alhambra's ornament, closely associated with Rafael Contreras (1824–1890), who was appointed restorer of the palace in 1847 and established a workshop producing plaster casts and scale models. The Victoria and Albert Museum holds another photograph by Clifford of the same triple-arched model catalogued as 'Lindaraja Hall: detail of arches and lattices. Gypsum model' (acc. no. 35514); and another example of the same photograph of the single-arched example ('Alhambra, model of a Mirador de Lindaraja', acc. no. 35513). Both are dated to circa 1859.
