description_block:
The Alhambra Collection: Part IEspaÃ±a: Recuerdos de Viaje, A rare album of photographs by Charles Clifford (1819-63) 
Spain, circa 1854-1862
44 albumen prints, the folio album of black cloth with leather spine, gilt embossed title to spine and to cover, the 42 album pages, 40 with one albumen print to one side, 2 with two albumen prints to one side, with original pen captions and later pencil numbering, some albumen prints with Charles Clifford blindstamp, the original album pages removed from original binding and mounted and rebound in two modern albums with marbled paper covers, brown leather spine and edges, applied black leather panel to each spine with gilt embossed title 
the original album covers 42 x 55.5 cm, the pages 38.3 x 54.5 cm.; the modern albums 54.4 x 65.5 cm.(3)

Provenance
Acquired in Paris in 2003.

Charles Clifford (1819–1863) was one of the principal photographers to document Spain's monuments during the early years of photography. Established in Madrid in 1850, he travelled extensively through the country, recording historic buildings, works of art and major engineering projects. His association with the Spanish court included photographic commissions connected with the royal journeys of 1860 and 1862. The latter, through Andalusia and Murcia, provided an important occasion for photographing the monuments of southern Spain under the patronage of Isabella II (reg. 1833–1868).

The present album, España: Recuerdos de viaje, contains a substantial group of Alhambra photographs, including general views, the Court of the Myrtles, the Court of the Lions, galleries, doorways and studies of ornament, together with the Generalife. Related photographs survive in major institutional collections. The Royal Collection holds Clifford's Alberca Court, dated circa 1858 (RCIN 2700098), while the British Library preserves a view of the fountain and pavilion in the Court of the Lions dated October 1862 (1704.d.9(55)). These examples demonstrate that Clifford's Alhambra photographs were made over several campaigns.

The architectural details are particularly relevant to the 19th Century study and reproduction of Alhambra ornament. The British Library's photograph of the Sala de Lindaraja, dated 1858 (1704.d.9(37)), is catalogued with the suggestion that it depicts a model by Rafael Contreras (1826–1890), rather than the original architecture. This provides an important comparison for the Lindaraja study in the present album and connects Clifford's photography with the production of architectural replicas (see also lot 144). The inclusion of such models places the album at the intersection of architectural documentation and the reproduction of ornament, through which the Alhambra's designs became available for study beyond Granada. The Córdoba and Seville photographs extend the album's coverage to the Mosque of Córdoba, the Giralda, the Alcázar and Casa de Pilatos, encompassing both buildings constructed under Muslim rule and the subsequent use of Islamic forms in Mudéjar architecture. 

Other Clifford albums survive, although their contents vary. The Royal Collection's two-volume Photographic Souvenir of Spain, published in 1861, contains 159 photographs (RCIN 2700021 and 2700109). The British Library holds Photographic Views in Spain, a bound collection of 98 albumen prints (1704.d.9), while the Biblioteca Tomás Navarro Tomás, Madrid, preserves a 92-print album commemorating the royal visit to Andalusia and Murcia in 1862 (SXIX/306870). 

The Royal Armoury section of the present lot includes the photograph captioned 'Yelmo del Rey Boabdil'. The helmet appears to be the sallet now identified as belonging to Philip the Handsome (reg. 1506), attributed to the Negroli workshop, Milan, circa 1496 (Real Armería, D.13). Its Islamic-inspired decoration explains the 19th Century misconception that it belonged to the last Nasrid Sultan of Granada, and adds an interesting counterpart to the architectural photographs.

The album is a rare and substantial survival of early photography of the Alhambra, bringing panoramic views, courtyard studies and close examinations of ornament into a sustained architectural sequence. Its significance extends beyond Granada: the photographs of Córdoba, Seville and the Royal Armoury place the Nasrid palace within a wider account of Spain's Islamic heritage and its artistic legacy. Preserved together, these images offer an important record of both Clifford's photographic achievement and the 19th Century formation of the Alhambra's international reputation.

The Alhambra Collection: Part IVoyage en Espagne: L'Alhambra, A rare album of photographs of the Alhambra by Charles Mauzaisse (1823-1885) 
Granada, Spain, circa 1860-70
24 albumen prints, captions in pen and ruled margins, green leather binding with marbled endpapers, fitted storage box 
each photograph 181 x 256 mm. approx.; the album 352 x 400 mm.

Provenance
Acquired in Paris in 2003.

Charles Mauzaisse (1823–1885) was a French photographer established in Granada by 1857. He produced portraits and views of the city and its monuments for the growing market of travellers and collectors, with the Alhambra forming a principal subject of his work. His connections with Granada's artistic circles are documented by his photograph of the Madrazo family in the palace's Court of the Golden Room, taken on 31 August 1871 and now preserved in the Museo Nacional del Prado (HF00878). His architectural photographs belong to the early commercial recording of Granada, alongside those of visiting photographers such as Charles Clifford (1819–1863).

The attribution of the present album to Charles Mauzaisse is supported by a closely comparable album in the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (inv. RP-F-2007-41), comprising thirty-six albumen prints of the Alhambra and catalogued as attributed to 'C. Maufsaise,' an erroneous rendering of Mauzaisse's name. Most significantly, the photograph of the Alhambra vase entitled 'Vase Arabe' in the present album (see also lot 147) is from the same negative as a print in the Rijksmuseum (inv. RP-F-2007-41-29). Other prints from the same negatives in the Rijksmuseum album include the 'Porte du Vin', the 'Tombeaux des Rois Catholiques' and the 'Bas-relief du palais de Charles (cinq)'. The Rijksmuseum album also contains many of the subjects represented in the present volume, including the Court of the Lions, the Generalife, the Halls of the Ambassadors, Abencerrajes, Justice and the Two Sisters, and the Mirador de Lindaraja. This substantial correspondence in photographic repertoire, together with the confirmed repetition of several negatives provides persuasive support for the attribution. The architectural state recorded in the present photographs, including the distinctive glazed dome installed over the eastern pavilion of the Court of the Lions during Rafael Contreras's restoration of 1859, is consistent with a date in the 1860s, although this feature remained in place until 1934

155 x 240 mm.; the mount 250 x 324 mm.

Charles Mauzaisse (1823–1885) was a French photographer and painter who first visited Granada in January 1857, subsequently establishing a photographic studio in the city by 1859. Among the earliest photographers to recognise the commercial potential of the Alhambra, he produced an extensive series of architectural views for travellers and collectors, remaining active in Granada until at least 1879. The present lot depicts the famous 'Alhambra' or 'Gazelle' vase, produced in Spain during the rule of the Nasrid Dynasty in the 14th Century. It was rediscovered in the late 18th Century at the Alhambra and by the mid 19th Century had become an icon of Spain's Islamic past, being reproduced by numerous potters of the time including Theodore Deck. Another copy of the photograph is in the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, and is attributed to C. Maufsaise, an erroneous rendering of Mauzaisse's name (obj. no. RP-F-2007-41-29). An album of photographs including the same photograph and also attributed to Mauzaisse is lot 146 in this sale.

description_block:
The Alhambra Collection: Part IAn album of photographs compiled by Major Herbert Cecil Money (1857â1939) on his travels to Malta, Greece, Italy, Spain (including Granada and the Alhambra), Morocco, Palestine and Syria 
circa 1889
60 albumen prints, some with inscribed dates (between March and August 1889) and captions, the album in contemporary red cloth, half leather 
each approx. 263 x 215 mm.; the album 377 x 273 mm.

Provenance
Sotheby's, Natural History, Travel, Atlases and Maps, 18 Nov 2008, lot 153 (part lot).

Herbert Cecil Money (1857–1939) was a British Royal Marines officer who eventually attained the rank of Major-General. Born on the 20th of September 1857, he entered the Royal Marines at Chatham in 1876 and subsequently saw distinguished active service during the Anglo-Egyptian War of 1882, participating in the actions at Kassassin and Tel-el-Kebir. At Kassassin on the 9th of September, Money and Captain Roger Pine-Coffin (1845-1921) led a successful charge by the Royal Marines against an Egyptian artillery position, capturing two Krupp guns; Money was specially mentioned in despatches for his gallantry. He returned to Egypt and the Sudan in 1884, serving at Suakin. 

By the date of the present album, 1889, Money was a Major in the Royal Marines. The album opens with a photograph, captioned 'H.M.S. "BENBOW", Malta, Mar: 1889', showing the recently completed Admiral-class battleship Benbow, which had been commissioned in June 1888 for service with the Mediterranean Fleet. Although Money's precise connection with the vessel remains to be established, its prominent position at the beginning of the album, together with the dated Malta inscription, provides an important context for the journey recorded in the photographs. 

The album subsequently forms an extensive visual record of travel through the Mediterranean and Near East, containing photographs of Malta, Greece, Italy and Spain, including Granada and the Alhambra, as well as Morocco, Palestine and Syria. Combining commercially produced photographs and amateur prints perhaps by Money himself, it reflects both the flourishing market for travel photography in the later 19th Century and the travels of a serving Royal Marine officer. The sequence concludes, intriguingly, with a photograph of Dartmouth, perhaps marking Money's return to England at the end of the journey.

A particularly well-documented episode in Money's journey is his visit to Granada on the 24th and 25th of July, 1889. The photographs themselves preserve an unusually precise record of his movements, several being inscribed in Money's hand with the dates. His selection ranges from a large panoramic view of Granada and views across the old town, to the celebrated commercial photographs of Rafael Garzón Rodríguez (1863–1923), including the Alhambra's Court of the Lions, Hall of the Abencerrajes and Tower of the Captive, together with a striking interior of a cave dwelling at Sacromonte. The group is therefore more than a conventional assemblage of Alhambra views. Money's dated annotations anchor the photographs to an identifiable two-day visit and show him purchasing contemporary photographs in Granada as a record of places he had personally seen. The inclusion of Garzón is particularly appropriate. One of the leading photographers of Granada and the Alhambra in the late 19th Century, Garzón developed a substantial business supplying photographs to the growing international tourist market, and the present group captures this trade at an early stage in its development.

Money's subsequent career included service as Senior Officer of Marines in the Mediterranean Fleet from 1897 to 1899 and active service during the South African War. He was appointed Companion of the Order of the Bath (C.B.) in 1902 and was ultimately promoted to Major-General in 1910.

Enrique Linares García (1866 – circa 1930) was a Granada antiquarian, photographer and producer of architectural models, born in the city on 20 June 1866. Together with his brother Abelardo, he ran The Old Curiosity Shop, a business closely associated with the burgeoning market for photographs (see lot 152), antiquities and reproductions of Andalusian architecture created for the increasingly international tourist trade. Linares belonged to a generation of Granada craftsmen and dealers who capitalised upon the enormous 19th Century enthusiasm for the Alhambra. His workshop, recorded at 7 Plaza Nueva, followed the precedent established by Rafael Contreras and his celebrated workshop of architectural casts and models, alongside competitors including Diego Fernández Castro and Rafael Rus Acosta. Linares's activities extended beyond the manufacture and sale of architectural models to photography. Surviving signed and numbered models indicate that the workshop maintained a repertoire of repeatable designs, of which the present No. 51 was among the most ambitious in scale.

description_block:
The Alhambra Collection: Part IAn impressive painted gesso and alabaster Alhambra plaque by Rafael Contreras MuÃ±oz (1826â1890) 
Granada, Spain, 19th Century
of rectangular form, depicting a double arched doorway within an archway, decorated in gilt and polychrome in the Nasrid style, alabaster column and threshold, inscribed within mould to right of arch 'De la ALHAMBRA por Contreras', painted and gilded wood frame, printed Contreras label to reverse 
53 x 80 cm. including frame

Rafael Contreras Muñoz (1826–1890), architect and restorer of the Alhambra, was instrumental in popularising its architecture through highly detailed plaster models and reductions produced by his Granada workshop. This plaque belongs to this important 19th Century tradition of architectural souvenirs, which influenced subsequent Granada makers including Enrique Linares García (1866-c.1930) and Diego Fernández Castro (1847-1920).

The label to the reverse confirms that the present model reproduces one of the great lateral arches of the Hall of Comares at one-twelfth scale. The hall was commissioned under the Nasrid sultan Yusuf I (reg. 1333–1354), whose name appears among the inscriptions reproduced on the model. The full label reads:

MODELO 
DE LOS GRANDES ARCOS LATERALES DE LA SALA DE COMARES
EN LA ALHAMBRA, 
á la dozava parte de la escala original. Los mosaicos y ornamentos de esta sala son de los mas bellos del PALACIO ARABE: véase á propósito esta inscripcion de su recinto: "Loor á Dios. Aventajo á las mas hermosas con mi adorno y mi diadema, y se me inclinan amorosamente los luceros desde el zodiaco." 
Sobre este modelo se encuentran las siguientes: 
"¡Oh Dios; para tí las alabanzas constantemente; para tí las acciones de gracia incesantemente!" 
"La gloria perenne á Dios. El imperio perpetuo á Dios único." 
"Solo Dios es vencedor". — "Bendicion". — "Gloria á nuestro Señor Abul Hachach." 
"Sobre su familia salud y paz. Di: yo me refugio al Señor de la aurora, huyendo de la maldad de sus criaturas, y de los males de la noche oscura cuando nos sorprende, y de la maldad de las que soplan en los nudos y de........." 
En el reverso de este arco se lee: 
"Me vistió mi Señor, el favorecido de Dios, Yúsuf, con un traje de gloria é hizo de mí el trono de su Imperio." 
Reduccion hecha por CONTRERAS, restaurador de la Alhambra en GRANADA, el cual conserva la propiedad de estos modelos.

The Alhambra Collection: Part IA painted gesso and alabaster Alhambra plaque 
Granada, Spain, 19th Century
of rectangular form, depicting an arcade, decorated in the Nasrid style, alabaster columns and threshold, backed by a photograph depicting the Court of the Lions, maroon velvet frame 
54.6 x 71.2 cm. including frame

The Court of the Lions (Patio de los Leones) forms the celebrated centrepiece of the Nasrid Palace of the Lions, constructed principally under Sultan Muhammad V (reg. 1354–59 and 1362–91). The photograph incorporated into the present model appears to derive from a negative taken by Charles Clifford (1819–1863) during his visit to Granada in October 1862. The distinctive glazed dome visible beyond the Fountain of the Lions had been added to the eastern pavilion by Rafael Contreras (1824–1890) in 1859. Clifford photographed the newly altered Court of the Lions in 1862 as part of his series recording the royal visit to Andalusia and Murcia.

Rafael Rus Acosta (circa 1846-1912) was a Granada craftsman specialising in decorative architectural models inspired by the Alhambra. His workshop was among those that developed the commercial tradition established by Rafael Contreras (1824–1890), producing reduced-scale reproductions of Nasrid architectural ornament for visitors and collectors. Asun González Pérez identifies Rus among the Granada model-makers active from the late 19th into the early 20th Century and attributes the present lot to him.

description_block:
A large gold temple offering or token depicting Hanuman making obeisance to Rama (ramtanka) 
India, possibly 16th/ 17th Century
of concave circular form, struck with Rama enthroned with Sita and flanked by attendants, Hanuman kneeling before him with monkey attendants 
6.1 cm. diam.; 100 g.

Provenance
Private UK collection since the 1970s.

Indian Hindu temple tokens, commonly known as Rama-tankas or Ramatankas, were produced in gold, silver and base metals as devotional objects rather than currency. Frequently depicting scenes from the Ramayana, particularly Rama and Sita enthroned with Hanuman and other attendants, they were associated with temple worship, pilgrimage and the presentation of votive offerings. Gold examples, sometimes of considerable size and weight, were particularly prestigious and may have been commissioned as offerings to temples or for private religious devotion. A distinctive feature of some early examples is their concave or cup-shaped (scyphate) form, occasionally with an undecorated reverse. The tradition is generally associated with southern India and the Deccan, particularly the Vijayanagara and post-Vijayanagara periods, although dating individual examples remains difficult. For a smaller gold example dated to the 16th/ 17th Century depicting a very similar scene, see the British Museum (inv. no. 1890,0604.82).

provenance: Private UK collection since the 1970s.

Private UK collection, acquired by the vendor's mother in the 1980s.

Hair-braid ornaments of this type were worn by women in South India, attached to and extending along the plait, combining personal adornment with auspicious and protective imagery. The present example is surmounted by Krishna subduing the multi-headed serpent Kaliya (Kaliya Mardana), an episode symbolising the triumph of divine power over destructive forces. The adjoining kirtimukha or 'face of glory' motifs also have an apotropaic function and occur widely in South Indian temple architecture and jewellery. Such elaborate gold braid ornaments formed part of festive and bridal dress, the long articulated form following and embellishing the wearer's plait.

A silver-hilted steel sword (tulwar) presented by Ahmed Izzet Pasha (1864-1937), former Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire and later Minister of Foreign Affairs, to Lieutenant J. B. Rickatson-Hatt in Constantinople in September 1921 
India, 19th Century
the steel blade of curved form with flattened spine, becoming double-edged towards the point, engraved to one side 'PRESENTED TO LIEUT. J.B. RICKATSON-HATT / COLDSTREAM GUARDS / BY MARSHAL IZZET PASHA / GRAND VIZIER OF TURKEY / CONSTANTINOPLE, SEPTEMBER 1921', maker's stamp and punched inscriptions to the other, the silver hilt with engraved rosettes and foliate decoration, hinged element to pommel of floral form, the wood scabbard clad in velvet and mounted in silver engraved and decorated in openwork with floral and foliate bands, rosettes and floral interlace 
73.5 cm. long

Provenance
Formerly in the collection of Bernard Rickatson-Hatt (1897-1966).

Bernard Rickatson-Hatt, an officer of the Coldstream Guards during the First World War, exemplifies the transition from traditional military service to the more ambiguous spheres of intelligence and international influence that characterised the early twentieth century. Following active service on the Western Front, he was subsequently posted to Constantinople. In the unsettled conditions of the post-Ottoman city, then a focal point of Allied occupation and political intrigue, Rickatson-Hatt undertook duties connected with military intelligence and internal security, ostensibly serving as a provost marshal. This experience, acquired in a milieu defined by competing powers and covert negotiation, appears to have been formative in shaping his later career. He was presented this sword in 1921 by Ahmed Izzet Pasha who had been a general during Wolrd War I and was at the time Minister for Foreign Affairs under Sultan Mehmed VI (reg. 1918-1922).

After leaving the army, he entered journalism and rose to prominence within Reuters, eventually serving as editor-in-chief. In this capacity he operated at the intersection of information, diplomacy, and influence, a role that drew upon the discretion and strategic awareness developed during his earlier service. His career coincided with a period in which the control and dissemination of news carried increasing political significance, and he became known for his ability to navigate these complexities.

Rickatson-Hatt was also acquainted with Ian Fleming, whose own background in intelligence informed the creation of James Bond. Although not identifiable as a direct prototype for Bond, Rickatson-Hatt belonged to the same cultivated and discreet milieu of internationally experienced figures whose careers spanned military service, intelligence work, and high-level communication. His experiences, particularly those in Constantinople, resonate with the cosmopolitan and politically charged settings that would later characterise Fleming's fiction.

description_block:
An unusual contemporary manuscript account, by an anonymous British officer, of the British conquest of Dutch coastal territories in Ceylon, covering the period from June 29th 1795 to February 29th 1796, and with a thirty-page description of the 1793 siege of Pondicherry by the British 
South India and Ceylon, [1796]
pp. 50, five blanks at end, marbled paper covers 
318 x 205 mm.

An unpublished eye-witness account of the British conquest of the Dutch coastal territories in Ceylon during the Napoleonic Wars. Following the French Revolution in 1789, the Netherlands had increasingly fallen under French influence, culminating in the proclamation of the pro-French Batavian Republic in 1795. The British launched this invasion to prevent the Dutch colony of Ceylon falling into French hands – a prime example of political upheavals in Europe having a direct impact in Asia.

This account is anonymous, the author only describing himself at one point as 'the journalist of the 73rd Flank Companies'. Each British Army regiment had two flank companies made up of its elite troops. Judging by the emphasis throughout on details of enemy fortifications, building batteries, and ordnance in general, the author was an officer in charge of either an engineers or artillery company. In this campaign he served under Captain Barbut who would later be taken prisoner and executed during the First Kandyan War (1803-1805). The same author has described his regiment's earlier experience taking part in the British capture of the French settlement of Pondicherry in 1793. From Ceylon the 73rd returned to India to take part in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War and the capture of Seringapatam in 1799, before returning to Britain in 1806.

The journal begins with the assembling of the British expeditionary force on the Coromandel coast under Colonel James Stuart. On 29th June 1795 the 73rd Regiment received orders to march from its station at Pondicherry via Cuddalore, Chidambaram, and the Danish colony of Tranquebar, where 'Several Danish officers came to our tents, and told us a number of fibs with the greatest effrontery'. At Nagore, which they reached on 11th July, they were joined by the 71st Regiment of Foot. On 24th July the 73rd embarked at Negapatam on board HMS Diomede in a thirteen-strong fleet. On 2nd August the Diomede struck a rock and sank, but 'it did not however alter the plans of our commanders; on the contrary all the arrangements were made for landing tomorrow morning, as if nothing had happened'. The troops were transferred to HMS Heroine and Suffolk, and the whole army disembarked near Trincomalee before dawn on 3rd August 'without the smallest opposition or difficulty'. But Major Fornbauer, the Dutch commander of the Fort, initially refused to surrender, citing a bureaucratic technicality. The letter from Colombo ordering him to allow British troops to enter was, he claimed, not mandatory but 'informal', having been signed only by the Governor and not by the Governor and Council. The nearby more powerfully-gunned Fort Ostenburg took longer to capture – the author surveyed its fortifications for weak points, describing it as having:
four bastions, a cavalier, and citadel redoubt. 3 of the curtains are covered by the sea, the one on the west face has a sod ravelin, with twelve embrasures – the rampart of the rest of the Fort is built of stone, but the rampart is in several parts of sod – the ditch and glacis are both sod, as is also the palisade round it – the dry ditch has a palisade and hedge in its center.

To breach the walls required large gun emplacements to be built under enemy fire:
20th Aug. Our howitzers had no sooner opened which they did between 7 and 8 than they completely fulfilled their intention by drawing the enemies [sic] fire in a great measure from our working parties at the breaching battery ... 21st Aug. Lieut Quayle received no damage from a 12 pound shot, which made a hole in the crown of his hat ... 23rd Aug. At 20 minutes after 5 this morning our three batteries opened upon the fort... Every shot of the very first discharge went thro as many embrasures, and in a very few minutes there was hardly a man to be seen on the works, or a gun fired from them.
On 31st August the Trincomalee and Ostenburg forts both surrendered (British losses suffered in their capture are recorded as are the articles of surrender). Swift capitulations followed as the British troops marched southwards via Jaffnapatam, Mannar, and Chilaw near Negombo. On 12th February 1796 they finally caught a first glimpse of Colombo and its defenders:
The country opened towards the sea, and not only gave us a view of Colombo, but of 600 Dutch and Malays drawn up to receive us, with a bamboo fence in their front. They gave us their fire while we were forming up by files to front them, but this being done, Captain Barbut ordered his 6 companies (about three hundred men) to charge, which they did, and the enemy broke, and fled in confusion, so that we were able to bayonet but a few of them, when we were ordered to halt, being little more than two thousand yards from the Fort.
On 16th February Johan Gerard van Angelbeek, the Dutch Governor of Ceylon, surrendered Colombo:
The 6 Flank Companies went in alone, but found the Dutch garrison so drunk, mutinous and riotous, that the other corps and guns were sent for in order to keep them in awe. Upon this the Dutch marched out (three thousand two hundred well armed men of which 1200 were Europeans) with all the honours of war, and grounded their arms on the glacis of the place. It was impossible for men to have behaved worse than the Dutch garrison marching out. They did not appear to be under the smallest control. Indeed their officers exerted themselves very little to put a stop to the irregularities of their men.
By contrast, the strict British Army discipline was harshly enforced:
A drum head general court martial sat and tried a man of the 77th Grenadiers immediately on getting into the Fort for having robbed a Dutch man of his watch. He was sentenced 1000 lashes and received 950. – This was the only irregularity committed by the British troops in taking possession of the city and fort of Colombo.
The author proudly listed the 876 pieces of ordnance captured during the campaign, but his final entry stressed the most significant outcome of the expedition:
Feb 29th. It is said that cinnamon and spices taken here at Colombo and Point De Galle may be valued at 30 lacks of rupees, or 300,000 £.
In removing the French threat, a considerable economic benefit to Britain had been gained.

The journal is followed by an unpublished account of the part played by the Flank Companies of the 73rd (Highland) Regiment of Foot in the 1793 siege of Pondicherry. From a small trading post established in 1674, Pondicherry had grown in importance to become the chief settlement of French India. After its earlier capture by the British in 1761, it had been restored to France two years later under the terms of the Treaty of Paris ending the Seven Years' War. This second siege took place early on in the French Revolutionary Wars, the Convention Nationale having declared war on Britain on 1st February 1793, and was the last occasion on which Pondicherry changed hands during the eighteenth century. It would not be returned to French control until 1814. 

The anonymous author of this journal was an officer in charge of an engineers or artillery company in the Regiment. By the time of the siege of Pondicherry, the 73rd had already been in India for some twelve years. Sent out in 1781, it had taken part in the 1783 siege of Mangalore during the Second Anglo-Mysore War and the 1792 siege of Seringapatam during the Third. The regiment was still stationed at Pondicherry when ordered to march to Negapatam to take part in the conquest of the Dutch coastal territories in Ceylon (described above). 
Two epigraphs provided by the author, the first from Canto 3 of Voltaire's La Pucelle d'Orléans, a satirical poem on Joan of Arc: Qui me dirâ si nos ardents Français / Dans ce grand art, l'art affreux de la guerre, / Sont plus savants que l'entrepide Anglais?; and the second from Act III Scene 3 of Shakespeare's Richard II: 'He is come to ope the purple testament of bleeding war' - suggest some literary pretension and perhaps an intention to publish.
The manuscript opens with a description of the build-up of British troops for the siege under the command of Colonel Sir John Brathwaite, acting Commander-in-Chief of the Madras Army. The force comprised three British Army regiments (the 19th Light Dragoons and the 72nd and 73rd Regiments of Foot) plus a regiment of Madras Native Cavalry. On 28th June the march on Pondicherry began, and on 11th July the force set up camp 'within sight of Pondicherry flag staff, and about 3 miles and a half from that fortress'. The engineer/artillery officer author details the work of his men in reconnoitring the fort's defences from 14th to 17th July and then from 19th to 24th July 'clearing the ground' for a series of gun battery emplacements to be constructed. Altogether 107 pieces of ordnance were deployed, including sixteen 24-pounders and twenty-five 18-pounders, as well as mortars and howitzers. By 28th July Rear Admiral William Cornwallis, Commander-in-Chief of the East Indies Station, had also put in place a naval blockade:
The working and covering parties in front today had a beautiful view of the ships in the roads before Pondicherry, consisting of His Majesty's frigate The Minerva and three Indiamen commanded by the Honourable Admiral Cornwallis.
On 2nd August an exchange of letters took place between Colonel Brathwaite and Rear-Admiral Cornwallis and the Governor-General of French India, Colonel Dominique Prosper de Chermonte. Brathwaite wrote: 
Sir, I have received orders to dispossess the French of Pondicherry, and have in consequence encamped before the place with a force which gives me the strongest reason to hope for success. Conceiving it to be my duty to avoid all unnecessary effusion of blood, I summons you to surrender the place, with its garrison, artillery, and provisions, warlike stores, and all kinds of publick property.. If this is complied with, without delay, I promise life, and good treatment to individuals, and that no one shall be deprived of his private property.
Chermonte's polite but firm response was delivered the following day:
You inform me that you have received orders to take Pondicherry, the defence of which has been entrusted to me, and the brave troops I have under my command. You must be well aware that with soldiers such as we are nothing can over-balance what duty and honour command. I have therefore to acquaint you that it is our intention to defend it.
He wrote to Cornwallis in similar terms:
We perceive but too clearly how much embarrassments multiply around us, both by sea, and land; but you must know, Sir, that in our situation these only add to our resolutions of perseverance.
In the face of this French defiance, preparations for bombarding the fort intensified under cover of darkness. On 5th August a large working party of 14 companies of infantry and 500 lascars was employed in 'carrying gabions and fascines' and making 'pickets and mallets'. On 12th August Brathwaite met with his senior commanders to finalize plans for the attack:
The NW Bastion of Pondicherry having been fixed upon as the proper point of attack, ground was broke this evening in front of the Blancherie by His Majesty's 52nd Regiment and three battalions of sepoys directed by the commanding officer of the Left Wing, Lieut. Col. Maxwell. The detail for the enfilading battery, consisting of sepoys, a very heavy fire was kept up all night against this last detail, by which we lost a number of men, and Captain Galpine of the 73rd Regiment ... Heavy rain during this night – which interrupted the work much.
As the dangerous work continued, the author allowed a personal note to interrupt his narrative:
14th Aug. Soon after going to work this evening, the 73rd Regiment had to bewail the loss of one of its worthiest members, Lieutenant Todd, who was killed by the same cannon shot with two soldiers of the Regiment. A journal is not a place to express the poignancy of my feelings, on the occasion of losing a friend whose memory I shall ever revere.
A massive artillery barrage was launched on 22nd August and had an almost instantaneous effect. Within a few hours the French sued for peace:
The north battery opened upon the Fort consisting of 14, 24, and eighteen pounders with two mortars, and in two hours almost silenced every gun on the north face ... At about 5 [p.m.], a number of white flags were seen along the whole of the north face, our batteries ceased.
On 23rd August Brathwaite formally announced the news of Pondicherry's capitulation, and the author includes here the text of the seven articles of surrender. His account ends with a detailed return of the troops captured and casualties suffered. On the French side, 1,780 men surrendered, comprising 766 Europeans (including 121 officers) and 1,014 natives (including 29 officers). 165 artillery pieces were taken. On the British side, 37 Europeans and 56 natives were killed; and 87 Europeans and 97 natives wounded.

A manuscript map, Sketch Plan of the Remains of the Ancient City of Shevensamudra, and of the Cataracts of the River Cauvery at that place, by Thomas Fraser, an officer of engineers 
South India, Madras, dated December 1800
pen and ink and watercolour on two conjoined sheets of paper, single-ruled frame, with title, key, and compass arrow, latitude and longitude unmarked, caption title to reverse, vegetation, structures and water in green, pink and blue respectively, signed by Thomas Fraser and dated December 1800

Thomas Fraser (1776-1823) was an engineer officer who served in the fourth Anglo-Mysore War attached to the infantry. He fought at the siege of Seringapatam. He was briefly attached to the Mysore Survey, under the command of Colin Mackenzie, which surveyed Seringapatam in 1799, but he was forced to return to Madras after a few months because of illness. He most probably prepared our map in Madras for presentation, after a completed map or from rough sketches executed in 1799.

description_block:
A rare manuscript map, Sketch of the country lying between Seringapatam and Coimbetore, by Lieutenant John Warren (1769-1830), presented to Lady Henrietta Clive (1758-1830) 
South India, dated 1800
pen and ink and watercolour on a single sheet of paper, quadruple-ruled frame, with scale (1 inch to 5 miles), lines of longitude and latitude, and compass, title and dedication within pen and wash cartouches, routes picked out in blue watercolour, cities in pink, vegetation in green, with contours in pen and wash 
560 x 400 mm.

The map was drawn in the immediate aftermath of the fourth Anglo-Mysore war of 1799. It depicts the territory between the East India Company's land and the domain of the late Tipu Sultan. The artist, John Warren, was a prominent Anglo-French officer and surveyor; the recipient the wife of the governor of Madras.
John Warren (1769-1830), baptized Jean-Baptiste François Joseph de Warren, was the descendant of English Jacobite émigrés. He first served with Dillon's Irish regiment, but left France in 1791 following the revolution, and reached London in 1793. That year he emigrated to India, and spent the next four years as a struggling indigo planter at Bihar. In 1798 he purchased a commission in the 33rd Regiment of Foot, then commanded by Arthur Wellesley. Warren served with distinction under Colin Mackenzie at Seringapatam and in December 1799 Wellesley appointed him Assistant Surveyor to the Mysore Survey, in which capacity he served until 1802, when he joined Charles Lambton's Trigonometrical Survey. Warren continued in British service until 1814, when, upon the restoration of the French monarchy, he returned to France, where he was reinstated in the French army and inherited the title of Comte de Warren in 1816. He returned to India and retired to Pondicherry.

The Wellesley papers contain a note on a map prepared by Warren, dated 6th April 1800, of the same area; our copy, inscribed to Lady [Henrietta] Clive, would have been prepared after the April map by Warren as a gift. Lady Clive's husband, Edward Clive, served as Governor of Madras from 1798 to 1803; she joined him from 1798 to 1801.

A letter, dated 5th July [1800] to her husband mentions that 'Captain Warren has given me three very pretty drawings done by himself of the town and other views near Zundredroog which you will like to see', (Birds of Passage, p. 157). The officer in question is clearly the same Warren; other letters mention meeting Warren surveying and note his service with the 33rd, but he was not in fact promoted to captain until 1806.

A letter from Lord Hobart, the Governor of Madras, to Hugh Inglis, the Chairman of the East India Company, referring to Tipu Sultan and his renewed machinations in southern India 
Fort St. George, Madras, dated 30th March 1797
autograph manuscript on paper, four sides of text, one folded sheet, with envelope addressed to Hugh Inglis Esq/East India House/London 
222 x 184 mm. (folded)(2)

Robert Hobart, 4th Earl of Buckinghamshire (1760–1816), styled Lord Hobart from 1798 to 1804, was later Secretary of State for War and the Colonies from 1801 to 1804. He had begun his political career as an MP in the Irish House of Commons for Portarlington in Ireland (1784-1790) and thereafter for Armagh Borough (1790-1797). He acted as aide-de-camp to successive Lord Lieutenants of Ireland from 1784 onwards, and from 1789 to 1793 he was chief secretary to the Lord Lieutenant, exerting his influence to prevent any concessions to Roman Catholics.

In 1793 he became a member of the Privy Council, and appointed Governor of Madras. In 1798 he was recalled to England by the President of the Board of Control responsible for Indian affairs, and summoned to the House of Lords through a writ of acceleration in his father's junior title of Baron Hobart. Hobart, the capital of Tasmania, is named after him.

Sir Hugh Inglis, 1st Baronet (1744–1820) first went to India in 1762, and returned to England in 1775. He was chosen as a Director of the East India Company in 1784, and served as deputy-chairman from 1796 to 1797 and 1799–1800, and chairman from 1797 to 1798 and again from 1800 to 1801. In June 1801, he was created a baronet. In 1802 he was elected MP for Ashburton and held the seat until 1806.

Hobart begins by saying that the letter has been sent by a neutral ship which should reach England five weeks before the remainder of the Company's fleet. There follows a discussion of the loading of ships and monetary equivalents of their cargoes.

...We are making every preparation for an attack on Manilla, and I should hope with every prospect of success - although it would afford me real pleasure to have our enterprise put an end to, by intelligence of Peace, which we are looking for with very great anxiety. The Nizam is dying, and I am afraid the succession to him will be disputed. The Mahrattas are quarrelling among themselves amongst themselves and Tippoo has an army on foot waiting Events. The arrival of a French force, which he seems to expect, but which I think improbable, would unquestionably induce him to break with us, otherwise he will avoid it if possible - tho' if a fair opportunity should occur by which he may calculate on recovering a part of those possessions he relinquished at the last Peace either to the Nizam or to the Mahrattas, he will run some risk for that purpose. Perhaps an attentive observation of recent proceedings may have induced him to believe that nothing but an attack upon the Company's possessions can awaken our interference.
Before this letter can reach you, you will learn whether I remain in India or not - [...] I continue, I shall esteem myself much flattered by your private correspondence.

description_block:
A manuscript letter from the Duke of Wellington, addressed to his elder brother, Richard Wellesley, 1st Marquess Wellesley (1760-1842), regarding the seal of Tipu Sultan and its presentation as a gift to Queen Victoria 
London, 'at night', dated 8th April 1842
one sheet, folded, three sides of text, reverse with D. of Wellington 
181 x 115 mm. (folded)

The letter almost certainly refers to the seal of dark red cornelian, engraved in Persian with an inscription bearing the name Haidar and dated 1217 in the Mauludi calendar/AD 1788-89, in the Royal Collection, Windsor (RCIN 65358). The inscription around the edge roughly translates as 'God give me the victory as long as the sun and the moon shine'.

When Tipu's son Ghulam Muhammad and grandson Feroz Shah were in England in 1854, Queen Victoria granted them permission to visit Windsor to view the trophies of Seringapatam, which was captured by British forces in 1799. Among them was this seal, of which they made a wax impression under which they signed their names. This was then pasted into a book on the history of Mysore (RCIN 1197007) which Ghulam Muhammad presented to the Queen. It is recorded in the North Corridor Inventory of Windsor Castle with the note 'This seal is believed to have been the private seal of Tipoo Sahib.' The Royal Collection notes that it is 'believed to have been presented by Richard Wellesley, 1st Marquess Wellesley' - who had of course been Governor-General in India (1798-1805), and who had commanded the forces which had defeated Tipu in 1799.

The text reads:
My dear Wellesley
I have just now received your note of this day. I quite concur in your opinion of the Queen's intention to appropriate an apartment in Windsor for the reception of [...]
You presented to me the great seal of Tippoo Sultaun; which certainly ought to be deposited in the deposit [sic]. But you should present it to the Queen herself.
If however you should wish me to present the seal to Her Majesty, and will give your permission for my making mention thereof, I will present it, leaving with it in the report [?] that your kindness had wished you to present it to me; and that I had laid it at the feet of Her Majesty and be deposited in the apartment in Windsor Castle appropriated for the reception of [...]
I shall be very much obliged to you for the book which you intend to present to me.
I am going tomorrow morning to Buckingham Palace to attend the reception of the Lord Mayor by Her Majesty. But I hope to be able to go to Apsley House in the afternoon.
Believe me ever yours most affectionately

description_block:
Lieutenant-Colonel Mark Wilks, Historical sketches of the South of India, in an attempt to trace the history of Mysoor; from the origin of the Hindoo government of that state, to the extinction of the Mohammedan dynasty in 1799, 3 volumes 
London, Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme and Brown, 1817
first edition (but new 1820 impression of first volume), three volumes, pp. xxxvi, 517, [1]; xxiii, 580; xiv, 557, [1], 2 folding maps hand-coloured in outline, armorial bookplates of Christopher Turnor, Stoke Rochford Library, marbled endpapers, contemporary calf, spines richly gilt 
273 x 225 mm.(3)

Provenance
Christopher Turnor (1809-86), Conservative MP, Stoke Rochford Hall, Lincolnshire (armorial bookplates on front endpapers).

Full title: Historical sketches of the South of India, in an attempt to trace the history of Mysoor; from the origin of the Hindoo government of that state, to the extinction of the Mohammedan dynasty in 1799. Founded chiefly on Indian authorities collected by the author while officiating for several years as Political Resident at the Court of Mysoor.

Mark Wilks (circa 1760-1831) served the East India Company military from 1782 to 1808, as, among other posts, military secretary and ADC to Colonel James Stuart in the war against Tipu, and Private Secretary to the Governor, Lord Clive.

The three volumes comprise a detailed history of the Hindu Wadiyar dynasty which ruled Mysore from the decline of the Vijyanagara Empire in 1565 until its reduction to a vassal state under Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan. In the words of Sir James Mackintosh, the Recorder of Bombay and a fellow historian, it was 'the first book on Indian history founded on a critical examination of testimony and probability'.

Wilks was uniquely well-placed to compile such a history, having served as Political Resident at the Court of Mysore from 1803 to 1808. After gaining a cadetship in the East India Company's Madras Army in 1781, Wilks had filled a number of important posts: Adjutant at Fort St. George in 1788, Aide-de-Camp to Colonel James Stuart during the Third Anglo-Mysore War 1790-92, and in 1799 Private Secretary to the Governor of Madras, Lord Edward Clive.

Wilks's wide-ranging linguistic skills allowed him to access an impressive variety of sources. In addition to consulting East India Company documents in London as well as Madras, Wilks also used the large collection of manuscripts in Kannada and other South Indian languages amassed by Colin Mackenzie, the first Surveyor-General of India. Wilks even commissioned a new historical memoir of Mysore from 'Poornia, the present able and distinguished minister of Mysoor, and his intelligent assistant Butcherow', which was compiled from 'the best informed natives of the country who were known to possess family manuscripts or historical pieces'. Finally his knowledge of Persian enabled him to use the military memoirs compiled 'under my own direction' by Abba Ali, Haidar Ali's Field Secretary 'from the written memoirs, or oral statements, of two distinct assemblies of the oldest and most intelligent military officers of the late dynasty'. The work was largely compiled during Wilks's return voyage to Britain in 1808, ill-health having obliged him to leave India permanently.

description_block:
Krishnaraja Wadiyar III, Rajah of Mysore (reg. 1799â1868) 
by S. W. Reynolds, Engraver to the King, after A. Stuart, early 19th Century
mezzotint, parallel English and Cananese text and coat of arms of His Highness the Rajah of Mysoor in lower border 
660 x 430 mm. (sight)

After the final defeat of Tipu Sultan in 1799, Lord Wellesley restored the region's former Hindu rulers and installed the five-year-old Krishnaraja Wadiyar III on the Mysore throne on 30th June 1799 and placed him under his mother Lakshmi Devi's regency. The ceremony took place in a special pavilion constructed near the Lakshmiramana Swamy temple in Mysore. Lakshmi Devi managed to have Tipu's adviser Purnaiah (who had acted against his master Tipu) continue as the Dewan of Mysore with the instruction that he should be loyal to the new king till the latter himself attained the age of independence. This occurred in 1810, though the British Resident, Arthur Cole, mentioned as the dedicatee in the text below the image, was very much in control. This became the de facto reality in 1831, after disturbances and British accusations of irregularity in the Rajah's government, and the British took direct control. Literature and art flourished during the reign, however, and the Rajah himself wrote poetry and was a literary scholar.

Another example of this engraving is in the National Trust's collection at Powis Castle, Wales (NT 1180781).

description_block:
A Mughal gilt glass bottle 
Gujarat, 18th Century
of rectangular form with a domed shoulder tapering to a short cylindrical neck, decorated in gilt and gesso with floral sprays to each side, floral interlace to shoulders and vertical stripes to neck, diagonal seam to square base 
14 cm. high

This is a so-called 'case' bottle whose name and form originates from Dutch and German models which were designed to be stacked within compartments of a case or box. Produced largely in 18th Century Gujarat and Kutch, some were made in the factories of the Dutch East India Company. Case bottles were distinguished by the fact that they were blown in a two-part mould: the two triangular halves were fused together diagonally and the corners painted over to conceal the join. The only visible seam in an archetypical case bottle is a diagonal line under the base (Stefano Carboni, Glass from Islamic Lands: The Al-Sabah Collection, Kuwait National Museum, London: Thames & Hudson, 2001, p.389). For a set of similar case bottles, see Christie's, Art of the Islamic and Indian World, 7th October 2008, lot 230.

description_block:
A Mughal rock crystal scent bottle 
North India, 18th Century
of piriform, carved and decorated with floral sprays, foliate bands to base and neck, flowerhead to base, accompanying padded velvet box and note detailing provenance 
6 cm high.

Provenance
Private US collection, acquired by vendor's father in Jaipur, circa 1958. 

Under the reign of Shah Jahan, Mughal craftsmen reached new heights of technical virtuosity with carved rock crystal gaining a greater luxury status than jade in some courtly circles. The emperor's so-called 'floromania' saw craftsmen specialising in depictions of poppies, tulips, irises and lilies which would permeate rock-crystal production for years to come. Such motifs mimicked the perfumes held in these flasks, which would be worn by both Mughal men and women. For further discussion, see Welch, Stuart Cary, India: Art and Culture, 1300-1900, New York, Metropolitan Museum of Art, pp. 256-257.

For a Mughal rock-crystal cup with similar decoration, see Christie's, The Saeed Motamed Collection Part 1, 22nd April 2013, lot 307.

description_block:
An impressive spinel and gem-set enamelled gold bazuband later mounted as a bracelet 
Jaipur, North India, circa 1870
the bazuband of octagonal form, set with a large central octagonal-mixed cut spinel, surrounded by a band of rose-cut diamonds and a band of teardrop gem-stones on a blue enamelled ground, suspension loops to each side in the form of flowers set with rubies and rose-cut diamonds, with hinged openwork elements also in the form of flowers surmounted by a tripartide arch, decorated to the reverse in polychrome enamels with floral interlace and perching birds, the later bracelet straps comprising two strands of octagonal gold elements alternately set with rubies and gem-stones, decorated ensuite in polyhrome enamel, fitted box of Jagat Narain & Sons, New Delhi, India 
the bazuband 7.2 x 3.7 cm. including hinged elements; the spinel approximately 23.5 x 18.7 mm.; the bracelet 16.8 cm. long; 91.8 g.

Provenance
Private collection, Brazil. Acquired by the vendor's grandfather (1915-1973) in India in the 1940s. 

Accompanied by a report from the Brazilian Gemmological Association stating that the spinel is natural and weighs approximately 20.49 carats, classifying it as a 'rare gemstone due to its size'. Report number 1336, dated the 14th of June 1973.

The present lot was originally conceived as a bazuband, or upper-arm ornament, and appears to belong to the celebrated tradition of gold enamelling and gem-setting practised at Jaipur in the third quarter of the 19th Century. Particularly close comparisons for its polychrome enamel decoration are found among the works presented by Maharaja Sawai Ram Singh II of Jaipur (reg. 1835–80) to Albert Edward, Prince of Wales (1841–1910; later King Edward VII, reg. 1901–10) during the latter's visit to Jaipur in 1876. These include an enamelled gold covered cup and saucer, dated to circa 1870–75 in the Royal Collection (RCIN 11424.a–c), which has closely related floral and bird ornament, and an enamelled gold salver (RCIN 11469) also in the Royal Collection (see Kajal Meghani, Splendours of the Subcontinent: A Prince's Tour of India 1875–6, London, Royal Collection Trust, 2017, pp. 94–95 and 108–09). The covered cup and saucer has been tentatively associated with the Jaipur enameller Ghuma Singh, while the salver is recorded as the work of Ram Singh, demonstrating the exceptional quality of Jaipur enamel production during precisely the period at which the present lot is believed to have been made. 

At a considerably later date the bazuband was converted into a bracelet through the addition of the two double-strand gem-set gold straps. The completed bracelet is preserved in a purpose-made fitted case stamped 'JAGAT NARAIN & SONS JEWELLERS NEW DELHI, INDIA'. In conjunction with the provenance, according to which the jewel was acquired in India during the early 1940s, the fitted nature of the case provides compelling evidence that the adaptation had taken place by this period and raises the strong possibility that Jagat Narain & Sons either undertook the conversion themselves or supplied the bracelet in its newly adapted form. The resulting bracelet therefore documents two distinct moments in Indian jewellery manufacture: an important Jaipur bazuband of circa 1870–75 and its transformation into a bracelet for a 20th Century clientele some seventy years later.

North India, late 19th Century
of shallow rounded form, decorated in cobalt blue and turquoise on a white ground with the dragon, ostrich plumes and motto of the 98th Prince of Wales regiment to the centre, surrounded by floral sprays, a band of foliate motifs to border 
30 cm. diam.

Raised in Chichester in 1824, the men of the 98th were posted initially in South Africa, China and then in India from 1848-55. In the Punjab, they served in the Second Sikh War (1848-49), returning in 1857 to eventually join the Sittana Field Force in 1858. From 1876, the regiment was awarded the 'Prince of Wales' title. Shortly after, in 1880, they were stationed in India once more, merging with the 64th (2nd Staffordshire) Regiment of Foot.

Interestingly, the dragon traditionally featured in the regiment's insignia takes on a uniquely Indian aesthetic on this vessel. Its sloping head and snout recalls more the mythical makara than medieval and Celtic-inspired models.

description_block:
A photograph album commemorating the wedding of Princess Rohini Kumari of Ali Rajpur with Rajah Bahadur Narendra Singh of Sarila, depicting individual and group portraits, various ceremonies, large groups and processions 
Sarila, by K. L. Syed, State Photographer, Palanpur, 18th January 1945
25 gelatin silver prints, laid down on card album pages, front doublure with gold-stamped label of the State Photographer, front cover of red leather album and cover of box stamped in gold with the coat of arms of Ali Rajpur State, Central India, and the details of the event, lacking lower half of box 
236 x 288 mm. and slightly smaller; album 285 x 383 mm.; box 300 x 405 mm.

Raja Narendra Singh Sarila (1927–2011) was the last ruling prince of the state. He served as ADC to Lord Mountbatten during the crucial years of India's independence and partition. He later joined the Indian Foreign Service (IFS) and served as India's ambassador to several countries, including France and Spain. He was also an accomplished historian and author of the book The Shadow of the Great Game: The Untold Story of India's Partition, as well as Once a Prince of Sarila: of Palaces and Tiger-Hunts, of Nehrus and Mountbattens, London 2008.

The state of Sarila was established as an independent principality in 1755 by Raja Aman Singh, a son of Raja Pahar Singh of Jaitpur and a great-grandson of the Bundela warrior-king, Maharaja Chhatrasal. Raja Pahar Singh later granted the estate of Sarila as an appanage to his son, Aman Singh. He established his capital at Sarila and constructed a fort, which consolidated the political identity of the new state.

During the latter half of the 18th century, the region of Bundelkhand was caught in the midst of conflicts between local Bundela rulers, Mughal remnants, and the expanding Maratha Empire, to which Sarila lost much of its territory. By the turn of the 19th century, the British East India Company began establishing its hegemony over Central India through treaty alliances.

In 1807, during the reign of Raja Tej Singh (the grandson of Raja Aman Singh), the British recognized Sarila's autonomous status. The state was granted a formal sanad (charter) by the British government, which confirmed the ruler in his possessions. Sarila subsequently became a British protectorate under the political supervision of the Bundelkhand Agency, a subdivision of the Central India Agency. Throughout the colonial era, Sarila remained a small, non-salute state with an area of approximately 95 square miles.

description_block:
An ivory and gilt-silver mounted cased presentation sword by Howell, James & Co. presented by Edward Robert Lytton Bulwer-Lytton, 1st Earl of Lytton (1831â1891), Viceroy of India between 1876â1880, at the Imperial Assemblage at Delhi on the 1st of January 1877 
London, circa 1876
the single-edged steel blade becoming double-edged from yelman to tip, etched with decoration throughout blade and inscribed 'FROM THE VICEROY, 1ST JANUARY, 1877' to one side and 'HOWELL, JAMES & CO REGENT ST. LONDON' to the other, the gilt-silver crossguard mounted with polychrome enamel and gilt medallion containing the initial 'L' surmounted by a crown, the ivory grips engraved with an undulating vine, bullion knot, the wood scabbard clad in red velvet and with openwork silver-gilt mounts with hallmarks for Daniel & John Wellby, and the date 1876, the central mount with hand-coloured photographic portrait of Lytton, the fitted wood case containing additional metal-thread mounted leather fittings, the lid with gilt bronze royal coat of arms 
97 cm. long (2)

The item within this lot containing ivory has been registered in accordance with the Ivory Act (Section 10), reference no. SP46GXQ8.

Edward Robert Bulwer-Lytton, 1st Earl of Lytton (1831–1891), served as Viceroy and Governor-General of India from 1876 to 1880. On the 1st of January 1877 he presided over the Imperial Assemblage at Delhi, convened to mark the assumption by Queen Victoria (reg. 1837–1901) of the title Empress of India. At the conclusion of the Assemblage, Lytton entertained seventy-two Indian chiefs at a farewell banquet, contemporary reports recording that each was presented with a costly 100-guinea sabre as Lytton's personal gift and souvenir of the occasion, together with his portrait; a contemporary newspaper article records that Lytton expressed the hope that the swords would never be drawn except against their 'common enemies' (Clutha Leader, vol. III, no. 128, 2 March 1877, p. 3, 'The Imperial Assemblage at Delhi'). The present sword can be securely identified with this remarkable group of presentations: the blade is inscribed 'From the Viceroy 1st Jan 1877', the scabbard incorporates a portrait of Lytton, and the hilt bears an enamelled crowned initial 'L', evidently referring to Lytton himself. It is further marked for Howell, James & Co., Regent Street, London, one of the leading London luxury retailers and manufacturers of the 19th Century, established in 1819 and trading from 5, 7 and 9 Regent Street. By 1822 the firm had received a Royal Warrant and subsequently exhibited at the Great Exhibition of 1851 and the International Exhibition of 1862. A related sword presented by Lytton to Maharana Sajjan Singh of Udaipur (reg. 1874–1884) on the 1st of January 1877 is preserved in the Udaipur collections and is recorded as having been made by Henry Wilkinson of Pall Mall, London.

Lacquer work has traditionally been produced in two fashions in Sri Lanka. The first being Matale work, named niyapoten veda and meaning 'fingernail work'. This involves the reheating and repeated manipulation of the lac until it forms a thin thread. This is then applied to the object before being cut off between the finger nail and thumb. The Angalmaduva and Hurikaduva process entails items being spun on the lathe and the lace-like lac applied, producing the recognisable concentric patterns. For further discussion, see A.K. Coomaraswamy, Mediaeval Sinhalese Art, New York 1956, p.215-217.

In 1846, Nicholl was appointed as a teacher of landscape painting and drawing at the Colombo Academy in Ceylon, where he remained for three years. It is thought that he returned from Ceylon by 1849, as he exhibited some views of the island at the Royal Academy that year.

Andrew Nicholl was from Belfast and established a local reputation as a landscape painter by his early twenties and became a founding member of the Belfast Association of Artists. In 1832 he exhibited at the Royal Academy and by 1837 he was elected as an Associate Member of the Royal Hibernian Academy. In 1846, Nicholl was appointed as a teacher of landscape painting and drawing at the Colombo Academy in Ceylon, where he remained for three years. There, with the backing of his most significant patron, the Belfast MP and Colonial Secretary James Emmerson Tennent, Nicholl produced a number of views of local scenery and also provided illustrations for Tennent's book Ceylon: An Account of the Island - Physical, Historical and Topographical, published in 1860. It is thought that he returned from Ceylon by 1849, as he exhibited some views of the island at the Royal Academy that year. He divided his time between London and Belfast, and exhibited at both the Royal Academy and Royal Hibernian Academy. In 1870 he offered twelve watercolours of views of Ceylon to Queen Victoria, who bought two of them.

John Davidson (1778–1850) was a British colonial administrator and merchant who served as Resident of Rembang, became a partner in Macquoid, Davidson & Co., and was the first director of De Javasche Bank. In 1815 he married Eliza Breithaupt (1788–1827), as noted on both of the labels on the reverse of the canvas.

The British occupied Java from 1811 to 1816 under the leadership of Thomas Stamford Raffles as Lieutenant-Governor (better known as the founder of Singapore) and installed Residents in the same way as they had in India. After the fall of Napoleon (the invasion was originally intended to oust French forces) Java was made over once more to the Dutch after this brief period of British control.

A portrait possibly identifiable with the present work appeared in an Amsterdam sale in 1915: 'J. F. Sand. Portret van een Indischen landvoogd, Java. 1845. Doek, vergulde lijst' [Portrait of an East Indian colonial governor, Java, 1845; canvas, gilt frame]. See H. G. Bom, Boekveilingcatalogus, Amsterdam, 12 tot 16 juni 1915, lot 703, p. 33.

of compressed globular form with domed conical neck and spout, engraved and decorated with depictions of wayang characters to the body including Sita, Arjuna and Bhima with inscriptions below each figure, flower-filled cartouches to the neck, mouth and spout

The Wayang, translatable as puppetry, is an Indonesian shadow puppet theatre that dramatises the epics of the Mahabharata, Panji tales and the Ramayana. Plots revolve around a battle between good and evil with stock characters including halus, gusen, and dhalgelan. John Fryer, A New Account of East India and Persia 
London, Printed by R.R. for Ri[chard] Chiswell, at the Rose and Crown in St. Paul's Churchyard, 1698
first edition, pp.[x], xiv, 427, [1], xxiv (index); engraved portrait frontispiece on verso of half-title, 5 engraved plates (3 folding) and 3 maps, woodcut illustrations in the text, two contemporary ownership signatures on title crossed through in ink, contemporary calf, neatly re-cased, head-cap repaired 
folio (324 x 210 mm.)

Full title: A new account of East-India and Persia, in eight letters. Being nine years travels, begun 1672. And finished 1681. Containing observations made of the moral, natural, and artificial estate of those countries; namely of their government, religion, laws, customs. Of the soil, climates, seasons, health, diseases. Of the animals, vegetables, minerals, jewels. Of their housing, cloathing, manufactures, trades, commodities. And of the coins, weights, and measures, used in the principal places of trade in those parts.

John Fryer (circa 1650-1733) set sail from Gravesend in December 1672 and arrived seven months later at Masulipatam, the first British settlement on the Coromandel coast. He continued via Madras and Bombay to Surat to take up a post as surgeon. In 1677 he travelled to the Persian Gulf to continue his investigations into the effect of climate on health. He returned to England after ten years in the east.

He published this account some years later in the form of eight letters. The first gives an account of his voyage from Gravesend to Fort St. George, and describes the Malabar and Carnatic coasts. The second letter covers Bombay, Bassein, and a visit to Elephanta. The third is on Surat. In the fourth Fryer visits Goa and discusses precious stones. The fifth recounts his voyage to Persia with visits to Persepolis and Isfahan. The sixth and seventh describe the Mughal court, and the eighth letter concerns his return to England.

description_block:
Benjamin Schultze, Compendiaria Alcorani Refutatio Indostanice 
Halle, In Typographia Instituti Judaici, 1744
first (and only) edition, edidit D. Jo. Henr. Callenberg, pp. [117], Arabic and some Latin text, original wrappers, modern cloth box 
102 x 172 mm.; box 230 x 165 mm.

This was not the first refutation of the Qur'an to be printed by Christian missionaries. In 1698 Ludovico (Luigi) Marrucci published his Latin translation of the Qur'an (Alcorani textus universalis) at Padua, with notes refuting Qur'anic doctrines. But Schultze's work is probably the first such refutation to be published by Protestant missionaries.

The Institutum Judaicum was founded in 1724 or 1728 at Halle by the Pietist Johann Heinrich Callenberg (Professor of Oriental Languages as well as Professor of Theology) who was a great promoter of missionary activity amongst Jews in Europe and amongst Muslims. The Institute's full title was Institutum Judaicum et Muhammedicum and its role was to train Protestant missionaries for work in converting Jews and Muslims. Apart from such polemics, the Institute also produced translations of the New Testament in Hebrew and Yiddish. Schultze also published a grammar of Hindustani in 1745, using the same printer.

There are apparently no copies of the text outside Germany and St. Petersburg.

description_block:
Eustace Carey, Satya darshan, arthat Ishvarer samast bakyete manushyer tran o acharanarthe yaha prakash haiyache tahar pradarshak. Kalikata chapa haila san 1818 sal, View of the Truth, a very rare publication in Bengali by the Baptist Missionaries in India 
Calcutta, Baptist Mission Press, 1818
pp.[2], 24, text in Bengali, engraved frontispiece, original thin blue paper wrappers and original simple stitching still in place, manuscript inscription on front wrapper The true Durshun by Mr. E. Carey 
8vo (182 x 110 mm.)

A Bengali tract extolling the truth of Christianity composed by Eustace Carey, nephew of William Carey as the son of his younger brother Thomas. This was one of the earliest Bengali tracts issued by the Baptist Mission Press, Calcutta during its first year of operation, as recorded in the memoir of Eustace Carey by his wife Esther: 'the fourth, by Brother E. Carey, is the first in a series of tracts, to be written upon the evidences, the doctrines, and duties of Christianity, and consists of remarks on the importance and necessity of an immediate revelation from God' (Eustace Carey, A missionary in India, London 1857, p. 214).

It is also recorded in William Hopkins Pearce's journal: 'In December we published 1000 Pandit and Sirkar in Bengali and English, and 2000 Bengali only, with 2000 of The True Dershan, first part being the first tract in the series ordered by the Auxiliary Society'. (Memoirs of the Rev. W. H. Pearce, son of the Rev. S. Pearce, A. M. Birmingham (Calcutta, printed at the Baptist Mission Press, 1841), p. 92).

The title-page is emblazoned with a dramatic woodcut of the sun shattering the dark clouds of 'heathenism' to reveal the Bengali Bible (Dharmma Pustak) lying open on the Cross. This was the work of Eustace's friend John Lawson who had trained as a wood-engraver in England before joining Serampore in 1812. 

Eustace Carey received his training for the Baptist ministry first under John Sutcliff at Olney and from 1812 at the Bristol Baptist Academy under John Ryland. In 1814 he embarked for India intending to work at Serampore but persuaded by William Carey to become co-pastor, together with John Lawson, of a church in Calcutta, since the so-called 'pious clause' in the East India Company's charter renewal the previous year had lifted the ban on missionary activity. Eustace excelled at preaching in Bengali but after ten years ill-health forced him to return to Britain in 1825. After William Carey's death in 1834, Eustace was commissioned by the Committee of the Baptist Missionary Society to compile a Memoir of William Carey, D. D. (London 1836) consisting mostly of extracts from William Carey's own letters and journals. Eustace died in 1855.

Historically recorded by Murdoch as tract no. 3 among the publications of the Calcutta Baptist missionaries: Eustace Carey's Satya Darshan, Part I (1818), printed in an edition of 2,000 copies. No other surviving copy has yet been located (see John Murdoch, Comp. Catalogue of the Christian Vernacular Literature of India: With Hints on the Management of Indian Tract Societies, Madras 1870, p. 7.). No other copy is recorded, and not listed in either WorldCat or the Bengali STC-1 (1801-1867) at https://granthsouthasia.wordpress.com/sct.

description_block:
Achille Auguste & Georges Augustin GÃ©ringer, Fifty-eight hand-coloured lithographs of South Indian personalities, castes, Hindu iconography and religious ceremonies from EugÃ¨ne Burnouf and M.E. Jacquet's L'Inde FranÃ§aise 
Paris, GÃ©ringer et Chabrelie; Imprimerie de E. Pochard, 1827-[1830?]
fifty-eight hand-coloured lithograph plates, loose, with original paper wrappers for 11th livraison 
folio (460 x 230 mm.)

These lithographs, from one of the most important plate books on India published in France, represent a stunning visual record of the French possessions in South India in the early 19th century. Much admired when published, not least by the French artist Eugène Delacoix, they remain little known today.

The lithographs were based on original paintings, some by Achille Auguste Géringer and his father Georges Augustin Géringer, others by moutchis, the South Indian caste of professional painters on cloth. The Géringers, gifted amateur artists, ran an artists' materials business in central Paris and visited India several times – perhaps in search of pigment supplies – between 1822 and 1826.

This selection comprises thirteen Hindu iconographic representations, most notably of the incarnations of Vishnu; ten portraits of the Géringers' personal servants, officials and professionals they met, and religious figures who seem to have held a particular fascination; twenty-five castes or types – barbers, bracelet-sellers, shoe-makers, carpenters, shepherds, palanquin-bearers, etc.; and ten religious ceremonies including a Brahmin funeral, fire-walking and the Pongal harvest festival. The exceptionally sensitively and sympathetically rendered life-studies are the earliest portraits of named individual Indians painted by a European artist to appear in book form.

The plates were originally issued in more than one version, as the two variant depictions of Rajputs and Marathas included here with their differences in detail and hand-colouring demonstrate. This intermittent publication is confirmed by the variations in the captions: some French only, others with Tamil added, and others still with Sanskrit in Devanagari script. The arrangement of the plates reflects the fact that the work was originally issued to subscribers in 24 parts (livraisons), each of six plates (planches). Our plates are all from the first volume which contained a total of 90; the second volume published in 1835 added a further 54. As our complete parts three, seven and fourteen here show, the contents of each part followed a regular pattern: a representation of a Hindu god or goddess, followed by a portrait from life, and then four topographical views, religious ceremonies or most frequently caste occupations. Part 25 was a text-only appendix on the religion of the Malabars.

Calcutta, 1800-1806
twenty aquatints, in card mounts 
19 with plate marks approximately 370 x 510 mm. on untrimmed sheets, 490 x 600 mm.; one trimmed within plate mark to 240 x 370 mm.(20)

A striking set of twenty landscape aquatints published between 1800 and 1806 by James Moffat (1775-1815), one of the earliest artist-engravers working in Calcutta. Moffat arrived there in 1789; his first employment was with one of the printing houses producing official publications, but by 1797 he was advertising 'picturesque copper-plate engravings (performed on very moderate terms) [...] accurately delineated, and if required, transferred to plates of any size' in the Calcutta Gazette.

In 1798, Moffat issued his first aquatints by subscription, following the model used by Thomas Daniell in 1788 and William Baillie in 1794 with their respective twelve views of Calcutta. Moffat's aquatints were well-received, and he attracted subscriptions from numerous Company officials. Moffat clearly identified a need in the local market; Daniell had returned to England in 1793 and Baillie died in 1799. Moffat appears to have overcome the technical difficulties which bedevilled both his predecessors. Baillie and Moffat both engaged local artists to colour their prints, perhaps with an eye to obscuring any defect in their printing. Moffat probably issued his aquatints uncoloured, leaving the instruction of local artists to the buyer.

Moffat's images went beyond the conventional depictions of European buildings at Calcutta which dominate the sets issued by Daniell and Baillie. The majority of these aquatints are after his own drawings of Calcutta and sites he visited along the Ganges, including Benares, Monghyr, and Berhampore. Where he worked from other artists' originals, he marks himself as the engraver only, as in his views of China and Indonesia, and early view of Seringapatam, presumably produced to meet popular demand after the British conquest of Mysore in 1799.
These aquatints have a spare, selective geometric character, and are at their best depicting architecture and landscape, where Moffat's eye for detail excels. 

Despite Moffat's technical and artistic achievements, and his place in the history of British depictions of India, he is remarkably un-studied. Archer and Lightbown's India Observed (1982) gives him a brief mention; de Almeida and Gilpin's Indian Renaissance (2005) is the first work to give Moffat any serious consideration, albeit over a few paragraphs. The sheer rarity of Moffat's work may explain this. His total output between 1798 and his death in 1815 may be no more than fifty prints, with a small number of impressions produced of each. His prints were apparently issued in sets, but there is no uniformity among the sets of his prints which survive, suggesting that Moffat sold them as the customer desired, rather than in fixed groups. No sets with title pages or contents lists are known.

Little is known of Moffat. Mildred Archer writes that he 'was a Scotsman living in Calcutta from 1789 to 1815. He appears to have learnt his profession of painting and engraving in India. In 1798 and from 1805 to 1810 he produced views of towns on the Ganges and Hooghly, and in 1808 engravings from Henry Creighton's drawings of Gaur'. British Drawings in the India Office Library, 1969, vol. II, p. 621).
