Captain Philip Meadows Taylor, Sketches in the Deccan, portraying Goa, Aurangabad, Hyderabad and the surrounding region 
London, Charles Tilt, 1837
drawn on stone by Weld Taylor, Edward Morton, and George Childs, first edition, lithographic title page and 19 tinted lithograph plates with descriptions facing, original half calf, dark wine boards, all edges gilt 
folio (485 x 382 mm.)

The plates are as follows:
Doorway of a Hindoo temple, near Kooladgee (title page).
Entrance to Goa harbour.
Cross of St Francis Xavier, Goa.
Tomb of Aurungzeeb's daughter, Aurangabad.
Bridge and part of the city wall, Aurangabad.
Temple of Bhowanee, Tooljapoor.
The Ghat Seele, Tooljapoor.
Tombs and part of the fort of Golcondah.
A street in the Karwan, Hyderabad.
Principal Room in the Indra Subba Cave, Ellora.
Tomb of Mohobut Sahib, or Peer Padshaw, near Hyderabad.
Tomb of Zur Zurree Zur Buksh, at Rozah.
Temple of Rameswur, Ellora.
Waterfall in the Tandoor Hills.
Purendah.
Tomb of a Mahomedan Saint, on the bank of the River Godavery.
Hindoo Temple at Houndah.
Medressa, or college, at Beeder.
Assur Mahal, Beejapoor.
Mausoleum of Mahmood Adil Shah, Beejapoor.

For an album of twenty-four drawings covering fortifications, temples, archaeology, architecture, topography and cantonment life in Aurangabad, Ellora, Belgaum, Bolarum, Daulatabad, Hyderabad, Goa and Trichinopoly, dated circa 1826-29, some of which were used for Sketches in the Deccan, see the sale in these rooms, Bonhams, Islamic and Indian Art, 22nd May 2025, lot 211.

Sketches in the Deccan was first book by one of 19th Century India's better known administrators who arrived in Bombay at the age of fifteen and entered the Nizam of Hyderabad's service. Meadows Taylor was an enthusiastic and competent artist who worked on his sketches on his tours through the Nizam's dominions.

While on furlough in England, Taylor published the first of several Indian novels, Confessions of a Thug (1839), in which he reproduced the tales he had heard about the Thuggee cult, described by the chief actors in them.

In 1860, Taylor's health failed and he returned to England, where he wrote five more Indian novels. He also wrote an autobiography (published posthumously in 1877), the letterpress for the monumental eight-volume The People of India: A Series of Photographic Illustrations, with Descriptive Letterpress, of the Races and Tribes of Hindustan (London, 1868–75), and a students' manual of Indian history. He was made a companion in the Order of the Star of India in 1869.

description_block:
Herzog & Higgins, The Abu Album, 1895-96, with 43 photographs showing Mount Abu and the Jain temples near Mhow, Central India 
[Mhow,] 1896
Forty-three photographs, including one panorama, handwritten captions, leather album, gilt ornamented 
photographs mostly 210 x 185 mm.; album folio (365 x 505 mm.)

This presentation album of photographs depicts the famous Jain temples of this area, and others of local attractions, including the lake, sports grounds, schools, the church and various residencies. There is also a portrait of Maharao Sir Keshir Singh Bahadur, KCSI, ruler of Sirohi. To quote the opening preface: 'For ages Abu has been held sacred by Hindus and Jains as the abode of gods, sages and holy men, hence its Sanscrit name of Ar-budha, or "Mountain of Wisdom". Colonel Tod was the first European to visit it in 1822, and it began to be used as a Sanitarium for British troops in 1840; three years afterwards the first barracks were built, and about the same time the Agent to the Governor-General for Rajputana first made it his headquarters. At the present time the Sirohi and other Chiefs of Rajputana, as well as many Europeans, use Abu as a summer resort'.

P. Adolf Herzog and P. Higgins had gained their photographic experience as assistants with several established photographers in India before going into partnership. Herzog is known to have worked for the Jabalpur photographer John Blees in the late 1880s and the pair were also both employed in the studios of Lala Deen Diyal and Johnston and Hoffmann around 1890.

This presentation album appears to be one of the earliest productions of their studio established in Mhow around 1894. The small town of Mhow had been a military centre since the early 19th century. The selection of this cantonment town for their studio was clearly aimed at exploiting a ready European market. Herzog and Higgins was the premier portrait studio in the area during the first two decades of the 20th century, remaining in business until around 1924.

artwork_title: The Abu Album, 1895-96

description_block:
Jacques Guiaud, The Ruins of Mandoo, the ancient Mahommedan Capital of Malwah, in Central India, from the original sketches of Captain Claudius Harris 
London, Day and Son, Lithographers to the Queen, 1860
With descriptive and historical notices, and an appendix, first edition, pp.[iv], 20, 6 tinted lithograph plates, original cloth 
Folio (507 x 343 mm.)

A fine set of lithographs produced by the French painter Jacques Guiaud (1810-76), a specialist at reproducing landscapes as lithographs for luxurious colour plate books. Guiaud had moved from Paris to Nice in 1847 to be able to seek commissions from the wealthy expatriate community, and there he encountered the Maharaja of Dhar who commissioned this work. Subscribers bought 159 copies. It is likely only around 200 were published. There appear to be three copies, in the British Library, the Bodleian, and the V & A.

The original watercolours on which Guiaud based his work were by Claudius Richard William Firth Harris, an amateur artist who served with the 8th Madras Light Cavalry between 1845 and 1860.

The plates are as follows:
1. View of the modern village of Mandoo, and of the ancient Mosque, the 'Jumah Musjid'.
2. Front view of the ruined Mosque, the 'Jumah Musjid'.
3. The 'Jahaz Mahal' or 'Water Palace'.
4. The palace of Sultan Baz Bahadoor, and pavilion of Roop Muttee, his Queen.
5. The marble mausoleum of the Sultan, Hoossain Shah Ghuree.
6. The Delhi gate.

description_block:
Colesworthy Grant, Lithographic Sketches of the Public Characters of Calcutta 
Calcutta, [1847]
first collected edition, lithograph title, 126 lithograph portraits, some on India paper and mounted, modern leather, the artist's presentation inscription, To the Revd. James Charles D.D. a small token of respect with the kind regards & best wishes of the artist, Calcutta Decemr. 18th 1847 
4to (277 x 222 mm.)

A rare artist presentation copy, predating other versions and including far more portraits.

This collection of lithographic plates of the notables of Calcutta published over nine years between 1838 and 1847 was the most important work of Colesworthy Grant, the greatest exponent of the new medium of lithography for portraiture in early 19th-century India.

The subjects cover the entire range of the Calcutta elite - administrators such as Governors-General the Earl of Auckland and Sir Charles Metcalfe, lawyers like Sir Edward Ryan, Chief Justice of Bengal, and Advocate-General John Pearson, churchmen including the Rev Alexander Duff and Dr William Yates, doctors such as Surgeon John Grant, and soldiers including Lieutenant-General Sir Hugh Gough and Lieutenant-Colonel Pogson. Most, but not all, are identified. A few Indian notables are included, such as the Nawab of Murshidabad and the 'Claimant of the Burdwan Raj'. Some portraits must have been copied from other drawings rather than taken from life, for example Henri Christophe, the First King of Haiti, who had died in 1820.

Between 1837 and 1850 Grant produced no less than 245 portrait studies, which appeared in various Calcutta journals, before selections were published in two volumes. But it was this collection which made his name.

'The lithographs of the public characters were so striking and full of life, that Colesworthy's reputation was established, and he was sought for by private individuals to take their water-colour likenesses', as stated in the only published study of him, Peary Chand Mitra's Life of Colesworthy Grant (1881). He has surely been unjustly neglected. Today he is best remembered not so much as an artist but as the founder of the Calcutta Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals in 1861, following the worrying to death of his favourite Persian cat by a neighbour's dogs.

According to Mitra, Grant produced portraits of 167 'public characters'. But, rather like the albums issued by Charles D'Oyly's Behar Amateur Lithographic Press, there may have been no such thing as a standard edition of this work, and no specific year of issue. In surviving copies the number of plates varies widely – a copy in the British Library dated 1850 contains no less than 188.
Thirteen of the plates are titled 'Private Sketches' and were presumably not published elsewhere.
artwork_title: Colesworthy Grant, Lithographic Sketches of the Public Characters of Calcutta
subject_matter: portraits, men, women, churchmen, administrators, lawyers, doctors, soldiers, Indian notables, elite society

J. Forbes-Watson, The Textile Manufactures and the Costumes of the People of India 
London, the India Office, 1866
pp. xxi, 173, 12 plates, of which 9 are mounted Forbes photographs, and one a chromolithograph, contemporary half calf, rebacked

description_block:
A folio from a Gita Gauri series, depicting Parvati seated in a bower approached by a brahmin 
Mewar, circa 1675-80
gouache and gold on paper, yellow panel at top with three lines of text in nagari script, red border, numbered 12 [?] at lower right 
292 x 235 mm.

Provenance
Spink and Son, London, Painting for the Royal Courts of India, 1976, no. 76.
Acquired by the seller's father from Spink, August 1980.
Private collection, Australia, since 1980.

Exhibited
Intimate Encounters, Art Gallery of New South Wales, 22nd February-4th May 2008.

The text is not in standard Sanskrit but a mix of Rajasthani and Hindi, perhaps because its intended audience may have been women of the zenana who were more likely to be familiar with the local dialect than courtly prose.

Gīta Gaurī patra || 12 || brahmaṇ pūche he || tuṅ tapa kyuṅ kare he || jadī pārvatī kahyo || huṁ mahadeva heṅ ichuṅ huṅ || jadī brahmaṇ kahyo || thāre vaṇ se kyuṅ || tuṅ hāthī caṛhe || o baladh caṛhe || tuṅ sajyā sue || o masāṅṇ || tuṅ hāra pere || o ruṅḍamālā || tuṅ caṅdan lagāve || o vibhūti ||

Page from the Gita Gauri. 12.
The brahman asks: 'Why are you practicing asceticism?'
Then Parvati said, 'God is my only desire'.
Then the brahman said, 'Why would you leave your forest [grove]? You ride an elephant, he rides an ox! You sleep in a bed, he sleeps in a cremation ground! You wear a necklace, he wears a garland of skulls! You adorn yourself with sandalwood, he uses sacred ash!

(Translation by Dr Richard Williams, Reader (Associate Professor) in Music and South Asian Studies, SOAS, London).

Siva has heard that Parvati is practicing extreme austerities in her love and devotion to him. He disguises himself as a brahmin to interrogate her. We see that Parvati is ready to leave behind her sumptuous bed, her box of luxury accoutrements and perfumes, and the sensory pleasures of the bower, even her Royal elephant (on the left-hand side of the painting) out of love for Siva. The brahman challenges her, raising his right arm to gesture overhead to the bleak, grey, upper section of the painting where Siva sleeps in a cremation ground, adorned with snakes, human heads, and sacred ash.

The Gita Gauri, the song of Gauri ('the fair one', i.e. Parvati), a version of Kalidasa's poem Kumarasambhava, is a series about the love and 'pastoral dalliance' of Siva and Parvati 'recalling the amours of Krishna and Radha in the Gita Govinda or Rasikapriya' (Topsfield).

Parvati, seated in a leafy bower, is addressed by a Brahmin priest (apparently part of a nobleman's entourage) on the subject of the deeds of Siva, as related in the inscription. Siva himself appears four times at the top of the painting.

For another example with discussion, perhaps from the same series, see A. Topsfield, Court Painting at Udaipur, Zurich 2002, p. 93, fig. 56, and n. 51. For another example from a Gita Gauri series, see Christie's New York, Indian, Himalayan and Southeast Asian Works of Art, 22nd March 2023, lot 408.

A painting from this series which has been attributed to Sahibdin is in the collection of the San Diego Museum of Art (acc. no. 1990.603). Other paintings can be found in the collections of the Art Institute of Chicago (acc. no. 2004.454) and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (acc. no. 66.123 and 66.124).

Rajasthan, dated Samvat 1903/AD 1846
Prakrit manuscript on paper, 46 leaves including cover pages, possibly incomplete and misbound, nagari text in black ink with headings and section divisions in red, minute commentary text, text and images recto and verso throughout with the exception of one leaf, numbered in black ink throughout in lower right corner on recto of all folios, 16 leaves with illustrations in gouache, most other leaves with tables outlined in yellow and red, cover pages with stylised floral and sunburst motifs, between modern card covers, not bound

description_block:
Shaykh Ibrahim Adham of Balkh fed by angels 
Oudh, Lucknow or Faizabad, late 18th Century
gouache and gold on paper, trimmed from its original mount and laid down on an album page with dark blue paper inner border and gold sprinkled buff outer border, inscription in nagari and nasta'liq verso 
painting 200 x 146 mm.; album page 325 x 235 mm.

Provenance
Sotheby's New York, Indian and Southeast Asian Art, 4th June 1994, lot 351.
Private collection, Japan, since 1994.

The Persian calligraphic composition on the reverse reads: tasvir-e shah adham padshah-e balkh, 'The image of Shah Adham, the King of Balkh'.

The subject of this miniature was a popular one in 18th Century Mughal painting. Based on the legend by Farid al-Din 'Attar, Sultan Ibrahim bin Adham (d. 776-77) gave up the Kingdom of Balkh to become a Dervish. He was visited by angels who bought him ten dishes of food inciting the jealousy of another poor dervish, also painted into miniatures of this subject, as here, at the lower right.

One such miniature, attributed to the Lucknow/Faizabad artist Hunhar and dated circa 1760-70 is in the Polsky collection (see Andrew Topsfield (ed.), In the Realm of Gods and Kings: Arts of India, London 2004, no. 80, pp. 196-97). The same painting was previously with Spink, London, Gopis, Goddesses and Demons, 2000, no. 76, where there is a comprehensive discussion of the subject. 

Others, from Lucknow and Murshidabad respectively, are in the India Office Library (T. Falk and M. Archer, Indian Miniatures in the India Office Library, London 1981, nos. 325 and 367); and in the St. Petersburg Muraqqa' (G. Bailey, The St. Petersburg Muraqqa', Milan 1996, pl. 90 folio 53 recto).
Another of the same subject, Oudh, circa 1750, is published in P. Carr, Dieux, tigres et amours: Miniatures indiennes du XVe au XXe siecle, Spain 1993, pp. 112-113.
See also the sales in these rooms, Islamic and Indian Art, 4th October 2011, lot 331; Bonhams New York, Indian, Himalayan and Southeast Asian Art, 14th September 2015, lot 102; A Modern Antiquarian: the collection of Graham Slater, Part 1, 15th April 2025, lot 186.

description_block:
Two Kathak dancers 
Provincial Mughal, Oudh, late 18th Century
gouache and gold on paper, inner margins ruled in colours and gold, gold-sprinkled outer borders 
163 x 144 mm. with borders

For a very similar depiction of the subject, painted in Bilaspur, circa 1700, see the sale in these rooms, Bonhams New York, Indian, Himalayan and Southeast Asian Art, 19th March 2012, lot 1180; Sotheby's, Fine Oriental Miniatures and Manuscripts, 20th July 1977, lot 12, oval, attributed to the Deccan, first half of the 18th Century; and Sotheby's, Fine Oriental Miniatures, Manuscripts, Qajar Paintings and Lacquer, 24th April 1979, lot 31 (illustrated), again oval, Mughal, 18th Century, with two oval portraits, all laid down on an illuminated album page. Compare also with an 18th Century Mughal version in the Art Institute of Chicago (1919.956), of oval shape, with the dancers on a terrace.

Kathak evolved from a blend of Hindu and Islamic culture. It was in origin a Hindu devotional dance, combining movement and story-telling, and later became a highly sophisticated court dance under Mughal rule, where it was considerably modified for the purpose of entertainment. The main repertoire of Kathak is based on the divine love between Krishna and Radha and on the Hindu epics, but also includes a wide variety of other lyrical genres, such as love songs (thumri) or danced poetry (gazal).

description_block:
Two portraits of the Emperor Jahangir (reg. 1605-27) and the Emperor Muhammad Shah (reg. 1719-48) 
Oudh, Lucknow or Faizabad, late 18th Century
gouache and gold on paper, red inner borders, plain outer borders, each with identifying inscription in nasta'liq in upper border, Jahangir Badshah; Muhammad Shah Badshah, each inscribed verso in a 19th Century hand Jahangir and Muhammad Shah respectively 
290 x 220 mm.(2)

Both figures stand against landscapes typical of Oudh painting, with puffy white cloud formations at the top of the page and a horizon placed at a low level with little vegetation or other detail. This trend, in which later copies of earlier Mughal portraits were redrawn, perhaps from a charba (a thin paper used for tracing), was popularised by Mihr Chand, reflective of the working practices of his studio and re-used by many artists in Oudh in the last quarter of the 18th Century. Mihr Chand (fl. 1759-86) is best known for his time in Faizabad where he served as the head of the workshop established by the Swiss-born East India Company officer, Antoine Louis-Henri Polier.

Comparison can be made with two pair of portraits in a Polier album in the British Museum, London (1920,0917,0.151v; 1920,0917,0.141v), depicting Sultan ʿAbdullah Qutb Shah (reg. 1626–72) and Nawab Vizier al-Mamalik Safdar Jang Abu'l-Mansur Khan Bahadur, both of which were probably produced in Oudh circa 1773–76.

description_block:
A Mughal nobleman, perhaps Nawab Najib ud-Daula (circaâ1707â1770) seated on a terrace smoking a hookah, and attendant with a flywhisk standing behind him 
Delhi, circa 1760
gouache and gold on paper, laid down on an album page with (possibly later) illuminated borders decorated with flowers and foliate motifs with animals and birds amidst them, inscription at lower left of painting sanah 990, 'The year 990'/AD 1582-83 
painting 212 x 140 mm.; album page 385 x 261 mm.

It has been suggested that the sitter in the painting is the Mughal general Najib ud-Daula. Portraits of this pivotal figure in 18th-century Indian history are rare. Although there is no identifying inscription on the present painting, comparison can be made with the features and dress of the sitter and his attendant with an 18th-century equestrian portrait of Najib ud-Daula, attributed to Mola Ram (1743–1833), in the Balak Ram collection, Srinagar (the great-grandson of the artist), published in Roopa Lekha, vol. XXII, no. 2 (1951).

Najib ud-Daula (circa 1707–1770), formerly a soldier of fortune named Najib Khan, was one of the most influential figures of 18th-century northern India. He began his military career as a Mughal serviceman and was granted land in Bijnor, the most northerly district of Rohilkhand, in the northwestern part of Uttar Pradesh. Here, he founded the city of Najibabad in the 1740s. Najib ud-Daula later shifted his allegiances to join Ahmad Shah Abdali when he invaded India for a third time in 1756. After capturing Delhi, the Afghan king returned to his own dominions in the following year, appointing Najib to the post of mir bakhshi. This was one of the Mughal empire's four ministers, broadly in charge of administering the military as paymaster general to the nominal Emperor, Alamgir II (reg. 1754–59). Najib was the master of a large tract in the upper Ganga-Jumna Doab, extending southwards from the mountains almost as far as Delhi. Through his ability and integrity, he upheld for a time the falling fortunes of the empire as the de facto ruler of Delhi. Immediately after the departure of Ahmad Shah in 1757, his forces clashed with the advancing Marathas, who captured Delhi. Najib ud-Daula surrendered after resisting the Maratha confederacy for more than five months, and withdrew to Najibabad. Despite losing control of Delhi, Najib ud-Daula continued to challenge the Maratha confederacy. In the autumn of 1759, after laying waste to his territories, they invaded Rohilkhand, being driven back by forces sent by Shuja ud-Daula, the nawab of neighbouring Oudh. Ahmad Shah Abdali was now beginning his fourth invasion of India, and Najib ud-Daula joined forces with him. In October 1760, Ahmad Shah marched towards Delhi and, in January 1761, the Maratha confederacy was destroyed at the great battle of Panipat. Before departing, Ahmad Shah entrusted the administration of Delhi to Najib ud-Daula, who assumed the title of amir al-umara ('prince of princes') with the office of mir bakshi. For nearly ten years as regent of the Mughal Empire, Najib ud-Daula was unsuccessful in halting the Jat and Sikh uprisings in imperial heartlands such as Delhi and Agra, in his own territory of Rohilkhand. He fell ill and died on 30 October 1770.

description_block:
Two paintings depicting Mirza Feroze Shah on horseback with attendants on foot; and an elephant with two riders, part of a Hindu religious procession in Madras 
Delhi, by Mazhar 'Ali Khan or an artist in his circle, circa 1840-42
gouache and gold on paper, black margin rules, Persian inscription in lower borders, card on reverse of each inscribed in French with a description of the scene, one with note regarding Alexis Soltykoff, late 19th Century brass frames 
93 x 125 mm.(2)

Provenance
Apparently formerly in the collection of Prince Alexis Soltykoff (1806–1859): acquired by a previous owner in 1882 (handwritten note on the backboard of one painting).

The Persian inscriptions read: Savar mirza firuz shah, 'Mirza Firuz Shah riding'; fil-e miratab, 'elephant [carrying the] Miratab [royal fish standard]'.

The French inscriptions read, respectively:
A. Cortege du Grand Mogol allant a la Mosquee le jour du Bairam, a Delhi/Collection du Prince Alexis Solstikof [sic] achetee en 1882, 'Procession of the Grand Mughal going to the mosque on the day of Bairam, in Delhi/Collection of Prince Alexis Soltykoff, acquired in 1882'.
'Le Grand Mogol' in 1841 would have been Bahadur Shah II (reg. 1837-58).

B. Procession religieuse Brachmane précédée de Bayaderes dans une rue de Madras; la marche est arretee pour la danse/Juillet 1841, 'Brahmin religious procession preceded by temple dancers in a street in Madras; the procession has halted for the dance/July 1841'.

Mazhar 'Ali Khan, son of the famed Ghulam 'Ali Khan (fl. 1817-52), stands out as one of Delhi's most important painters of the 19th Century. Active in the 1840s and 1850s, he is best known for his meticulous panoramic view of Delhi completed in 1846 (British Library, Add.Or.4126) and, more relevant to the present works, a group of topographical paintings commissioned by Sir Thomas Metcalfe, the governor-general's agent at the court of the Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, between 1842 and 1844. One hundred paintings executed by Mazhar 'Ali Khan depicting the monuments, ruins, palaces and shrines of Delhi – including a panorama in twelve sections showing the procession of the Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar surrounded by elephants, palanquins and ranks of soldiers to celebrate the feast of Eid in Delhi in 1843 – were later compiled by Metcalfe into an album. Containing 89 folios and completed with a small number of paintings by other Indian artists, it became known as 'The Dehlie Book' or 'Reminiscences of Imperial Delhi' (British Library, Add.Or.5475). The manner of execution of the present pair of works is clearly related to the small processional vignettes in Metcalfe's album (British Library, Add.Or.5475, f.59v, panels 7 and 8).

On the left page (top), the second elephant in the procession carries the royal standard and (bottom) the camel carries a nagara, a kettle drum (on the right page, a party of Skinner's Horse). The first of the pair shows a noble on horseback with attendants. The inscription identifies him as Mirza Firoz Shah, the grandson of Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar who fought against the British in Lucknow and Awadh. He is believed to have authored an influential rebel manifesto commonly known as the 'Azamgarh Proclamation' and published in the Delhi Gazette on 29 September 1857. In it, the prince aimed to rally both Hindus and Muslims against the East India Company and restore the Mughal government to power. He fought several actions against the British and managed to elude capture to survive for almost twenty years. 
The second painting shows an elephant with a driver and a rider carrying the Imperial Mughal insignia, the gold Panja ('Hand' or 'Palm') standard representing the power, protection and righteous justice of the emperor. Other standards that would be carried on elephants in procession included the Lion, which was the special sign of the emperor, the Round Ball or Orb representing the sun, the Scales of Justice and a Fish standard (Mahi o Maratib, or fish and dignities). This latter description has been inadvertently inscribed for this painting.

For a discussion of Mazhar 'Ali Khan's work and milieu, see: J. P. Losty, M. Roy, Mughal India: Art, Culture and Empire, London 2012, p. 229; J. P. Losty, 'Depicting Delhi: Mazhar Ali Khan, Thomas Metcalfe, and the topographical school of Delhi artists', in W. Dalrymple, Y. Sharma (eds.), Princes and Painters in Mughal Delhi, 1707-1857, London 2012, pp. 52–9; p. 165, cat. no. 73 (Jami Masjid); and for Ghulam 'Ali Khan, pp. 217–20; W. Dalrymple (ed.), Forgotten Masters: Indian Painting for the East India Company, London 2019, pp. 140–47.

Mazhar 'Ali Khan produced larger and more finished versions of the smaller scenes commissioned by Metcalfe, demonstrating the range of his output. His work also found its way (by repute, as evidenced by the inscription to the reverse of one of the paintings here) into the hands of other European visitors to Delhi.

One such traveller was Prince Alexis Soltykoff (1806–1859), a Russian diplomat who made two trips to India, in 1841-43, and then again in 1844-46. His letters written home to his brother were later published in the popular success Lettres sur L'Inde (1848), which also included some lithographs based on drawings he had made of the people, landscapes, processions, hunting scenes and ceremonies. In 1850, the drawings were engraved by De Rudder and published in Voyages dans L'Inde in a 36-plate elephant folio edition, as well as subsequent octavo versions. In these publications is an engraving based on Soltykoff's own sketch of the grand state procession of the Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah II, in November 1842 and titled Cortege du grand Mogol a Dehli [sic]. It is therefore possible that Soltykoff acquired the present pair of paintings (perhaps along with others) as points of reference for his own work capturing the royal procession.

description_block:
Percy Carpenter (British, 1820-95) 
Nine Indian hunting scenes, original paintings used for the lithographed plates in Hog Hunting in Lower Bengal (1861)
pencil, watercolour and bodycolour, all signed P. Carpenter and dated 1860 in pencil, contemporary handwritten titles embedded in mounts, The Tiffin with the names of the participants embossed on the mount 
the smallest 245 x 340 mm.; the majority 340 x 510 mm.(9)

Provenance
The artist.
Sir Archibald James Dirom Crawford, whose father was an indigo exporter in Calcutta.
Given to the seller in 1983 by the above.

The subjects are:
The Tiffin (340 x 490 mm.).
The Meet (330 x 510 mm.).
The Beat (340 x 510 mm.).
Tally Ho (340 x 510 mm.).
The First Spear (340 x 510 mm.).
The Charge (340 x 510 mm.).
The Hog at Bay (340 x 510 mm.).
The Death (340 x 510 mm.).
Last scene of All (245 x 340 mm.).

Hog Hunting in Lower Bengal, published in 1861, and now rare, was dedicated to the The Calcutta Tent Club. It had eight hand-coloured lithographed plates, and is described as 'one of the few books on pig-sticking and very difficult to find in good condition' (Schwerdt). 'The meet was held by the Calcutta Tent Club in March 1860 on the Sowerra Burrea Plains, near Tumluk, 50 miles south east of Calcutta. The hunt lasted three days during which time thirty-seven hogs were killed'.

Percy Carpenter studied painting at the Royal Academy where he exhibited in 1841. He travelled to Singapore, Ceylon and India between 1855 and 1860. By 1859, Carpenter was in Calcutta, and had developed his sporting speciality. The Calcutta Tent Club commissioned him to make drawings of their meet on the Sowerra Burrea Plains, near Tumluk, 50 miles southeast of Calcutta, in March 1860. The hunting party consisted of fifteen members of the Club, including their guests, with around four horses per person and attendants, numbering around sixty people. There were also eleven elephants to act as beaters in the long grass, jungle, and woods on the plain. The hunt lasted three days during which time they killed thirty seven hogs. Subsequently eight of Carpenter's works were lithographed.

description_block:
A view of the ghat at Benares, by Hercules Brabazon Brabazon (British, 1821-1906) 
circa 1875-76
pencil and watercolour on paper, signed H B B lower right, inscribed Benares lower left 
218 x 287 mm. (sight)

Provenance
With M. Knoedler & Co., 14 East 57th St, New York (gallery label on backboard), between 1925 and 1970.

Knoedler was one of the longest-established commercial galleries in the USA, founded in 1846, and finally closing in 2011. In 1925 its premises moved to 14 East 57th Street, near Madison Avenue, and remained there until 1970, when it moved to a refurbished town house at 19 East 70th Street.

Brabazon spent several months in India from 1875 to 1876, travelling with his nephew Harvey T. B. Combe, during the Prince of Wales's tour of the Eastern provinces. His experiences caused a profound change in the direction of his work and the watercolours he produced exhibit a much looser style than his previous work. The Taj Mahal was his favourite subject and C. Lewis Hind writes in his biography of the artist 'Perhaps in no subject was he so personal, so sure of his "audacities and omissions," so apparently careless, yet so completely the artist, as in his impressions of the Taj Mahal, near Agra...It hardly looks like a real building in Brabazon's rendering. It is an Eastern dream, that may vanish into air before the wave of a magician's wand.' (Hercules Brabazon Brabazon: His Art and Life, London, 1912, pp. 22-23). India saw the start of what is known as Brabazon's later 'short hand'.

description_block:
A calligraphic composition bearing the name of General John Baillie Ballantyne Dickson (1842-1925), copied by the scribe Muhammad 'Ali Rampuri 
North India, Rampur, dated 10th March 1907
the main composition in stylised intertwining thuluth in painted lacquer, interspersed with gold, below this two lines of text in large naskhi in black ink within gold cloudbands, floral inner border, inner margins ruled in colours, brown outer border 
album page 395 x 540 mm.

The tughra reads: 'General John Baillie Ballantyne Dickson CBC MG'.
The text in the lower panel reads:
'The tughra of the one with the most glorious celebrated and the revered, excellent attribute the Great Commander (amir kabir), the prudent chief with wisdom of Aristotle and generosity of Plato, the helper of devotees, the protector of lands, His Excellency General John Baillie Ballantyne Dickson CBC MG, may his prosperity be everlasting, the traveller of India, The needy Mirza Muhammad 'Ali, attached to the Rampur governor, wrote it on tenth of March of the Christian [year] 1907'.

John Baillie Ballantyne Dickson was born in 1842 and entered the army in 1860. He served in the Bengal Cavalry and the Indian Staff Corps, and was on special service to South Africa in 1879 to take part in the Zulu War as an officer in the Native Carrier Corps. He was promoted to major in 1881 and later transferred to the 5th Dragoon Guards with the rank of Lieutenant-Colonel. He was DAA and QMG on the Nile Expedition of 1884-85 in which he was severely wounded. He was appointed commanding officer of the 5th DG in 1887 and commanded until 1893. In 1897 he was a colonel on the Staff, commanding a cavalry brigade in Eastern District and then the Straits Settlements, Malaya in 1899. He reached the rank of Major-General, and in the Boer War commanded the 4th Cavalry Brigade. He died on 15th Aug 1925.

The scribe Muhammad 'Ali Rampuri is recorded as a highly skilled 19th Ccentury court scribe and calligrapher, who worked under the patronage of Nawwabs of Rampur State in Northern India, where it became a centre for Indo-Islamic art, scholarship and literature.

For the distinctive type, see J. Jain, Kalighat Painting: Images from a Changing World, Ahmedabad 1999, pp. 182-185, figs. 162-165; p. 111, fig. 105 (referred to as 'Herwitz Series C', 'in an unparalleled idiom'). A group of five was sold in these rooms, 12th-13th October 2005, lot 432.

'The artist, apparently with great delight, has used his brush with rapid powerful zigzag strokes in grey and blue to indicate the sky, and pink and grey to depict the earth, displaying a taste for playing with his brush and creating abstract forms. This may be the only instance in pre-modernist Indian painting where purely abstract forms resulting from a playful, undirected movement of the brush have been consciously used by an artist who appears to have been revelling in the very act of painting' (Jain, op. cit. p. 185).

Siva and Parvati seated with Nandi on Mount Kailasa 
Bengal, late 18th Century
gouache and gold on paper, orange border, seal impression of Elijah Impey verso, also inscribed Parbuttee ou [...], nagari inscription at top 
303 x 227 mm.

For a painting depicting Siva in a very similar, idiosyncratic style, and also bearing Impey's seal impression, dated 1775, see the sale in these rooms, Bonhams, Islamic and Indian Art, 14th June 2012, lot 319.

Sir Elijah Impey was Chief Justice of Bengal from 1774 to 1782. Along with his wife, Lady Impey, he was a well-known patron of Indian artists. They are better known for the studies of flora and fauna they commissioned, but Sir Elijah was also an avid collector of Indian miniature paintings. The present lot is an example of this interest, and its subject may well reflect Impey's desire to form an almost documentary group of portrayals of aspects of Hindu religion in the same manner as the natural history paintings.

For examples of miniatures from his collection, see S. C. Welch, Room for Wonder: Indian Painting during the British Period 1760-1880, New York 1978, p. 32, no. 4 (a portrait of Muhammad Reza Khan, Murshidabad, circa 1770, bearing his seal impression, dated 1775); and West-East: the Niall Hobhouse Collection, Christie's, London, 22nd May 2008, lot 344 (Mughal, circa 1760, from the 'Husn Album').

An illustration from a Mahabharata series, depicting the assembly of the Kauravas and Pandavas before the blind king Dhritarashtra 
School of Purkhu, Kangra, circa 1820-30
gouache and gold on paper, red border, identifying inscriptions in nagari script, numbered 6 verso 
343 x 478 mm.

Provenance
Acquired in London at auction, late 1990s.
Private collection, Japan.

As noted by B. N. Goswamy and Eberhard Fischer, one of Purkhu's patrons was Maharajah Sansar Chand (circa 1725-1823) and that according to the traveller William Moorcroft, who stayed with the Maharajah in 1820, a great deal of Sansar Chand's collection was concerned with 'the performances and prowess of Arjun' and that these paintings often had complex perspective and several representations of the same act in one painting, as is true for the present example. (Pahari Masters, 1992, pp. 371-372).

For comparison, see in particular two paintings depicting a related point in the narrative, Christie's, Arts of India, 25th May 2017, lots 66 and 67. description_block:
Guru Nanak seated under a tree beside a raging fire 
Punjab, perhaps by the artist Kehar Singh (1820â1882), late 19th Century
pen and ink and watercolour heightened with gold on paper; verso a drawing of Vishnu seated on a lotus, by another hand, 19th Century 
136 x 134 mm.

Kehar Singh (1820-82) was one of the most famous Sikh artists of the 19th century. His artistic career led him to the royal court of Lahore, where it is said that he painted a picture of a dead sparrow and coaxed a sweeper of the court to place it on Maharaja Ranjit Singh's throne. The trick worked and Kehar Singh was hired as a court painter. He later became influenced by European watercolours, oil paintings and photography. In his series of painted sketches done around the 1860–70s, he portrayed men and women occupied in different trades and professions in great detail, even naming many of them as part of his accompanying notes, which were often inscribed on the face of the artworks in both Persian and gurmukhi.

Comparisons can be drawn between the style of the present sketch, with its stark ink lines balanced with loose brush work, and a work by Kehar Singh depicting Ajaib Singh Nihang (Government Museum and Art Gallery, Chandigarh, acc. no. 1701, published in R. P. Srivastava, Punjab Painting (1983), plate 
49).

For other works attributed to Kehar Singh, see the sales in these rooms, 20th November-5th December 2018, lot 45; 10th-18th November 2020, lot 176; 22nd May 2025, lot 302. For a group of possibly related ink and watercolour studies of tradespeople in a similar style to the above, see Sotheby's, The Stuart Cary Welch Collection, Part Two: Arts of India, 31st May 2011, lot 143.

description_block:
Sikh Priest reading the Grunth, Umritsur, from India Ancient and Modern: A Series of Illustrations of the Countries and People of India and Adjacent Territories, by William Simpson & Sir John William Kaye 
Day & Son, London, 1867
chromolithographic plate after Simpson, mounted on thin card 
plate 242 x 345 mm.; card 440 x 625 mm.

For a complete edition of India Ancient and Modern with 50 plates, see the sale in these rooms, Bonhams, Islamic and Indian Art, 22nd May 2025, lot 238.

William Simpson (1823–1899) made his name as an artist correspondent during the Crimean War, sketching from life as the conflict raged from the Baltic Sea to Balaclava, and sending his drawings back to Colnaghi & Son in London, where they were printed and published as The Seat of War in the East (1855–56). After the success of this publication and the subsequent exhibition of the original watercolours, Simpson was commissioned to undertake an even more ambitious project depicting life and landscape in India.

In the wake of the Indian Mutiny, Day & Son commissioned Simpson to make studies in India for a large-scale illustrated book. He arrived in October 1859 and joined the party of the governor-general, Lord Canning, on a tour of the area where the mutiny had taken place; he also sketched with Lady Canning. Over three years he visited much of the subcontinent, including Punjab, Tibet, Bengal, Lucknow and Kanpur (Cawnpore), central India, the Himalayas, Kashmir, Madras and Sri Lanka (Ceylon). On his return to England in 1862, he worked for four years on Day's project, completing 250 drawings. However, when the firm went into liquidation, his Indian watercolours were taken over and sold off as bankrupt stock. Simpson received no recompense for seven years of hard work.

Only fifty of his watercolours ultimately reached print and were published in the 50-plate edition with accompanying text provided by the military historian and civil servant, John Kaye (1814–1876), who had earlier served in the army in India. The subjects include topographical views, trade scenes, architecture, and depictions of specific events. Places shown include Delhi, Bombay, Lucknow, Udaipur, Amritsar and many others.

Simpson would go on to have a long and successful career working for the Illustrated London News, covering a vast array of conflicts and events the world over.

A Critical Study of the Life and Teachings of Sri Guru Nanak Dev, the Founder of Sikhism, by Sewaram Singh Thapar 
Rawalpindi: Printed at the Commercial Union Press, 1904
pp. 179, modern binding, 185 x 135 mm.; together with Bhagat Lakshman Singh, A Short Sketch of the Life and work of Guru Gobind Singh, the Tenth and Last Guru of the Sikhs, Lahore, The Tribune Steam Press, 1909, pp. 186, original green cloth, front cover with the title Guru Gobind Singh in gold 
225 x 140 mm.(2)

Sewaram Singh Thapar's monograph was the first book-length biography of Guru Nanak in English by a Sikh scholar. On the title page he is described as 'Pleader, Rawalpindi', and as the author of Anecdotes from Sikh History and The Indian Constitution and Parliamentary Sovereignty. His footnotes are often citations in gurmukhi, though he also renders religious texts into English verse, perhaps stemming from his obvious liking for the poetry of Matthew Arnold, whom he uses for his epigraph and endpiece.

Bhagat Lakshman Singh was Professor of History and Literature, Gordon Mission College, Rawalpindi; 'one of the Original Promoters of the Khalsa College, Amritsar'; editor of Khalsa, 'the first English Organ of the Sikhs' (see lot 339 in the current sale); this life of Guru Govind Singh; and Sikh Martyrs (1923).

description_block:
Brigadier-General John Malcolm, Sketch of the Sikhs, the first significant published European account of the Sikh nation 
Calcutta, printed by A. H. Hubbard, at the Hindoostanee Press, 1810
first edition (an extract from Asiatick Researches, vol. 11), pp. 95, modern replacement of title page, modern yellow morocco 
4to, 275 x 225 mm.

John Malcolm (1769-1833) began to assemble materials for his history while serving with British forces in the Punjab in 1805, noting that 'English writers, none of them had possessed more than very general information regarding this extraordinary race...' Malcolm made his own observations and notes in the Punjab, and acquired a number of Sikh manuscripts. When he returned to Calcutta, he interviewed a Sikh priest about his religion, and acquired a number of English translations of Sikh religious and historical texts from John Leyden.

The demands of Malcolm's military duties prevented him from compiling a full history, but his text effectively glosses the period from the birth of Guru Nanak in 1469 to the disordered Sikh states of the Punjab in 1805. Malcolm relied on Sikh sources, stating that 'it is of the most essential importance to hear what a nation has to say of itself; and the knowledge obtained from such sources has a value, independent of its historical utility'. He was aware of other contemporary accounts and histories, but preferred the Sikhs' own accounts to the somewhat hostile Mughal records.

The text was reprinted in London in 1812, in octavo (for an example of which see the sale in these rooms, Travel and Exploration, 8th-17th December 2025, lot 84, a presentation copy from the author's brother, Rear Admiral Sir Pulteney Malcolm). Its preface said that it had been published to provide a 'clear account of an oriental people, of singular religion and manners, with whose history the European reader can be but little acquainted'.

Malcolm rose to become Governor of Bombay in 1827-31. He is buried in St James's Piccadilly. There is a statue of him by Francis Chantrey in Westminster Abbey.

description_block:
The Maharajah Duleep Singh and the Government: a Narrative, published by the Maharajah for private circulation, and inscribed by him for presentation to Lord Henniker (1842-1902), on 20th July 1884 
Ballantyne Press, Edinburgh, 1884
183pp., contemporary dedication inscription on front flyleaf, black morocco gilt, in modern green leather solander box 
8vo (233 x 175 mm.); box 157 x 210 mm.

Provenance
John Henniker-Major, 5th Baron Henniker (1842-1902); bookplate of Thornham Hall Library (the family seat) on front doublure.

The dedication inscription reads: To/The Lord Henniker/With the/Maharajah Duleep Singh's compliments and/Sincere thanks/July 20th 1884.

A rare publication, inscribed by Maharajah Duleep Singh himself for presentation to Lord Henniker, who succeeded his father as 5th Baron in 1870. In 1877 he was appointed a Lord-in-waiting (government whip in the House of Lords) in the Conservative government of Benjamin Disraeli, a post he held until the government fell in 1880, and again under Lord Salisbury between 1885 and 1886, between 1886 and 1892, and briefly in 1895. He was appointed Lieutenant Governor of the Isle of Man in 1895, serving as such until his death in 1902.

For another copy, inscribed by Maharani Bamba Duleep Singh, Maharajah Duleep Singh's wife, for Henry Waldemar Lawrence (1845-1908), 3rd Baronet, and son of Henry Lawrence, British Political Resident in the Punjab in the 1840s, see the sale in these rooms, Bonhams, Islamic and Indian Art, 21st May 2024, lot 205.

Part I concerns the history of the Punjab, the reign of Maharajah Ranjit Singh, and events immediately after his death, until 1843. It explains 'the political position of the Maharajah at the time he came to the throne and his title to private estates and landed property in the Punjab, independently of his sovereign rights'. Part II is entitled The Life and Fortunes of the Maharajah Duleep Singh, and the Annexation of the Punjab. Part III discusses relations between the Maharajah and the British Government, his guardianship and the treaty of 1849. Several appendices deal with various treaties between the Sikhs and the British.

To quote the preface: The following narrative has been compiled, partly from historical sources, and partly from private information and documents furnished by the Maharajah Duleep Singh. The object of the work is to inform those of his friends who care to know it, the nature of the Maharajah's differences with the Government, and to disabuse their minds of any prejudices which may have arisen from what appeared in print on the same subject about a year ago.

description_block:
A Sikh sardar and two troopers on horseback 
by Egron Selif Lundgren (Swedish, 1815-1875), executed circa 1858
watercolour on paper, backboard with handwritten note in Swedish by the historian Karl Asplund, dated Stockholm, 5th August 1941 
450 x 350 mm.

Provenance
Formerly at Wyfold Court, Reading, home of Sir Robert Hodge, Bt., according to the note by Asplund.

Compare another watercolour of similar dimensions, depicting Sikh officers and three Gurkha soldiers, sold in these rooms, Bonhams, Islamic and Indian Art Online Sale, 20-28 October 2022, lot 231. Lundgren seems often to have been in the company of Sikhs and often depicted them: see for example a similar study in watercolour of Sikh cavalry, plate 26 in Karl Asplund's Med Egron Lundgren i Indien 1858-1859 [With Egron Lundgren in India, 1858-1859], Bonnier, Stockholm, 1931 (copies of which have been offered in these rooms).

Egron Selif Lundgren (1815-1875) was a Swedish traveller, artist and writer, who went to India to report on the Mutiny, or uprising, of 1857-58. He accompanied Lord Clyde in the campaign in Oudh, including the Relief of Lucknow. His work found much favour with the Royal Family: he was commissioned by Queen Victoria to record the wedding of the Princess Royal to Prince Frederick William of Prussia in January 1858, and sketches from his stay at Balmoral in September 1859 remain in the Royal Collection at Windsor. For further information see S. Nilsson and N. Gupta, Egron Lundgren and India, Malmoe, 1992.

An unusual sketch book of drawings in ink and wash, consisting of accomplished copies of originals by John Leech, Sir John Tenniel, Hablot Knight Browne ('Phiz'), and the illustrators of The Illustrated London News, combining satirical depictions of early Victorian society with depictions of Sikh Akalis, Rajah Suchet Singh, and General Ventura, the Italian officer serving with the Sikh army 
British School, circa 1846

Rajah Sucheyt Singh (Malek Adel); and General Ventura: after images from the Illustrated London News 1846 series The War in India: Sketches in the Punjaub and Sikh Country, perhaps ultimately deriving from G. T. Vigne.

description_block:
Papers relating to the Punjab, 1847-49, presented to both Houses of Parliament by Command of Her Majesty 
London, Harrison & Son, 1849
pp. 665 [but renumbered as 701 in ink], modern paper-covered boards retaining paste-down label 
330 x 223 mm.

A fascinating publication reprinting documents surveying relations between the British and the Sikhs, beginning on 4th April 1847, with a despatch from Major Lawrence, Assistant to the Resident, stationed at Peshawar, to the Resident at Lahore (Lt. Col. H. M. Lawrence), and closing almost exactly two years later on 7th April 1849, with a note from the Governor-General to The Secret Committee. As we look down the 'Chronological List of Papers', which goes on for almost forty pages, we see all the notable personalities and place-names of the Anglo-Sikh Wars: Lawrence, Viscount Hardinge, the Governor-General, Dost Mohamed Khan; Tej Singh, 'the expulsion of the Maharanee from the Punjab'; Mooltan, Goojerat, Sher Singh - ending on 24th March 1849 with 'Surrender of the Sikh Chiefs and army to Sir Walter Gilbert' - 'Occupation of Attock' - Disarming of the people of the Punjab'.

description_block:
A manuscript diary of J. W. Barber, a soldier serving in India with 3rd Company, 78th Regiment of Foot (later the Seaforth Highlanders), and apparently killed at Cawnpore during the uprising of 1857 
India, circa 1845-1857
manuscript diary on blue paper, 66 text leaves, many blank, brown chamois leather binding; together with a letter from E. R. G. Kerr, Edinburgh, dated 19th July 1943, addressed to the Secretary, Seaforth Highlanders Regimental Association 
205 x 160 mm.(2)

Provenance
The family of E. R. G. Kerr, who received the diary when a comrade of Barber's, returning from service in India, attempted to contact his family; unable to, he bequeathed the manuscript (according to the letter of 1943).

Barber's regiment first took part in the Anglo-Persian War, which ran from late 1856 to spring 1857, caused by a dispute over Persian claims to Herat. Lieutenant General Sir J. Outram KCB was in command of the Persian Field Force, as Barber notes. He recounts the regiment's embarkation at Bombay in January 1857 on expedition to Persia; landfall at Bushehr after minor mishaps at sea; bewilderment of Persian population at Highland dress; massive detonation of the enemy's ammunition magazine.

The action then shifts back to India in 1857. The unit is in Allahabad, then part of a mobile column under Brigadier-General Havelock, whose order to the troops Barber reproduces (July 1857). Barber was a witness to some of the worst atrocities of the uprising, the massacres at or near Cawnpore (Kanpur):
we encamped on the plain, and a party was sent to reconnoitre the City & town for the women & children with General Wheeler & his detachment — but to their horror found all them lying in a house Murdered! I believe it was a shocking sight to see children that had been rent asunder by the legs and women with their bellies ripped open — such horrible deeds — so I will not give you a description of its loathsome appearance which the House presented to the view of the Spectators.

The diary also contains a good deal of sentimental verse, songs, tables of kit and equipment, names of camps and remarks on their suitability and comfort.

description_block:
Thirty-Five Years in the East, by John Martin Honigberger, physician at the Sikh court in Lahore 
H. Bailliere, London, 1852
pp. 448, 2 vols. in one, pp. xxix of introduction to this English edition, lithograph frontispiece portrait of the author, numerous lithograph plates including portraits of Sikh notables; the second volume devoted to medical matters, with 31 plates of plants and glossaries of technical terms, contemporary brown leather gilt 
216 x 160 mm.

Martin Honigberger (1795-1869) was born in Krostadt in Romania, left Transylvania in 1815 and travelled though the Levant, Egypt, Arabia, Persia and then to India. He was in Lahore as physician at the Sikh court between 1829 and 1833, and then again between 1839 to 1849. His account is the main source for the activities of his guest, the artist August Theodor Schoefft (including his run-in with some ferocious akalis while he was sketching in preparation for many of the famous depictions of the Lahore Court). Honigberger's lithograph illustrations are based on the paintings of artists working in Lahore and Amritsar. (The foldout lithograph panorama of the fortress and city of Lahore is lacking).

The plates in vol. I include:
Map of Central Asia between Bokhara and Russia.
Plate with portraits of Ranjit Singh and other Sikh notables.
Three sepoys.
Plate with portraits of Rani Jindan, Duleep Singh and others.
Facsimile of a letter in nasta'liq.
Plate with portraits of Maharajah Gulab Singh and other notables.
A Sikh doctor, after the album paintings.
Portraits of Raja Tej Singh and others.
Two horsemen, one an akali.
Portrait of Hari Das.
A barber, after the album paintings.
A seller of perfumes.
Dervishes smoking bhang.
Distillers.

description_block:
The German first (original) edition of Leopold von Orlich's Reise in Ostindien in Briefen an Alexander von Humboldt und Carl Ritter (Travels in the East Indies in letters to Alexander von Humboldt and Carl Ritter) 
Verlag Mayer und Wigand, Leipzig, 1845
pp. 298, 22 engraved and lithographed plates, 10 of them coloured, and 40 coloured woodcuts in the text, bookplate of Carl Niessen, stamps of Staatsbibliothek, Bremen, blue paper-covered boards with gilt vignette of the Taj Mahal on front cover and title on spine, blindstamped ornamental borders on cover and spine 
320 x 235 mm.

Baron Leopold Adolph Ludwig von Orlich (1804–1860), a captain in the Royal Prussian Guards, visited India between August 1842 and April 1843. His original intention had been to travel with the British Army to Afghanistan to report on what he expected to be a lengthy war with the Afghans in response to the disastrous 1842 retreat from Kabul. However, being delayed, he only succeeded in joining up with the British at Ferozepore in the Punjab after their return from Afghanistan. He embarked instead on a personal voyage across India. 

The author describes his travels from London to India by way of Gibraltar, Cairo and Aden in a series of twelve letters to Alexander von Humboldt and Carl Ritter. He first came to Bombay and then travelled to Poona, Karachi, Sindh and then Punjab. Besides describing the customs and manners of the habitants, Orlich's narrative is especially important as an eyewitness account of Sindh on the eve of the British conquest and the events leading up to the First Anglo-Sikh War (1845–46), including a personal interview with Maharaja Sher Singh, whom he described as 'very corpulent and strongly built, but is light in his movements; his features are expressive of good-nature and a love of pleasure, and his fine dark eye beamed with kindness and affection: his black beard was very carefully dressed' (vol. I, p. 214).

The illustrations include colour lithographs and engravings depicting architectural views (e.g. the Jumma Masjid in Delhi and Agra respectively, the Qutb Minar, the Taj Mahal and the Gates of Somnath); and customs (e.g. Sati, festival of Muharram and a qazi reciting the Quran). The woodcuts show the customs and trades of the people of India (e.g. Akali Sikhs, musicians and various artisans). Most of these derive from Patna paintings on both paper and mica.

The work was subsequently issued in two volumes, both in German and an English translation by H. Evans Lloyd under the title Travels in India, including Sinde and the Punjab, London 1845. For the English edition, see the sale in these rooms, Islamic and Indian Art Online, 2nd-12th June 2025, lot 276.

Hardinge (1822-94) was present in India in 1845 when the Sikh army crossed the Sutlej and invaded British territory. He served as private secretary to his father, Sir Henry Hardinge, first Viscount of Lahore, who was Governor-General of India at the time.

'Hardinge was brought up among artistic influences, and was himself no mean painter in watercolours. In 1847 his friends in England published a folio volume entitled Recollections of India, consisting of twenty lithographs from his drawings made in India, particularly interesting for its portraits of Sikh chieftains and views of scenery in Kashmir, then an almost unknown country, which he visited in company with John Nicholson' (ODNB).

description_block:
Two illustrated leaves from a dispersed manuscript written in gurmukhi script 
Punjab, circa 1850
gurmukhi manuscript on paper, two or four lines recto written in black and red ink respectively, illustrations in gouache and gold within floral borders, two and eleven lines of text verso respectively 
238 x 320 mm.(2)

The two illustrations, depicting a noble warrior in discourse with a monkey in a forest, and then descending the tree and moving off, leaving his weapons behind, are clearly related, and perhaps actually consecutive episodes in the narrative.

These leaves come from a dispersed manuscript sometimes tentatively attributed to Patiala, and which appears to have contained at least 148 paintings. The text is unknown, though it has been suggested that such leaves might derive from either a Kathararitsagara, or the Kharatnakara, both compilations of stories. For another example see S. Stronge (ed.), The Arts of the Sikh Kingdoms, London 1999, p. 170, fig. 193; and V. Ducrot, Four Centuries of Rajput Painting, Turin 2009, pp. 240-244. For one of a number of examples which have appeared at auction, see Christie's, Arts of India, 25th May 2017, lot 65; Bonhams, Islamic and Indian Art, 19th November-4th December 2019, lot 172, a group of four leaves.

description_block:
The Jagannath trio, identified as Buddha avatar, the Ninth avatar of Vishnu 
by the artist Kapur Singh, Amritsar, Punjab, circa 1865
gouache and gold on paper, orange outer border, 19th Century English inscription in lower border 9th- Bhoodha, and further inscribed in pencil below this 9th Buddha avatara, and at upper right By Kapur Singh of Amritsar 1865 
270 x 198 mm.

Apparently part of a series of works by Kapur Singh on the avatars of Vishnu (though the subject seems more likely to be the Jagannath trio), probably from an album of paintings collected by Augustus W. Honner, an officer in the Indian Army, the 1st Grenadiers, stationed in Bombay circa 1865. Two other portraits from this album were sold at Maggs Bros. (see Oriental Miniatures and Illumination, Maggs Bros. Bulletin, London, June 1977, nos. 60 and 61). See also the sales in these rooms, Bonhams, Islamic and Indian Art, 14th October 2004, lot 154; 28th April 2005, lot 250; and 12th and 13th October 2005, lots 427 and 428; 4th-18th June 2019, lot 84.
Most recently 12th November 2025, lot 239, depicting Radha and Krishna, which bears stylistic similarities to other works depicting episodes in the life of Krishna by Kapur Singh from the Honner Album. They include a painting of Krishna under a flowering tree fluting to the gopis (Maggs Bros., Ltd., London, Oriental Miniatures & Illumination, Bulletin No. 3, June 1962, no. 93 (current whereabouts not known); and a scene showing Vasudeva carrying the infant Krishna across the swollen river Yamuna (Maggs Bros., Oriental Miniatures & Illumination, Bulletin No. 10, Vol. III, part 2, October 1966, no. 88 (now in the National Library of Scotland, MS.16490). For a discussion of the Honner album, see M. Archer, Company Drawings in the India Office Library, London 1972, pp. 225–26, no. 187.

Kapur Singh was the son of the artist Kishan Singh, and nephew of Bishan Singh. Members of the family were responsible for the murals and floral motifs on the walls inside the Golden Temple of Amritsar. After experimenting in murals, oil paintings and works on paper, Kapur Singh became one of the most famous Sikh painters of the 19th Century. In the 1860s, he began producing a great number of works depicting everyday life in the Punjab, including scenes of different occupational workers in varying crafts and trades. Some of his studies were inscribed in English, and others are depicted realistically but also clearly by an artist trained in the Mughal tradition with the miniaturist's attention to detail. The scholar, artist and historian, Percy Brown, wrote of him: 'In the Punjab, at Lahore and Amritsar, the productions of several Sikh painters found favour at the end of the nineteenth century, their work showing a strange mixture of the East and West. One, Kapur Singh, painted a large number of figure subjects, miniature in size, and showing a very fair knowledge of drawing with considerable action'. (P. Brown, Indian Painting, Calcutta 1917, p. 56, quoted in Archer, op. cit., p. 226).

description_block:
Thirty-three weekly issues of The Khalsa: an English Organ of the Sikhs, the first Sikh newspaper in English, including its first issue 
Lahore, January-December 1899
bound in one volume, 33 issues each of four leaves, eight pages, stamps and bookplate of Forman Christian College, Lahore, green cloth 
323 x 210 mm.

The Khalsa was the first English-language Sikh newspaper, founded by the Sikh reformer Bhagat Lakshman Singh to champion the Singh Sabha movement and to articulate Sikh issues. The contents of each issue is a fascinating mixture, beginning with world news, then moving on to 'local and provincial', followed by short passages from Sikh scripture, given in both gurmukhi and in English translation, and commentary, with other leading articles and homilies.

The Khalsa lasted for just over for two years and alongside, inter alia, The Khalsa Advocate and Sikhs and Sikhism (both est. 1903), was part of a flourishing newspaper and pamphlet scene (in both Punjabi and English) in the Punjab in the late 19th and early 20th Century.

Volume 1 no. 1 to volume 1 no. 15 run consecutively; thereafter the following issues in the year's run are lacking: 16, 17, 18, 22, 23, 26, 27, 28, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 40, 41, 44, 49 and 52. The last issue here is no. 51, 20th December 1899.

An engraved silver document holder by P. Orr & Sons, presented to Lord Hailey (1872-1969), Governor of the Punjab 
Madras, 1925
of cylindrical form, engraved with acanthus-filled bands to each end, to centre 'Presented to Sir W. M. Hailey K.C.S.I, C.I.E., I.C.S. Governor of the Punjab by the Members of the Anglo Indian & Domiciled European Association India Lahore Branch 14 January', stamped 'ORR SILVER 22'; An engraved repoussÃ© silver document holder, presented to Lady Hailey (1867-1939), Lucknow, dated 1928, of cylindrical form, decorated in repoussÃ© and chased with scenes of rural life, the central cartouche inscribed 'Presented to Alessandra Lady Hailey by the Girl Guides of the Punjab 6-9-1928', containing an address on silk from the Lucknow Women's Association and the Lady's response 
35.5 cm. long(2)

Lord William Malcolm Hailey (1872-1969) served as Governor of the Punjab from 1924-1928 after which he was appointed Governor of the United Provinces (now Uttar Pradesh). He later was a major British figure in colonial reform in Africa after 1945. His work was recognised both through his peerage and his burial at Westminster Abbey. His wife, Andreina Balzani (1867-1939), was not just revered as a notable hostess during her husband's tenures, but also a budding pilot and fellow of the Royal Geographical Society. Her time in India is recounted in her journals, Indian Diary of a Female Big Game Hunter, Kashmir, 1916-1919.

description_block:
A signed photograph of Anita Delgado Briones, Princess Prem Kaur of Kapurthala, the 'Spanish Maharani' 
dated April 1911
albumen print, oval, signed in ink Prem Kaur of Kapurthala/4 1911, in leather easel frame; together with two printed cards from the memorial service for the Maharani, Madrid, 7th July 1962, the first with details of the service, in Spanish, the front of the card depicting the Virgin Mary, the second black-edged, depicting the crucified Christ and the Virgin Mary 
photograph 200 x 150 mm.; frame 260 x 208 mm.; the largest card 115 x 145 mm.(3)

Anita Delgado Briones (1890-1962) was a Spanish dancer who in 1906 fascinated the Maharajah of Kapurthala, Jagatjit Singh (reg. 1877-1949), when he was visiting Madrid for the wedding of the King of Spain. They married in 1908 in France, and after a Sikh wedding in India, she changed her name to Maharani Prem Kaur. They travelled extensively in both Europe and India, and wrote a memoir Impressions de mes Voyages aux Indes (1915). When the Maharaja married his seventh wife in 1925, they divorced and Prem Kaur returned to Spain.

description_block:
HH Raja-i-Rajgan Sir Raghubir Singh, GCSI, CIE, the ruler of Jind (reg. 1864â1887), seated in a western-style interior 
Punjab, Jind, circa 1882-83
gouache and gold on paper, laid on card, gold inner border, inscribed verso in Urdu detailing how the painting was based on a photograph taken in 1882 
painting (including inner borders) 255 x 190 mm.; card 285 x 230 mm.

The Urdu inscription verso reads: awwal aks tasvīr kā photograph se 17 Jūn 1882 mein liyā gayā thā, par rangat aham tasvīron mein (?), ne hāth se lagāyā thā...; 'The first photograph of this image was taken on 17 June 1882, but the colouring of the important picture was applied by hand by ...[?]'. 

Raghubir Singh became heir apparent to his father, Raja Swarup Singh of Jind (reg. 1812–64), when his older brother died in 1848. During the Sepoy Uprising of 1857–58, he fought alongside his father in armour and mail at some of the major battles against the rebels. Following Swarup Singh's death in 1864, Raghubir Singh ascended to the Jind throne. He established his main residence at Sangrur and began the process of remodelling his state, rebuilding the bazaar, constructing the gardens and building temples, water tanks, public buildings and paved roads. In 1872, he contributed a contingent of the Jind artillery for service in the outbreak of the Kuka movement. Two years later, he faced a serious revolt in fifty villages in his territory of Charkhi Dadri, as well as in some other lands acquired after 1857, but he took personal command of his troops and subdued the revolt in a month. In 1875, he received the highest imperial dignity, being appointed as Knight Grand Commander of the Order of the Star of India (GCSI). He received the 1876 Prince of Wales gold medal and became a Councillor of the Empress of India the following year. During the Second Afghan War (1878–79), he sent 700 cavalry and infantry to the aid of the British forces in Afghanistan. In 1881, shortly before this painting was made, he was granted the hereditary title of Raja-i-Rajgan.

This painting appears to be based on a photograph, possibly taken by Bourne and Shepherd Studio, around 1882 (the year as stated in the Urdu inscription verso) when the raja was fifty years old. The only other painted portraits of Raghubir Singh known to exist were both by Val Prinsep (1838–1904), executed in 1877–78. Prinsep was commissioned by Lord Lytton, Viceroy and Governor-General of India, to mark the Imperial Assemblage held on 1 January 1877. This gathering of the chiefs and rulers of India was organised to commemorate Queen Victoria's assumption of the title of Empress of India on 1st May 1876. 

Prinsep initially captured the Jind ruler's individual portrait wearing his assorted awards at Simla in 1877 (now in the Victoria Memorial Hall, Calcutta). This, along with nearly 160 recognisable portraits of the princes of India, were then, on his return to England, worked into his monumental final painting of the Assemblage (1877–80, Royal Collection, Windsor, RCIN 407181).

In his memoir of his Indian travels, Prinsep recorded the history of the Jind state and his interactions with the rajah: 'Nabha, Jheend, and Puttiala are small Sikh states, which were in the way of being snapped up by the devourer of small states, Runjeet Sing. We, however, interfered, and saved them. Unlike most natives, these chiefs were true to us to the backbone, and it was mainly owing to them that we were not turned out of India [...] The present Jheend is universally esteemed. He is a good ruler, a kindly old man, and, moreover, has what to me is much more important, a very fine head. He is only forty-two, but looks over fifty'. (Val. C. Prinsep, Imperial India: an Artist's Journals, London 1879, pp. 252, 266).

description_block:
Joseph FÃ©lix Bouchor (French, 1853-1937) 
Portraits of three Indian soldiers stationed at the Indian Army Depot at Daours, on the Somme front, France, in 1916: Sepoy Daulat Khan, Rajput; Natha Singh, Punjabi, of the 12th Bengal Cavalry; and Maninder Singh, a Gurkha
oil on board, signed, inscribed and dated CAMP INDIEN DE DAOURS/157bn 1916/J.F.BOUCHOR lower right, inscribed with the soldiers' names and titles at lower edge, handwritten label verso Hindous [sic]/radjput, Sikh et gurka and with the artist's name and Paris address 
24 x 33 cm.

The 12th Bengal Cavalry was an Indian regiment which served in Mesopotamia (present-day Iraq) during the First World War. Originally established as the 12th Regiment of Bengal in 1861, it formed part of the Indian Army's forces in the region.

The 157th Company of the Machine Gun Corps (to which 157bn may refer) was formed in Mesopotamia on 30 September 1916, through the transfer of machine-gun sections from the battalions of the 35th Indian Infantry Brigade.

The Rajput Sepoy and the Gurkha were infantrymen, but the central Sikh figure was a trooper of the 12th Bengal Cavalry who wears the ribbon of the India Medal 1895. This was originally issued to those who took part in the Chitral campaign of 1895, but in 1898 it was again issued for campaigns in the Punjab, Malakand, Samana and Tirah. When the medal was worn, all of these campaigns or actions would be shown by silver clasps mounted on the medal ribbon, but not when the ribbon was worn, as here, on its own.

The painting was executed at Daours, which was a depot of the Indian Corps in France on the Somme. Largely because of the difficulties Indian soldiers experienced in relation to the wet and cold climate of France and Belgium, the Indian infantry divisions were withdrawn and sent to Mesopotamia in November 1915. The cavalry divisions, however, remained in France until March 1918, and were then transferred to Egypt.

It seems likely therefore that the artist simply composed this painting from sketches and put the three faces together with a date and a location that was not appropriate to two of them.

We would like to thank Anna Lavelle, National Army Museum, and Andrew Cormack, Hon. Editor, Journal of the Society for Army Historical Research, for their comments and advice.
